metadata.title: Greenhouse gas concentrations in high-Arctic streams in northeast Greenland and their relationships with stream chemistry and catchment characteristics
metadata.description:
Description:

Dataset on greenhouse gas concentrations and driver variables in headwater streams in the Zackenberg area, Northeast Greenland measured during three field campaigns 2021-2023. Methods are described below.

 

Field sampling methods

            The 18 study streams are located in the Northeast Greenland National Park, near the Zackenberg Research Station (74°28’N, 20°34’W). The area has a polar tundra climate with mean annual air temperature of -9.1 °C; July is the warmest month with a mean of 5.8 °C, and February the coldest month with a mean of -22.4 °C and continuous permafrost. Annual mean precipitation is 261 mm of which approximately 10% falls as rain (Hansen et al., 2008). The 18 catchments spanned a gradient from steep, sparsely vegetated slopes with shallow, coarse mineral soils and limited snow retention, to low-gradient, wetter catchments with peat accumulation and more continuous vegetation cover.
            At each site (50-70 m reach), we measured stream discharge using the salt tracer release method (Gordon et al. 2004), and specific conductivity with a Cond 3110 WTW portable meter. We measured stream width at 10 points, and water depth at 50 points along the reach. We filtered water samples in the field: for dissolved nutrient analyses, we used 0.2 µm membrane filters (Supor 200 PES, Pall Corporation, Port Washington, New York, US), and for DOC/TDN analyses we used 0.7 µm pre-combusted glass fibre filters (GFF, Whatman, UK). Samples for nutrients were kept frozen until analysis, while samples for total dissolved nitrogen (TDN) and DOC were acidified with HCl 10% to pH 2-3 and stored refrigerated at 5 °C. We also measured pH in the field. All water samples and measurements were made in the middle of the streams’ width and depth.
            We estimated dissolved CO2, CH4, and N2O concentrations in stream water using the headspace equilibration technique (McAuliffe, 1971). In the field, we collected replicate (n=3) 50 mL water samples from the upper 10 cm of the water column using a 60 mL polypropylene syringe. We then introduced 10 mL of N2 gas into each syringe to create a headspace and shook each syringe vigorously for ∼60s. Finally, the 10 mL headspace was transferred into a 5.9 mL pre-evacuated borosilicate glass vial (Exetainer, Labco, High Wycombe, UK) until analysis.

Sample analysis
            We analyzed nitrate (NO3-) and ammonium (NH4+) using standard methods on a Lachat QC-8500 Flow Injection Autoanalyzer (colorimetric analysis; Lachat Instruments, Loveland, Colorado, US; APHA, 2005), and quantification limit for NO3-N  and NH4+-N were 4 and 10 µg N L-1, respectively. Samples for TDN and DOC were analyzed on a TOC-Vcph/TNM-1 analyzer (chemiluminescence analysis; Shimadzu) with QL of 0.055 mg N L-1. The QL for DOC was 0.02 mg C L-1. Dissolved organic N (DON) was calculated by subtracting DIN (NO3--N + NH4+-N) from TDN. All data below the QL were expressed as half of the QL (QL/2).
            In the laboratory, we measured CO2, CH4, and N2O concentrations using a dual-inlet Agilent 7890 GC system interfaced with a CTC CombiPal autosampler (Agilent, Nærum, Denmark), configured and calibrated using standard gases as described in detail by Petersen et al. (2012). We converted headspace gas concentrations to dissolved aqueous concentrations according to Henry's law, using Henry's constant to correct for water temperature and atmospheric pressure at the time of sampling (Weiss 1974; Weiss and Price 1980; Wiesenburg and Guinasso 1979). For each gas and sampling event, we calculated the % saturation as %sat = 100 × Cw/Ceq, where Cw is the measured dissolved gas concentration and Ceq is the concentration in equilibrium with the atmosphere, calculated from Henry’s law as Ceq = KH(T) × pgas. Here, KH(T) is the solubility coefficient at the in-situ water temperature (Weiss 1974; Weiss and Price 1980; Wiesenburg and Guinasso 1979), and pgas is the atmospheric partial pressure of the gas, calculated from atmospheric mixing ratios of 415 ppm for CO2, 1.80 ppm for CH4, and 0.330 ppm for N2O and the atmospheric pressure at the time of sampling. Thus, water temperature was used both to calculate the dissolved gas concentrations and their equilibrium concentrations

Catchment characteristics
           Terrestrial vegetation density across the study area was quantified using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) derived from Sentinel-2 imagery. Images were obtained from the ESA Copernicus Open Access Hub, selected for lack of cloud cover, with a spatial resolution of 12 m. The temporal window for NDVI data was specifically delineated to early July, August, and September 2021, and early August 2023, to coincide with the field measurements of GHGs. The data were corrected for atmospheric bottom effects, with acquisition dates stamped as follows: 9Jul2021, 1Aug2021, 4Sept2021, and 2Aug2023. All NDVI values were computed from the Red (B4) and Near-Infrared (B8) bands using the formula (NIR−R)/(NIR+R) within a raster calculator, subsequently producing GeoTIFFs of the NDVI. For each catchment area, NDVI distribution was examined, and the median NDVI was calculated using the zonal statistics tool in ArcGIS pro.
            In addition, for each stream catchment, snow cover was also derived from Sentinel-2 satellite imagery. Scene classification maps were downloaded from the ESA Copernicus Open Access Hub for the same days and regions as the NDVI imagery. The classification map was then overlaid with the catchments using the zonal statistics tool to estimate the snow cover for each catchment. The scene classification maps have a spatial resolution of 20 m, i.e. coarser than the NDVI data, but fine enough to resolve snow patches within the study catchments (0.24–11.3 km2). Finally, the catchment area, mean elevation, and terrain slope were derived using ArcticDEM, a high-resolution global Digital Elevation Model (DEM) for territories north of 60° latitude, sourced from the Polar Geospatial Centre at the University of Minnesota (USA). For this study, processed mosaics with a 2 m spatial resolution were used and subsequently down-sampled to a 7 m spatial resolution using average resampling to reduce imagenoise. Arctic DEM was employed in ArcGIS Pro with spatial analyst tools to precisely delineate and model characteristics of the small-scale headwater stream catchments.

 

References

Gordon, N. D., McMahon, T. A., Finlayson, B. L., Gippel, C. J., Nathan, R. J. (2004) Stream hydrology: An introduction for ecologists (p. 444). John Wiley & Sons.

Hansen, B. U., Sigsgaard, C., Rasmussen, L., Cappelen, J., Hinkler, J., Mernild, S. H., Petersen, D., Tamstorf, M. P., Rasch, M., & Hasholt, B. (2008) Present‐day climate at Zackenberg. Advances in ecological research 40: 111–147.

McAuliffe, C. (1971). Gas chromatographic determination of solutes by multiple phase equilibrium. Chemical Technology 1: 46-51.

Petersen, S. O., Hoffmann, C. C., Schäfer, C. M., Blicher-Mathiesen, G., Elsgaard, L., Kristensen, K., Larsen, S. E., Torp, S. B., Greve, M. H. (2012). Annual emissions of CH4 and N2O, and ecosystem respiration, from eight organic soils in Western Denmark managed by agriculture. Biogeosciences 9(1): 403-422. https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-9-403-2012

Weiss, R. F. (1974). Carbon dioxide in water and seawater: the solubility of a non-ideal gas. Marine Chemistry 2(3): 203-215. http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/B6VC2-488GBCK-1N/2/ab0520fd152200d62e291715e1b9c888

Weiss, R. F., Price, B. A. (1980). Nitrous-oxide solubility in water and seawater. Marine Chemistry 8(4): 347-359. https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4203(80)90024-9

Wiesenburg, D. A., Guinasso, N. L. (1979). Equilibrium solubilities of methane, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen in water and sea water. Journal of Chemical & Engineering Data 24(4): 356-360. https://doi.org/10.1021/je60083a006

metadata.title: A 1-km monthly surface air temperature dataset for Arctic land (2000–2025)
metadata.description:
Monthly mean near-surface (2 m) air temperature at 1-km resolution over Arctic land for March 2000 to December 2025 (310 monthly fields), reconstructed by an ensemble of Random Forest, LightGBM and XGBoost regressors trained separately for each calendar month on station observations (CRUTEM5 station archive, release 5.1.0.0) with MODIS predictors: Terra and Aqua day-time and night-time land surface temperature (MOD11A2, MYD11A2), Terra and Aqua NDVI (MOD13A3, MYD13A3), MCD12Q1.061 LC_Type5 land-cover fractions, latitude and longitude. Elevation is deliberately not a predictor; the reasons, and the measured consequence, are given in the accompanying paper.

What changed in version 3.0. The predictor values of the training table are now pooled from the same gridded stacks the prediction reads, rather than from a separate extraction of the granules, so that training and prediction use one source. The land surface temperatures entering training are screened with three checks of the GHCN-Daily quality-assurance system at their published thresholds (world-record exceedance, a climatological outlier check at six biweight standard deviations, and spatial corroboration against the nearest neighbours); 3860 values, 0.50 % of the land surface temperatures, were found to be invalid — seven satellite month-year composites had reached the table with MODIS fill values that had not been masked when the monthly means were formed — and are treated as missing. The gridded predictor stacks were checked for the same signature and carry none of it, so no field of version 2.0 was affected by that defect. The models were refitted and the whole record re-predicted. Hold-out accuracy at the 120 withheld stations improves from 1.50 to 1.48 °C root-mean-square error.

Data are on the native MODIS 1-km sinusoidal grid (34 tiles h09–h26, v00–v02, mosaicked to 3600 × 21600 cells, pixel 926.625433 m) with 2-D latitude/longitude and a CF grid mapping, so no resampling has been applied to the values. Water pixels are removed with the MOD44W mask and Greenland is excluded.

Each annual file (ArcticSAT1km_monthly_YYYY.nc, CF-1.8 netCDF4) contains:

  • sat — monthly mean near-surface air temperature (°C), ensemble mean of the three models;
  • sat_model_spread — the per-pixel standard deviation of the three individual model predictions for the same month, a measure of structural (model-choice) uncertainty.

Both are stored as int16 with scale_factor 0.01 °C (precision 0.01 °C), zlib-compressed, chunked one MODIS tile per chunk. ArcticSAT1km_grid.nc holds the static 2-D lat, lon, the MOD44W land_mask and tile_index; ArcticSAT1km_climatology.nc holds the monthly climatologies, the warm (April–October) and cold (November–March) seasonal means, the number of valid years per pixel and the mean inter-model spread.

Note on coverage: a fixed subset of land cells never has a valid MODIS/Terra night-time LST retrieval. The pattern is static — identical in every month and year of a given tile — and varies strongly between tiles (measured examples, as a fraction of the tile's land cells: h22v02 0 %, h24v02 12.3 %, h19v02 43.4 %). There the missing night-LST predictor enters the models as zero, so the prediction rests on the remaining predictors and is less well constrained. Nothing is blanked and no quality-flag variable is provided; every file carries this note in its comment global attribute, and README_data.md lists it under "Known limitations".

The climatologies in ArcticSAT1km_climatology.nc use the period 2001–2025 (25 years), the earliest period in which all twelve calendar months are complete, since January and February begin in 2001.

MANIFEST_md5.txt allows md5sum -c verification, MANIFEST_sizes.tsv lists file sizes, PROVENANCE.json gives a machine-readable provenance record, and README_data.md documents every variable, the method and the known limitations.

Processing code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23490034 (https://github.com/SeoyeonLee-rosee/arctic-1km-sat).

metadata.title: Global Monthly Mean Burned Area (km², 0.25°) Averaged Across 2019–2024 — Derived from ESA FireCCI Sentinel-3 SYN v1.1
metadata.description:
This dataset provides global monthly mean burned area (in square kilometers) averaged across the years 2019 to 2024. It is derived from the European Space Agency (ESA) Fire Disturbance Climate Change Initiative (FireCCI) Sentinel-3 SYN Burned Area Grid Product, version 1.1. The FireCCI product (FireCCIS311) combines multispectral reflectance data from the Ocean and Land Color Instrument (OLCI) and Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR) sensors onboard the Sentinel-3A and 3B satellites, complemented by VIIRS thermal anomaly detections, to identify and quantify burned areas globally.

The FireCCIS311 grid product summarizes pixel-level burned area information into a regular global grid at 0.25 × 0.25 degree spatial resolution and monthly temporal resolution. For this derived dataset, all available monthly grids from 2019 to 2024 were processed to calculate the long-term mean burned area for each calendar month (January–December). The resulting layers represent the climatological mean monthly fire activity, smoothing inter-annual variability and highlighting consistent spatial and seasonal patterns in global fire occurrence and extent.

Each GeoTIFF file corresponds to one calendar month and contains the mean burned area per 0.25° grid cell, expressed in km². The dataset is suitable for use in ecological and environmental analyses, including studies of fire-climate interactions, vegetation dynamics, biogeography, ecological niche modeling, and assessments of disturbance regimes.

All rasters cover the global extent (-180° to 180°, -90° to 90°) at 0.25° (~25 km) resolution in the WGS 84 coordinate reference system (EPSG: 4326). Pixel values indicate the mean burned area (km²) per grid cell; zero values correspond to grid cells where no burned area was detected across the 2019–2024 period.

metadata.title: ESA Fire Climate Change Initiative (FireCCI): MODIS FireCCI Burned Area GRID product, version 5.1 (2023-2024)
metadata.description:
This dataset includes only the monthly FireCCI51 burned area grids for 2023 and 2024. The files are derived from the MODIS FireCCI v5.1 product, developed within the ESA Fire Disturbance project of the Climate Change Initiative (CCI), but only the burned area variable aggregated onto a regular global 0.25-degree grid is provided here.

Specifically, the dataset includes only the burned_area variable, expressed in m². No additional auxiliary variables from the original product are included, standard error, fraction of observed area, fraction of burnable area, or other ancillary layers.

The files are organized by year and month for 2023 and 2024, and represent the monthly burned area in each cell of the global grid. These data were used as input to train the harmonisation model applied in the development of the MRBA60 product (Torres-Vázquez et al., 2026).

The data are distributed in NetCDF (.nc) format, using a WGS84 geographic coordinate system and a spatial resolution of 0.25 degrees. The file structure preserves the essential metadata associated with the burned_area variable from the original FireCCI51 product.

Previous years of the FireCCI51 product, covering the period 2001–2022, are the official release of the dataset and can be accessed through the original product record: Chuvieco, E.; Pettinari, M.L.; Lizundia-Loiola, J.; Storm, T.; Padilla Parellada, M. (2018): ESA Fire Climate Change Initiative (Fire_cci): MODIS Fire_cci Burned Area Pixel product, version 5.1. Centre for Environmental Data Analysis, 01 November 2018. doi:10.5285/58f00d8814064b79a0c49662ad3af537. https://dx.doi.org/10.5285/58f00d8814064b79a0c49662ad3af537

Algorithm reference: Lizundia-Loiola, J., Otón, G., Ramo, R., and Chuvieco, E. (2020). A spatio-temporal active-fire clustering approach for global burned area mapping at 250 m from MODIS data. Remote Sensing of Environment, 236, 111493. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2019.111493.

metadata.title: State of Wildfires 2025-26: Regional Summaries of Burned Area, Fire Emissions, and Individual Fire Characteristics for National, Administrative and Biogeographical Regions
metadata.description:
This dataset supports the State of Wildfires 2025-26 report under review at Earth System Science Data (Burton et al., under review). It is an update of the State of Wildfires 2024-25 report (Kelley et al. 2025). The dataset provides annual data and final-year anomalies in burned area (BA), fire carbon (C) emissions, and fire properties (e.g. distributional statistics for fire count, size, rate of growth). Annual data relate to the global fire season defined as March-February (e.g., March 2024-February 2026), aligning with an annuall lull in the global fire calendar (see Kelley et al., 2025). The complete methodology is described by Burton et al. (under review).

Citation

Work utilising our regional summaries should cite both Burton et al. (under review) AND the primary reference for the variable(s) of interest as follows:

  • Giglio et al. (2018) for MODIS MCD64A1 BA.
  • van der Werf et al. (2017) for GFED4.1s fire C emissions.
  • Kaiser er al. (2012) for GFAS fire C emissions.
  • van der Werf et al. (2025) AND Kaiser er al. (2012) for the average of GFED5 and GFAS fire C emissions.
  • Andela et al. (2019) for the Global Fire Atlas.
  • Giglio et al. (2016) for the Fire Radiative Power (FRP) observations.
  • Torres-Vázquez et al. (in revision) for the MRBA60 BA product.
  • Giglio et al. (2024) for VIIRS VNP64A1 BA.

Input Data

Burned Area (BA)

  • BA data from NASA’s MODIS BA product (MCD64A1) are extended from Giglio et al. (2018) and are available from NASA EarthData. 
    • Period: 2002-February 2026
    • Resolution: 500m, daily
  • BA data from ESA's BA product (MRBA60) are extended from Torres-Vázquez et al. (in revision), which harmonises products FireCCI51 (Lizundia-Loiola et al., 2020) and FireCCIS311 (Lizundia-Loiola et al., 2022).
    • Period: 2019-February 2026
    • Resolution: 300m, daily
  • BA data from NASA’s VIIRS BA product (VNP64A1) are extended from Giglio et al. (2025) and are available from NASA EarthData.
    • Period: 2012-February 2026 (only the data after 2019 are used for consistency in the comparisons between MCD64A1, FireCCIS311, and VNP64A1).
    • Resolution: 500m, daily

Fire Carbon (C) Emissions

  • GFED5 fire C emissions data are extended from van der Werf et al. (2025) and are available at https://globalfiredata.org/.
    • Period: 2003-February 2026
    • Resolution: 0.25 degree, daily
  • GFAS fire C emissions data are extended from Kaiser et al. (2012) and are available from the CAMS Atmosphere Data Store (ADS).
    • Period: 2003-December 2025 from ADS; January-February 2026 on request
    • Resolution: 0.1 degree, daily

Global Fire Atlas (Individual Fire Properties)

  • Global Fire Atlas data are extended from Andela et al. (2019) and are available from the repository maintained by Andela and Jones (2026). 
    • Period: 2002-February 2026
    • Driven by 500m MODIS BA data (collection 6.1)

Fire Intensities

  • FRP from NASA’s MODIS MCD14ML product (Giglio et al., 2016) and are available at NASA FIRMS.
    • Period: 2002-February 2026
    • Resolution: 1km, daily

Regional Analysis

We performed "cookie-cutting" (spatial and temporal masking) of the above input data sets to features in each of the following regional layers (e.g. per country in the "Countries" layer). 

The statistics derived from cookie-cutting are listed below. Full details in Burton et al. (under review).

metadata.title: GFED5NRT: Global Fire Emissions Database Near-Real-Time Extension
metadata.description:
GFED5NRT: Global Fire Emissions Database Near-Real-Time Extension

[Version] 
5.1

[Authors]
Yang Chen, Guido R. van der Werf, Mingquan Mu, Dave van Wees, Joanne V. Hall, Louis Giglio, Roland Vernooij, Douglas C. Morton, Li Xu, Tianjia Liu, Rebecca C. Scholten, Shane R. Coffield, Melanie B. Follette-Cook, Lesley Ott, James T. Randerson

[Overview]
This repository contains the 2023–2024 dataset for the Global Fire Emissions Database Near-Real-Time extension (GFED5NRT). GFED5NRT provides daily global estimates of burned area and emissions for multiple trace gases and aerosols, using active fire observations from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS).

This dataset is designed to provide continuity with the long-term GFED5 record (1997–2022) by using biome- and region-specific lookup tables of effective fire area and fuel consumption to bridge the transition from MODIS to VIIRS sensors.

[Data Description and Source Sensors]
The data are categorized based on the VIIRS sensor(s) used for the derivation:
    CMB (Combined): Data derived using both Suomi NPP (SNPP) and NOAA-20 (JPSS-1) VIIRS active fire observations.
    VNP: Data derived using Suomi NPP (SNPP) VIIRS observations only.
    VJ1: Data derived using NOAA-20 (JPSS-1) VIIRS observations only.

[Directory Structure]
The data are organized by temporal resolution (Daily/Monthly), data type (Species/Ecosystem), and sensor source (CMB/VNP/VJ1). Each sensor subfolder contains separate directories for the years 2023 and 2024.

Root/
├── Daily/
│   ├── Species/          (Trace gas and aerosol emissions)
│   │   ├── CMB/ [2023, 2024]
│   │   ├── VNP/ [2023, 2024]
│   │   └── VJ1/ [2023, 2024]
│   └── Ecosystem/        (Ecosystem-specific burned area and emissions)
│       ├── CMB/ [2023, 2024]
│       ├── VNP/ [2023, 2024]
│       └── VJ1/ [2023, 2024]
└── Monthly/
    ├── Species/
    │   ├── CMB/ [2023, 2024]
    │   ├── VNP/ [2023, 2024]
    │   └── VJ1/ [2023, 2024]
    └── Ecosystem/
        ├── CMB/ [2023, 2024]
        ├── VNP/ [2023, 2024]
        └── VJ1/ [2023, 2024]

[Data Content]
    Species: Includes daily and monthly gridded emissions for carbon (C) and various trace gases and aerosols (e.g., CO, CH4, NOx, PM2.5, BC, OC).
    Ecosystem: Includes burned area and emissions partitioned by fire type (e.g., boreal forest fires, temperate forest fires, tropical deforestation and degradation, peat fires, agricultural waste burning, and savanna/grassland/shrubland fires).

[Contact]
Yang Chen (yang.chen@uci.edu)

metadata.title: Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED5) Burned Area
metadata.description: The monthly GFED5 burned area data produced in this study are available in netCDF files. For years between 2001 and 2020, five layers of burned area (Norm: normal type, Crop: cropland burning, Defo: deforestation burning, Peat: peatland burning, Total: the sum of all burning) are provided at 0.25°×0.25° resolution. The ‘Norm’ layer contains burned areas in each grid cell (in km2) separated by 17 major land cover types. For the pre-MODIS era (1997-2000), only the ‘Total’ burned area layer with reduced spatial resolution (1°×1°) is provided. We also provide two global maps of burnable area (with water and snow/ice cover excluded) in each grid cell (0.25°×0.25° for the MODIS era and 1°×1° for the pre-MODIS era). Please refer to readme.html or readme.pdf for more detail about the dataset.

metadata.description:
Please note this dataset is undergoing peer review and may be subject to changes. 

The Global Cropland Area Burned (GloCAB) dataset represents the first attempt at a global cropland-focused burned area product. The dataset provides monthly, cropland burned area files at 0.25-degree spatial resolution from July 2002 - December 2020 for our upper (high) and lower (low) estimates. The data is provided in annual GeoTIFF stacks, where the 2002 tiff file only contains 6 layers (July - December), compared to 12 layers for 2003 - 2020 (January - December). 

Please refer to the readme file for more details about the dataset.

metadata.title: State of Wildfires 2025-26: Protected Areas Exposure to Fire
metadata.description:
This dataset supports the State of Wildfires 2025-26 report under review at Earth System Science Data (Burton et al., 2026, under review).

The dataset provides annual data summaries and final-year anomalies in the exposure of global protected areas to wildland fires.

Annual data relate to the global fire season defined as March-February (e.g., March 2025-February 2026), aligning with an annuall lull in the global fire calendar. The complete methodology is described by Burton et al. (2026).

Input data

  • Burned areas from NASA's MODIS MCD64A1 Collection 6.1 Burned Area product (Giglio et al., 2018) available at Giglio et al. (2021).
  • MODIS MCD12Q1 Collection 6.1 Land Cover product (Sulla-Menashe et al., 2019) available at Friedl and Sulla-Menashe (2022) to filter for semi-natural, burnable vegetation areas.
  • Protected areas dataset derived from Resco De Dios et al. (2025) and updated to the March 2026 version of the Protected Planet’s World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) (UNEP-WCMC and IUCN, 2026).

Regional Analysis

We performed "cookie-cutting" (spatial and temporal masking) of the above input data sets to features in each of the regional layers descriped in Burton et al. (2026).

Citation

Work utilizing our regional summaries should cite both Burton et al. (2026) and the previous reference on the global analysis of protected areas, as follows:

metadata.title: Update of: The Global Fire Atlas of individual fire size, duration, speed and direction
metadata.description:
This is an updated and extended record of the Global Fire Atlas introduced by Andela et al. (2019). Input data (burned area and land cover products) are updated to the MODIS Collection 6.1 (the original version featured in Andela et al. (2019) was based on collection 6.0 burned area and collection 5.1 land cover products, respectively). The timeseries is extended to cover the period 2002 to February 2026.

Methodological Notes:

The method employed to create the dataset precisely follows the approach described by Andela et al. (2019).

The input burned area product is MCD64A1 Collection 6.1. It is described by Giglio et al. (2018) and available at: https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/mcd64a1v061/. 

The input land cover product is MCD12Q1 Collection 6.1. It is described by Sulla-Menashe et al. (2019) and available at: https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/mcd12q1v061/. 

Note that while the methods have remained the same compared to Andela et al. (2019), we do observe small differences between the Global Fire Atlas products originating from differences between the MCD64A1 collection 6.1 burned area data used here and the collection 6 data used in the original product. In addition, we observe more substantial differences in the dominant land cover class associated with each fire due to the differences between the MCD12Q1 collection 6.1 data used here and collection 5.1 data used in the original product. 

Please note that the year string in filenames refers to the locally-defined fire season in which the fire ignited, not the calendar year. For each MODIS tile, the fire season is defined as the twelve months centred on the month with peak burned area (see Andela et al., 2019). For example, for a MODIS tile with peak burned area in December, the 2023 fire season would be defined as the period from July 2023 to June 2024. This is particularly relevant in the Southern extratropics and the northern hemisphere subtropics, where the fire seasons often span the new year. The local definition of the fire season is based on climatological peak in burned area as described by Andela et al. (2019).

Here we extended the time-series to include the fire season of 2002, and extended the time-series until February 2026.

Usage Notes:

Recommendation: Do Not Mix Dataset Versions 

We recommend downloading and using each version of the Global Fire Atlas as a complete dataset. Users should not extend an earlier version by adding only the final years from a newer release, as updates between versions may affect the full-time series. This is because each release includes a recalibration of model parameters, including fire persistence and fire season, which are derived on a per-tile basis using the complete available time series. Consequently, changes to the length of the input time series can alter these parameters for individual pixels, leading to minor differences throughout the dataset rather than only in the newly added years.

Incomplete Observations for the Latest Fire Seasons:

Please note that the year string in filenames refers to the locally-defined fire season in which the fire ignited, not the calendar year. As such, the time-series can be incomplete for the latest fire season (e.g. the "2026 fire season") and also for the penultimate fire season (e.g. the "2025 fire season") due to the way that fire seasons are defined (see above). For example, if the month with peak burned area for a tile is December, then full data covering the 2025 fire season in that tile are not available until midway through the 2026 calendar year. This contrasts with the original dataset from Andela et al. (2019), which only included the data for entire fire seasons between 2003 and 2016.  

Observational Outages and Time-series Consistency:

For the purpose of time-series analysis, we note that the 2002 product may have been affected by outages of Terra-MODIS (most notably, June 15 2001 - July 3 2001 and March 19 2002 - March 28 2002), which affects the burn date estimates and Global Fire Atlas product. Following the launch of Aqua-MODIS in May 2002 burn date estimates are more reliable as estimated from both MODIS sensors onboard Terra and Aqua. We also note that, as Terra and Aqua approach the end of their operational lifetimes, the effects of orbital changes (e.g. changes in overpass time, sampling, and pixel size) may have affected the final years of the time series, although the extent of these impacts on the MODIS product suite remains under investigation.

File Naming Convention:

GFA_v{time-stamp}_{data-type}_{fire_season}.{file_type}

{time-stamp} = Date that code was run.

{data-type} = “ignitions” or “perimeters” for vector files; “day_of_burn”, “direction”, “fire_line”, or “speed” for raster files.

{fire_season} = the locally-defined fire season in which the fire was ignited (see more below).

{file_type} = ".shp" for vector files; ".tif" for raster files. 

Please note that the year string in filenames refers to the locally-defined fire season in which the fire ignited, not the calendar year. Hence the file GFA_v20260408_perimeters_2003.shp can include fires from the 2003 fire season that ignited in the calendar years 2002 or 2004. 

Coordinate systems (Map Projections):

Vector data are provided on the WGS84 projection.

Raster data are provided on the MODIS sinusoidal projection used in NASA tiled products. The WKT string defining this projection is:

'PROJCS["unnamed",GEOGCS["Unknown datum based upon the custom spheroid",DATUM["Not_specified_based_on_custom_spheroid",SPHEROID["Custom spheroid",6371007.181,0]],PRIMEM["Greenwich",0],UNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433,AUTHORITY["EPSG","9122"]]],PROJECTION["Sinusoidal"],PARAMETER["longitude_of_center",0],PARAMETER["false_easting",0],PARAMETER["false_northing",0],UNIT["metre",1,AUTHORITY["EPSG","9001"]],AXIS["Easting",EAST],AXIS["Northing",NORTH]]'

 

Data Layers:

Table 1: Overview of the Global Fire Atlas data layers. The shapefiles of ignition locations (point) and fire perimeters (polygon) contain attribute tables with summary information for each individual fire, while the underlying 500 m gridded layers reflect the day-to-day behavior of the individual fires. In addition, we provide aggregated monthly summary layers at a 0.25° resolution for regional and global analyses.

File name Content
SHP_ignitions.zip Shapefiles of ignition locations with attribute tables (see Table 2)
SHP_perimeters.zip Shapefiles of final fire perimeters with attribute tables (see Table 2)
GeoTIFF_direction.zip 500 m resolution daily gridded data on direction of spread (8 classes)
GeoTIFF_day_of_burn.zip 500 m resolution daily gridded data on day of burn (day of year; 1-366)
GeoTIFF_speed.zip 500 m resolution daily gridded data on speed (km/day)
GeoTIFF_fire_line.zip 500 m resolution daily gridded data on the fire line (day of year; 1-366)
GeoTIFF_monthly_summaries.zip Aggregated 0.25° resolution monthly summary layers. These files include the sum of ignitions, average size (km2), average duration (days), average daily fire line (km), average daily fire expansion (km2/day), average speed (km/day), and dominant direction of spread (8 classes). 

 

Table 2: Overview of the Global Fire Atlas shapefile attribute tables. The shapefiles of ignition locations (point) and fire perimeters (polygon) contain attribute tables with summary information for each individual fire.

Attribute Explanation / units
lat, lon Coordinates of ignition location (°)
size Fire size (km2)
perimeter Fire perimeter (km)
start_date, start_DOY Start date (yyyy-mm-dd), start day of year (1-366)
end_date, end_DOY End date (yyyy-mm-dd), end day of year (1-366)
duration Duration (days)
fire_line Average length of daily fire line (km)
spread Average daily fire growth (km2/day)
speed Average speed (km/day)
direction, direc_frac Dominant direction of spread (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW) and associated fraction
MODIS_tile MODIS tile id
landcover, landc_frac MCD12Q1 dominant land cover class and fraction (UMD classification), provided for 2002-2024
GFED_regio GFED region (van der Werf et al., 2017; available at https://www.globalfiredata.org/)
references: Andela, N., Morton, D.C., Giglio, L., Paugam, R., Chen, Y., Hantson, S., Van Der Werf, G.R. and Randerson, J.T., 2019. The Global Fire Atlas of individual fire size, duration, speed and direction. Earth System Science Data, 11, 529-552.
Giglio, L., Boschetti, L., Roy, D.P., Humber, M.L. and Justice, C.O., 2018. The Collection 6 MODIS burned area mapping algorithm and product. Remote sensing of environment, 217, 72-85.

Sulla-Menashe, D., Gray, J.M., Abercrombie, S.P. and Friedl, M.A., 2019. Hierarchical mapping of annual global land cover 2001 to present: The MODIS Collection 6 Land Cover product. Remote sensing of environment, 222, 183-194.

metadata.title: Burned Area Maps based on MODIS Surface Reflectance
metadata.description: Burned area (BA) was classified using in-house algorithms, described in detail by Woźniak and Aleksandrowicz (2019). This method utilizes images acquired before and after fire events. All MODIS surface reflectance products MOD09A1 (tiles 24_03 and 25_03) for the period 2002 – 2021 were investigated. Since the study area is obscured by clouds or covered with snow for most of the year, only images from the time window that maximized the number of available frames across most years were selected. Hence, only images acquired between the 145th and 241st day of each year (corresponding to the spring-summer period) were retained for further processing.
references: Woźniak E, Aleksandrowicz S. Self-Adjusting Thresholding for Burnt Area Detection Based on Optical Images. Remote Sensing. 2019; 11(22):2669. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs11222669

Vermote, E. (2021). MODIS/Terra Surface Reflectance 8-Day L3 Global 500m SIN Grid V061 [Data set]. NASA EOSDIS Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Center. Accessed 2024-05-28 from https://doi.org/10.5067/MODIS/MOD09A1.061

metadata.title: Global Monthly Burned Area Fraction Data at 0.25-degree Resolution (2001–2024)
metadata.description: This dataset provides monthly global burned area fraction at 0.25° resolution, covering January 2001 to December 2024. It was generated by aggregating the MODIS MCD64A1 Burned Area Monthly Global 500m (Collection 6.1) dataset from Google Earth Engine (https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/MODIS_061_MCD64A1). The burned area fraction for each 0.25° grid cell is calculated using area-weighted average, representing the proportion of land surface affected by fires within each grid cell. Data are provided in GeoTIFF (.tif) and NetCDF (.nc) formats for compatibility with GIS tools and climate models.

metadata.title: AMAP SLCF EG Pan-Arctic Fire Emissions Model
metadata.description: Custom pan-Arctic open biomass burning emissions model for the year 2018 using Suomi-NPP VIIRS active fire from day and night detections (Oliva and Schroeder, 2015). Each detect was assumed to completely burn each 375 m2 pixel. A ‘best-guess’ land cover was created, from three different land cover products. The 750 m VIIRS Surface Type land cover product (Zhang et al., 2018) was used for North America, Greenland, and the Russian Federation, augmented by the revised 1 km Circumpolar Arctic Vegetation Map (Raster CAVM; Raynolds et al., 2019). For Norway, Sweden, and Finland, the 10 m Land Cover Map of Europe 2017 from the Sentinel-2 Global Land Cover Project (Gromny et al., 2019) was used. All land cover maps were reclassified into the International Geosphere-Biosphere Program (IGBP) classes for ease of emission calculations. Fuel loadings and combustion completeness were taken from Van Leeuwen et al. (2014), with tundra values used for Greenland. Emission factors were taken from Akagi et al. (2011), with updates from Andreae (2019). Atmospheric species include black carbon, methane, and PM2.5.
references: Oliva, P. and Schroeder, W.: Assessment of VIIRS 375 m active fire detection product for direct burned area mapping, Remote Sens. Environ., 160, 144, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2015.01.010, 2015.

Zhang, R., Huang, C., Zhan, X., Jin, H., and Song, X. P.: Development of S-NPP VIIRS global surface type classification map using support vector machines, Int. J. Digit. Earth, 11, 212, https://doi.org/10.1080/17538947.2017.1315462, 2018.

metadata.title: Afforestation reshapes wildfire activity across global temperate biomes
metadata.description:
This repository contains the data and code used to evaluate how afforestation affects wildfire activity across global temperate biomes. Datasets are provided in spatial and CSV formats, alongside the complete analytical workflow and metadata describing variable definitions, units, and original data sources. The Supplementary Material (GlobalPlantationsFire_SuppMaterial) includes detailed descriptions of the afforested patches, statistical analyses, model outputs, and additional maps and visualizations supporting the study’s findings.

The dataset covers more than 67,000 afforested patches, defined as areas converted from non-forest land to planted forests. These patches were identified by combining land-cover transitions from the MODIS Land Cover Type Product (MCD12Q1, Collection 6.1) with officially mapped planted forests in the Spatial Database of Planted Trees (SDPT v2.0). Wildfire occurrence and burned area were derived from MODIS Burned Area products (MCD64A1.061). Each patch has paired observations before and after plantation establishment, with associated information on patch area and observation-period length.

The dataset also includes climatic variables, distance to roads as a proxy for human accessibility, and ecoregion and biome classifications. Continuous predictors used in the models were standardized to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one to facilitate model convergence and comparison of effect sizes. The analytical framework uses generalized linear mixed-effects models. Fire probability was modeled using binomial models with a complementary log-log link, and burned area was analyzed using zero-inflated lognormal models. Model offsets accounted for patch area and observation length, as appropriate. Post hoc contrasts based on estimated marginal means quantified multiplicative changes in fire occurrence and burned area following afforestation.

metadata.title: Model data for "Global biomass burning fuel consumption and emissions at 500-m spatial resolution based on the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED)"
metadata.description:
500 m fire carbon emissions and burned area as part of the publication:

"Global biomass burning fuel consumption and emissions at 500-m spatial resolution based on the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED)"

Dave van Wees1, Guido R. van der Werf1, James T. Randerson2, Brendan M. Rogers3, Yang Chen2, Sander Veraverbeke1, Louis Giglio4, and Douglas C. Morton5

1Department of Earth Sciences, Vrije Universiteit, Amsterdam, 1081 HV, The Netherlands
2Department of Earth System Science, University of California, Irvine, CA 92697, USA
3Woodwell Climate Research Center, Falmouth, MA 02540, USA
4Department of Geographical Sciences, University of Maryland, College Park, MD 20742, USA
5Biospheric Sciences Laboratory, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD 20771, USA

DOI: https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-15-8411-2022

 

UPDATE OF DATASET TO 2023:

This dataset has now been extended to 2023. Since the first release of this dataset, multiple updates to the model input data have been made:

- Update from MODIS C6 to MODIS C6.1 for all MODIS input data, including MCD12Q1 land cover types, MCD14ML active fires, MCD15A2H fPAR, MOD44B VCF, MOD44W land-water mask, and MCD64A1 burned area.
- Update of Hansen forest loss data from v1.9 to v1.11.
- Update of GLEAM evaporative stress data from v3.6b to v3.7b.
- Extension of ERA5-land data to 2023.
- Addition of land cover type layers to the 500-m resolution data files.

 

Files contain 500-m (per MODIS tile) and 0.25 degree aggregated (global grid) carbon emissions and burned area from biomass burning for 2002-2023, as part of the paper "Global biomass burning fuel consumption and emissions at 500-m spatial resolution based on the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED)" published in Geoscientific Model Development (https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-15-8411-2022). 500-m resolution files include land cover type grids. 0.25 degree global grid files also include biome partitioning and accompanying biome fractional cover grids.

Zip archives with filenames "500m_YYYY.zip" contain annual files named "Model500m_2002-2023yr_h##v##_YYYY.nc", which are the 500-meter resolution model results per MODIS tile using the MODIS sinusoidal projection. Carbon emission data layers are:

- Total biomass burning carbon emissions from aboveground; g C m-2 month-1 (/MOD_Grid/emissions/C_AG_TOT)

- Total biomass burning carbon emissions from belowground; g C m-2 month-1 (/MOD_Grid/emissions/C_BG_TOT)

- Fire-related forest loss carbon emissions from aboveground; g C m-2 month-1 (/MOD_Grid/emissions/C_AG_FL)

- Fire-related forest loss carbon emissions from belowground; g C m-2 month-1 (/MOD_Grid/emissions/C_BG_FL)

Total emissions are calculated as: C_AG_TOT + C_BG_TOT. Total fire-related forest loss emissions are calculated as: C_AG_FL + C_BG_FL.

Burned area data layers are:

- Total burned area; fraction of 500-m grid cell per month (/MOD_Grid/burned_area/BA_TOT)

- Burned area from fire-related forest loss; fraction of 500-m grid cell per month (/MOD_Grid/burned_area/BA_FL)

The Zip archive with filename "025d_2002_2023.zip" contains annual files named "Model500m_2002-2023yr_025d_YYYY.nc", which are the 500-m model results aggregated to a 0.25 degree global lat-lon grid. These files contain the same variables as the 500-m files, but aggregated to 0.25 degree resolution (MOD_CMG025). Furthermore, these files include biome partitioning of emissions and burned area (MOD_CMG025BIOME) and provide accompanying biome fractional cover grids for all 20 biomes (variable 'biomes'). Biomes are listed in detail in Table S1 of the van Wees et al. (2022) paper. The biomes 'water', 'snow/ice' and 'barren' were excluded from Table S1 because of their negligible share, but are included in the files provided here for completeness.

metadata.title: Supplementary Data: Global rise in forest fire emissions linked to climate change in the extratropics
metadata.description:
Supplementary Data for the paper "Global rise in forest fire emissions linked to climate change in the extratropics" by Jones et al. (2024, Science).

The records include mapped pyromes and data and code used to delineate the pyromes.

Mapped Pyromes

The data records include mapped pyromes in three forms:

  1. Shapefile (Jones_etal_2024_Global_Forest_Pyromes.shp.zip). Vector features in shapefile format containing data fields pyrome ID and pyrome name. The zipped file contains .shp, .dbf, .prj, .shx files.
  2. Lower-resolution NetCDF (Jones_etal_2024_Global_Forest_Pyromes_Qdeg.nc). NetCDF version 4 file containing gridded values of pyrome ID at quarter-degree resolution.
  3. Higher-resolution NetCDF (Jones_etal_2024_Global_Forest_Pyromes_005deg.nc). NetCDF version 4 file containing gridded values of pyrome ID at 0.05 degree resolution.

Shapefiles are accessible via GIS programmes such as QGIS or ArcGIS. All files .shp, .dbf, .prj, .shx files must be stored in a single directory

NetCDF files can be access by a variety of programming languages such as Python and R. For quick visualisations and access to the data structure, we suggest using the Panoply  tool https://www.giss.nasa.gov/tools/panoply/.

Correlation Data

The data records (Correlation_Qdeg.zip) include gridded quarter-degree correlations between forest burned area (BA) and each of the following variables:

  • Fire weather index
  • Atmospheric instability (continuous Haines index)
  • Lightning flash density
  • Soil moisture
  • Vegetation productivity (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index)
  • Population density
  • Cropland cover
  • Pasture cover
  • Road density
  • Potential fuel loads - surface fuels
  • Potential fuel loads - shrub fuels
  • Potential fuel loads - canopy and ladder fuels
  • Terrain ruggedness index
  • Forest area density

The BA data derive from MODIS MCD64A1 collection 6.1 (Giglio et al., 2018). BA data for forests is masked using the MODIS MOD44B product (DiMiceli et al., 2021) with a 30% tree cover threshold. The predictor data derive from multiple sources as desribed by Jones et al. (2024). See Supplementary Methods and Materials.

The gridded correlations data are provided in Hierarchical Data Format version 5 (.hdf5) files, zipped to Correlation_Qdeg.zip. File names describe the variables used. Cropland_Pasture_Qdeg.hdf5 contains data for both cropland and pasture. Each file contains layers describing the Spearman's rho (ρ) correlation coefficient and the related p-value.

As explained and justified by Jones et al. (2024), the correlation structure used depends on the variable (see Supplementary Methods and Materials) as per the following categories:

  • Fire Weather Index, Atmospheric Instability, and Lightning Flash Density: Monthly correlation between forest BA and each variable across all fire season months in the period 2001-2021 at the quarter-degree resolution.
  • Soil Moisture: Inter-annual correlation between (i) mean soil moisture during the fire season and (ii) accumulated forest BA during the fire season at quarter-degree resolution across years 2001-2021. 
  • Vegetation Productivity (NDVI): Inter-annual correlation between (i) mean NDVI during the prior growing season and (ii) accumulated forest BA during the fire season at quarter-degree resolution across years 2001-2021. 
  • Population Density, Cropland Cover, Pasture Cover, Road Density, Terrain Ruggedness Index, Forest Area Density: Spatial correlation between mean annual forest BA and each variable across the 0.05° cells within each quarter-degree cell during 2001-2021.

Note that these grids are provided for insights into spatial variation in the input correlation data. Pyromes are defined based on correlations fitted on the spatial scale of Olson ecoregions, not quarter-degree grid cells (see further details below).

Clustering Code

DEMO_Clustering.zip contains R Statistics code for clustering forest ecoregions into pyromes based on correlations observed between forest BA and 14 predictors at regional level. The Input directory contains a .RData data frame with correlations between forest BA and each predictor for ecoregions. For demonstrative purposes the code is applied to cluster forest ecorgions of North America into pyromes. The Regions directory contains ecoregions of North America in shapefile format. The Output directory contains output generated by M. Jones, which can be used for validation purposes once other users have trialled the code.
references: Jones et al. (2024) - UNDER REVIEW
Giglio, L., Boschetti, L., Roy, D.P., Humber, M.L. and Justice, C.O., 2018. The Collection 6 MODIS burned area mapping algorithm and product. Remote sensing of environment, 217, 72-85.
DiMiceli, C., Townshend, J., Carroll, M., Sohlberg, R., 2021. Evolution of the representation of global vegetation by vegetation continuous fields. Remote Sensing of Environment, 254, 112271.

metadata.title: Bitemporal Sentinel-1/2, forest-loss and forest-carbon cells for 16 disaster and clearing sites in Indonesia
metadata.description:
One row per 500 m forest cell inside an 80 × 80 km box around each of 16 Indonesian sites: 11 natural disasters (peat fires, a pyroclastic flow, eruptions, a tsunami, landslides, a cyclone, floods) and five human-clearing reference sites, 268,217 cells in total. Each cell has Sentinel-2 optical indices and Sentinel-1 radar backscatter before and after the event, the Hansen Global Forest Change loss label of the event years, terrain, ESA CCI above-ground biomass, and the carbon stock and carbon lost.

Also included: independent event footprints (MODIS burned area, a Sentinel-1 flood signal, hazard-zone rules), out-of-fold and leave-one-site-out model predictions, attribution and benchmark results, supplementary tables S1–S6, Hansen loss time series 2001–2024, daily weather, hazard records, a data dictionary, and a notebook that reproduces every number of the related article (204 checks). Dataset_Description_NusaCarbon.pdf (3 pages) explains every folder and column and links every source.

All inputs are public: ESA / EU Copernicus (Sentinel-1/2, Copernicus DEM, CCI Biomass), University of Maryland and Google (Hansen GFC v1.12), NASA (MODIS MCD64A1, POWER), ECMWF (ERA5), NOAA NCEI and USGS. See README.md for the folders, definitions and source terms.

How to use: unzip Indonesia_disaster_forest_cells_v1.zip, read README.md, and join any files on case_id, row, col. To reproduce the article, run pip install -r code/requirements.txt, open code/reproduce_paper_results.ipynb and Run All.

Related article: R. Hans et al., "Mechanism-Stratified Detection and Quantification of Disaster-Induced Forest Carbon Loss in Indonesia Using Bitemporal Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 Multispectral Observations", 2026.

metadata.title: Global human exposure to wildland fires dataset: 2002-2021
metadata.description:
Global human exposure to wildland fires dataset: 2002-2021

 

Seyd Teymoor Seydi1, John T. Abatzoglou2, Matthew W. Jones3, Mojtaba Sadegh1,4

1Department of Civil Engineering, Boise State University, Boise, ID, USA

2Management of Complex Systems Department, University of California, Merced, Merced, CA, USA

3Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research, School of Environmental Sciences, University of East Anglia (UEA), Norwich, UK

4United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health, Richmond Hills, ON, Canada

 

1.  Dataset Overview

This dataset contains comprehensive information on global fire events from 2002 to 2021, including fire characteristics, environmental variables, land cover properties, and detailed population exposure estimates separated by age group and gender. The data is organized into two separate dataset series:

1.      Fire Events Series (df_Fire_Events_2002 to df_Fire_Events_2021): Contains fire characteristics, environmental variables, land cover properties, and summary exposure information for each fire event. Each file includes global fire events for one year, as indicated in the file name.

2.      Age Groups Series (df_Fire_Age_Groups_2002 to df_Fire_Age_Groups_2021): Contains detailed demographic breakdowns of populations exposed to individual fire events by age group and gender. Each file includes global fire events for one year, as indicated in the file name.

2.  Data Structure

Each annual dataset contains the following information:

  • Temporal Coverage: Individual years from 2002 to 2021 (20 datasets total x 2 [environmental variables and summary exposure + exposures broken down by age and gender structures])
  • Spatial Coverage: Global
  • Unit of Analysis: Individual fire events identified by unique fire_ID
  • Fire Metrics: Location, size, duration, spread characteristics, active fire days, and fire radiative power
  • Environmental Variables: Vegetation indices (EVI, NDVI) and land cover fractions
  • Population Metrics: Total exposure and detailed breakdowns by 5-year age groups and gender
  • Geographic Context: Country and continent information

Column Definitions

Fire Characteristics

  • fire_ID: Unique identifier for each fire event
  • Latitude: Latitude coordinate of fire ignition point (decimal degrees)
  • Longitude: Longitude coordinate of fire ignition point (decimal degrees)
  • size: Fire area
  • perimeter: Fire perimeter length
  • start_date: Fire start date
  • duration: Fire duration (days)
  • spread: Fire spread rate
  • speed: Fire speed rate
  • Active_Fire_Days: Number of active fire days in each pixel within fire polygon, averaged for each fire polygon (Source: MOD14A1)
  • total_frp: Total fire radiative power summed from start to end date of fire, aggregated by sum for each fire polygon (Source: MOD14A1)

3.  Geographic Information

  • Country: Name of country where fire occurred
  • Continent: Name of continent where fire occurred

4.  Land Cover Characteristics (Source: MCD12Q1)

  • Agriculture-Fraction: Fraction of agricultural land cover within fire polygon
  • Urban-Fraction: Fraction of urban areas within fire polygon

5.  Vegetation Indices (Source: MOD13A1)

  • EVI: Enhanced Vegetation Index - maximum annual value for each pixel averaged across fire polygon
  • NDVI: Normalized Difference Vegetation Index - maximum annual value for each pixel averaged across fire polygon

6.  Population Exposure (Source: WorldPop)

  • Exposure: Total population exposure to fire, aggregated by sum for each individual fire event using contemporary population data for each year
  • Scenario-Exposure: Total population exposure to fire using constant 2002 population data across all years, with dynamic fire data for each year, aggregated by sum for each individual fire event. This is also referred to as counterfactual exposure.

6.1. Female Population Exposure (SUM_f_*)

  • SUM_f_0: Number of females aged <1 year exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_1: Number of females aged ≥1 to <5 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_5: Number of females aged ≥5 to <10 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_10: Number of females aged ≥10 to <15 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_15: Number of females aged ≥15 to <20 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_20: Number of females aged ≥20 to <25 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_25: Number of females aged ≥25 to <30 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_30: Number of females aged ≥30 to <35 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_35: Number of females aged ≥35 to <40 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_40: Number of females aged ≥40 to <45 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_45: Number of females aged ≥45 to <50 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_50: Number of females aged ≥50 to <55 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_55: Number of females aged ≥55 to <60 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_60: Number of females aged ≥60 to <65 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_65: Number of females aged ≥65 to <70 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_70: Number of females aged ≥70 to <75 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_75: Number of females aged ≥75 to <80 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_f_80: Number of females aged ≥80 years exposed to fire

6.2. Male Population Exposure (SUM_m_*)

  • SUM_m_0: Number of males aged <1 year exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_1: Number of males aged ≥1 to <5 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_5: Number of males aged ≥5 to <10 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_10: Number of males aged ≥10 to <15 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_15: Number of males aged ≥15 to <20 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_20: Number of males aged ≥20 to <25 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_25: Number of males aged ≥25 to <30 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_30: Number of males aged ≥30 to <35 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_35: Number of males aged ≥35 to <40 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_40: Number of males aged ≥40 to <45 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_45: Number of males aged ≥45 to <50 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_50: Number of males aged ≥50 to <55 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_55: Number of males aged ≥55 to <60 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_60: Number of males aged ≥60 to <65 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_65: Number of males aged ≥65 to <70 years exposed to fire

  • SUM_m_75: Number of males aged ≥75 to <80 years exposed to fire
  • SUM_m_80: Number of males aged ≥80 years exposed to fire

7.  Data Sources

  • Population Data: WorldPop Project demographic datasets

o    Source URL: https://hub.worldpop.org/project/categories?id=8

o    Population estimates are provided in 5-year age groups by gender at high spatial resolution

  • Land Cover Data: MODIS MCD12Q1 Land Cover Type product

o    Used to calculate agricultural and urban land cover fractions within fire polygons

  • Vegetation Indices: MODIS MOD13A1 Vegetation Indices product

o    Used to derive maximum annual EVI and NDVI values, averaged across fire polygons

  • Fire Activity Data: MODIS MOD14A1 Thermal Anomalies and Fire Daily product

o    Used to calculate active fire days and total fire radiative power within fire polygons

  • Fire Data: Global fire atlas is available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11400062

8.  Usage Notes

  1. Exposure Definition: Exposure is defined as population within fire polygon boundaries
  2. Exposure Scenarios:

o    Exposure: Uses contemporary population data for each year, allowing analysis of changing demographics over time

o    Scenario-Exposure: Uses constant 2002 population data across all years to isolate the effect of changing fire patterns while holding population constant

  1. Age Group Structure: Age groups follow standard demographic categories with the first year of life separate (0) and 4-year grouping for ages 1-4, followed by 5-year groupings
  2. Coordinate System: Fire ignition points are provided in decimal degrees
  3. Land Cover Fractions: Agriculture and urban fractions represent the proportion of each land cover type within fire polygon boundaries
  4. Vegetation Indices: EVI and NDVI values represent maximum annual values averaged across the fire polygon area
  5. Fire Activity Metrics:

o    Active Fire Days represents the average number of days with detected thermal anomalies within each fire polygon

o    Total FRP represents the cumulative fire radiative power from fire start to end date, summed across the fire polygon

metadata.title: Distinct drivers of extreme and non-extreme fires in the Brazilian Amazon
metadata.description:
The Amazon forests are pivotal in regulating the global terrestrial carbon cycle (1, 2) and providing habitats for a rich diversity of species (3). These forests are facing a growing threat from intense fire disturbances, especially in areas where forests are fragmented and converted to other types of vegetation (4, 5). Fire can alter vegetation structure and function (6, 7) and affect the regional and global energy budget by changing surface albedo (8) and emitting aerosols and greenhouse gases (9), posing a significant threat to the valuable ecosystem services of tropical forests. In recent years, extreme fires have occurred more frequently and caused more severe damage to tropical forests than non-extreme fires; however, it remains unclear whether the drivers behind extreme and non-extreme fires differ (10, 11). Understanding the drivers of fire disturbance while distinguishing between fire severity levels in the Brazilian Amazon region is therefore of great importance to understanding and protecting the world’s largest tropical forest from fire disturbances. 


Lightning-ignited wildfires and anthropogenic fires for farming expansion are two important sources of fire events in the Brazilian Amazon (12, 13). According to satellite observations, there is a significant variation in both the size and intensity of these events (14). Previous studies have identified climatic and anthropogenic drivers of fires in the Brazilian Amazon, including fire foci (15), El Niño-Southern Oscillation events (16-20), logging (21-23), and expansion of roads (24), stockbreeding and agriculture (12, 13, 25). One experiment showed how a fire can evolve into an extreme one under suitable conditions (26), but the main drivers of extreme and non-extreme fires in the Brazilian Amazon remain unclear. Understanding these drivers is crucial for preventing non-extreme fires from escalating and causing severe damage to forests, and for providing guidance to policymakers to prevent and reduce fires in the face of global warming.


Here, extreme fire is defined as 0.5°×0.5° grid cells with annual burned area exceeding the 90th percentile of the entire time series, while non-extreme fire includes 0.5°×0.5° grid cells with annual burned area greater than 0 but below the 90th percentile. In this study, we use machine learning models to build empirical relationships between climate, anthropogenic activities (represented by land use and land use change), and burned area in the Brazilian Amazon (see the workflow in Fig. S1). The spatial extent of the study region applied here is the Brazilian Amazon biome excluding the Cerrado (Methods). We first apply a random forest classification algorithm to categorize grid cells (0.5°×0.5°) into two types representing extreme fire and non-extreme fire, based on 4 different satellite-based burned area datasets covering the Brazilian Amazon during 1985~2020 (FireCCI51 (27), MCD64CMQ (28), MapBiomas Fire (29), and GABAM (30)). 


We then use random forest quantile regression models to establish non-linear relationships between burned area, climate and anthropogenic variables in grid cells with extreme fires and non-extreme fires, respectively (Methods). The combined classification and regression models follow a previous study for reconstructing historical burned area (31). These random forest models are applied to predict future burned area in two different climate and land use change scenarios under Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSPs) (32) and Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) (33). These are pairings of SSP1 & RCP2.6, SSP5 & RCP8.5. SSP1 & RCP2.6 represents a low-warming climate and more sustainable land use changes, whereas SSP5 & RCP8.5 represents a high-warming climate and less sustainable land use changes.

 

This dataset is currently for manuscript submission to the scientific journal 'Nature Communications'

metadata.title: Data and code supporting concurrent burned-area detections and persistent agro-pastoral conversion after first forest loss in the Peruvian Amazon
metadata.description:
This release supports the study “Concurrent burned-area detections are associated with persistent agro-pastoral conversion after first forest loss in the Peruvian Amazon”.

Version 1.1.0 adds Supplementary_Data_1_Active_Fire_Analysis.zip, containing the complementary historical NASA FIRMS MODIS and Suomi-NPP VIIRS analysis, the fixed protocol, input data, derived matching results, scripts, environment requirements, provenance, checksums, tests and independent verification results. Download and extract this ZIP without changing its folder structure, then open 08_VALIDACION_FUEGO_ACTIVO/START_HERE_REVIEWERS.md. The ZIP is 17,955,692 bytes and contains 59 files.

The original cohort archive fire_loss_conversion_peruvian_amazon_v1.0.0.zip and its separate companion files are preserved unchanged. Those historical companions retain the original title, DOI, version and figure numbering. For this release, read START_HERE_VERSION_1_1_0.md and use CITATION_VERSION_1_1_0.cff. The original release remains available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21881539.

The study uses a retrospective spatial cohort sampled on a systematic 0.01° lattice in stable forests of the Peruvian Amazon. Hansen Global Forest Change defines first loss during 2014–2021; MapBiomas Peru Collection 3 defines baseline and subsequent land cover; MapBiomas Fire and GABAM define concurrent burned-area detection categories. Persistent conversion requires anthropogenic cover in each of three consecutive post-loss years. The original archive reproduces analyses from derived panels, not the raster-to-panel extraction.

The estimates are associational. Thermal observations corroborate nearby combustion but do not validate individual 30 m burned pixels or subsequent land use. No field photographs or field campaign data are included. This dataset release does not publish the manuscript or confidential review correspondence.

Author-owned material is covered by the record-level CC BY 4.0 licence. Software in the preserved original code folder retains its included additional MIT licence. NASA data and other third-party materials retain their original terms, attribution and disclaimers and are not relicensed by this deposit. See START_HERE_VERSION_1_1_0.md for details.

metadata.title: MOSEV: A global burn severity database from MODIS (2000-2020)
metadata.description: To advance in the fire discipline as well as in the study of CO2 emissions it is of great interest to develop a global database with estimators of the degree of biomass consumed by fire, which is defined as burn severity. We present the first global burn severity database (MOSEV database), which is based on Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) surface reflectance and burned area (BA) products scenes since November 2000 to near real time. To build the database we combined Terra MOD09A1 and Aqua MYD09A1 surface reflectance products to obtain dense time series of the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) spectral index, and we used the MCD64A1 product to identify BA and the date of burning. Then, we calculated for each burned pixel the difference of the NBR (dNBR), and its relativized version (RdNBR), as well as the post-burn NBR which are the most commonly used burn severity spectral indices. The database also includes the pre-burn NBR used for calculations, the date of the pre- and post-burn NBR and the date of burning.

metadata.description:
This repository holds a dataset of lightning-ignited wildfires across the boreal biome. The BoLtFire dataset covers the period 2012 to 2022 and encompasses 6,902 fires - 4,201 in Eurasia and 2,701 in North America.

The layers included in this dataset are: FireID, StartDate, EndDate, FireYdear, AreaHa (burned area), ClassSize, BiomeName, EcoBiome, EcoName, EcoID, Realm, LCDN (Land cover number), LCName (land cover name), Country, Continent, HoldoverD (days), HoldoverRD (holdover rounded), IgnLat (Ignition location Latitude), IgnLong (Ignition Location Longitude), DisPol (Distance of the ignition location to the fire perimeter if it is located outside the polygon), and PerCheck (designates if the ignition location is within the fire perimeter or oustide the perimeter).

 

The datasets are available per continent (North America, Europe, and Asia) as shapefiles. The spatial reference system is Global LANd Cover mapping and Estimation (GLANCE) Grids - Version 01 CRS.

 

*Please note: Versions 1 and 2 are missing LIW from Canada between 2021-2022.

Update (v6.1, April 15, 2026): Key model output and other data used to create figures in the study have been uploaded in the differland_output_and_figure_data.zip file. The driver files (differland_driver_files_v6.zip) used to calibrate the model remain unchanged from version 6. 

This repository contains the driver files used in the manuscript "Differentiable Land Model Reveals Global Environmental Controls on Latent Ecological Functions." A full description of the driver datasets and the sources of different variables is available in our manuscript. If you would like to reproduce the results in our manuscript, please download and unzip the driver data, and place the respective files in the /data directory.

Data Availability Statement

The DifferLand driver files, including processed spatial predictors, forcing data, and model configuration files, are publicly accessible on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13984225. Additionally, processed model output used to generate the figures is also deposited in the same Zenodo repository. The DifferLand model code is available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19410424).

All datasets used in this study are publicly available from their respective repositories. Key datasets and their DOIs include: MODIS land cover product MCD12C1 (https://doi.org/10.5067/MODIS/MCD12C1.061), ERA5 reanalysis (https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.adbb2d47), Global 30 Arc-Second Elevation dataset GTOPO30 (https://doi.org/10.5066/F7DF6PQS), global forest age 1km dataset (https://doi.org/10.17871/ForestAgeBGI.2021), Harmonized World Soil Database v1.2 (https://doi.org/10.3334/ORNLDAAC/1247), NOAA global CO2 record (https://doi.org/10.15138/9N0H-ZH07), GRACE/GRACE-FO terrestrial water storage (https://doi.org/10.5067/TEMSC-3JC63), the LCSPP-MODIS photosynthesis proxy (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11658088), the reprocessed MODIS Version 6.1 Leaf Area Index dataset (https://doi.org/10.4121/21858717.v2), CMS-Flux Net Biome Exchange (NBE) (https://cmsflux.jpl.nasa.gov/get-data/gcp-2023/), and GLEAM v4.2a evapotranspiration data (https://www.gleam.eu/#downloads). GFED5 burned area data are available at https://zenodo.org/records/7668424, while GFED5 fire emissions data are available from the Global Fire Data portal (https://www.globalfiredata.org/). MODIS burned area fraction data are available via NASA EarthData Search (https://search.earthdata.nasa.gov/). Changes in global terrestrial live biomass dataset at 10 km resolution from Xu et al. (2021) can be accessed at https://zenodo.org/records/4161694 (2001-2019) or by contacting the authors of the dataset (for 2020-2021).

Additional datasets include: Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) global inversion-optimized greenhouse gas fluxes and concentrations (https://doi.org/10.24381/ed2851d2); Copernicus Leaf Area Index 1999–2020, 1 km, 10-daily (https://doi.org/10.2909/d5fdc595-2e03-4cbe-a39e-5f006f9cef07); Copernicus Leaf Area Index 2014–present, 300 m, 10-daily (https://doi.org/10.2909/219fdc9f-616b-444b-a495-198f527b4722); IB-AGC global live biomass carbon product (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15676176); GLAB-VOD vegetation optical depth dataset (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10306094); and CMS-Flux Fire L4 V2 carbon fluxes (https://doi.org/10.5067/HO07ZJEQBMHE). Full descriptions and usage details for all datasets are provided in the Datasets subsection of the Methods.

Eddy covariance observations used in this study were compiled from the FLUXNET2015 dataset, AmeriFlux FLUXNET, ICOS, and OzFlux networks. These datasets are publicly available under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license. Detailed site-level citations, dataset access links, and metadata are provided in Supplementary Data 1.

    • MSWEP: 17
  • MAT - Mean annual temperature from CRU)
  • MConc_xxx – Mean annual concentration of rainfall as defined by 18, where xxx denotes precip data source (see “MAP_xxx”)
  • MADD_xxx- Mean annual fractional dry days from CRU - i.e. seasonality of rainfall), where xxx denotes precip data source (see “MAP_xxx”)
  • MDDM_xxx – Mean fractional dry days of the driest month.
  • MADM_xxx – Mean annual precipitation of the driest month.
  • MTWM - Mean Maximum Temperature of the warmest month from CRU
  • MTCM - Mean minimum temperature of the coldest month from CRU
  • SW1 - direct downwards SW simulated using the SLASH model using CRU cloud cover
  • SW2 - diffuse downwards SW simulated using the SLASH model using CRU cloud cover
  • MaxWind (Mean Max Windspeed from CRU-(National Centers for Environmental Prediction 15

‘output_summary’ contains framework output. There are several directories for different experiments, each containing a netcdf file. Along with standard latitude and longitude,each file contains ‘model_level_number’ dimension, with each layer representing the 1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75, 90, 95 and 99% quantiles of the model posterior. The folder represents the experiment:

  • Control – standard full model reconstruction
  • noHumans – without human influence (from crop, pasture, population density or urban influence)
  • noMortality – without disturbance stress (burnt area, wind, heat stress, rainfall seasonality
  • noMAP – without mean annual precip influence.
  • noNoneMAT – without mean annual temperature influence.
  • noFire – tree cover without the influence of fire
  • noDrought – without the influence of rainfall distribution
  • noTasMort – without mortality from heat stress
  • noWind – without influence from max. windspeed
  • noPas – without exclusion from pasture
  • noCrop – without exclusion from crop
  • noPop – without reduction from population density
  • noUrban – without exclusion from urban
  • firePlus1pc – tree cover with burnt area was 1% higher.

metadata.description:
This dataset supports the State of Wildfires 2024-25 report under review at Earth System Science Data (Kelley et al., under review; !!!!ADD DOI LINK TO ARTICLE!!!!!). 

It is an update of the State of Wildfires 2023-24 report (Jones et al. 2024). The dataset provides annual data and final-year anomalies in exposed population and exposed physical assets. 

Annual data relate to the global fire season defined as March-February (e.g., March 2023-February 2024), aligning with an annuall lull in the global fire calendar (see Jones et al., 2024). The complete methodology is described by Kelley et al. (under review; !!!ADD DOI LINK TO ARTICLE!!!)

 

Citation 

Work utilising our regional summaries should cite both Kelley et al. (2025; !!!ADD DOI LINK TO ARTICLE!!!) AND the primary reference for the variable(s) of interest as follows: 

  • Giglio et al. (2018) for MODIS MCD64A1 BA. 

  • Eberenz et al. (2020) for the exposure layers (reference year: 2018).

  • Aznar-Siguan and Bresch (2019) and Aznar-Siguan et al. (2025) for the global risk assessment platform CLIMADA.



Input Data 

Burned Area (BA) 

  • BA data from NASAʼs MODIS BA product (MCD64A1) are extended from Giglio et al. (2018) and are available at Giglio et al. (2021). Period: 2002-February 2025 Resolution: 500m, daily. 

Exposure data LitPop from CLIMADA

  • Exposure data for population and physical assets are extended from Eberenz et al. (2020) and are available through the CLIMADA data API. Resolution: 150arc, static (reference years=2018).



Regional Analysis 

We performed "cookie-cutting" (spatial and temporal masking) of the above input data sets to features in each of the following regional layers (e.g. per country in the "Countries" layer). 

The statistics derived from cookie-cutting are listed below. Full details in Kelley et al. (2025).

metadata.title: California Wildfire Perimeters with Environmental and WUI Attributes
metadata.description:
This dataset contains processed fire perimeter records from four wildfire datasets: the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CalFire; 1990–2025), Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS; 1990–2024), the Global Fire Atlas (Atlas; 2001–2025), and the FIREDpy-based country-level dataset (FIRED; 2000–2024). Atlas and FIRED are derived from MODIS imagery. CalFire records are limited to fire events larger than 1 km².

All four shapefiles include fire identifiers, ignition date, year and decade, burned area (size_km2), Northern/Southern California flags, and WUI classification attributes from intersecting fire perimeters with WUI boundaries (FireType: WUI vs Wildland; reachWUI; reachUrban).

CalFire further includes containment date, ignition cause, climate and terrain variables (temperature, vapor pressure deficit, precipitation, wind, elevation, slope, NDVI, and land cover), ignition-based WUI classes derived by matching Global Fire Atlas ignition points to CalFire perimeters (IgnWUI; IgnType: WUIIgnite, WUISpread, or Wildland), the within-perimeter WUI burned-area fraction (WUIfrac), 4-day mean Canadian Fire Weather Index moisture codes (FFMC_4d, DMC_4d, DC_4d), Santa Ana wind occurrence flags for Southern California fires (SAW), and within-perimeter land-cover fractions from MCD12Q1 FAO-LCCS1 2020 (fracFor, fracGrass, fracShrub, fracSG). A full field list is provided in CalFire_added_fields.txt.

The four perimeter datasets are provided as compressed Shapefiles.

These data are intended to support research on fire size distribution, fire behavior, land-fire interactions, and WUI risk assessment.

metadata.title: Data and Code for: Climate–Fire Relationships Across Global Mountain Systems: A Six-Continent Analysis
metadata.description:
Datasets and Google Earth Engine code for analyzing climate–fire relationships across six global mountain systems.

Contents:

  • Processed panel datasets (6 CSV files) containing 229,178 pixel-year observations of fire severity (dNBR), climate variables (ERA5-Land), and topographic covariates (SRTM) for six mountain regions: Central Himalaya, Central Rockies, Central Andes, Western Alps, East African Highlands, and Australian Alps (2013–2023)
  • Google Earth Engine JavaScript code for data generation and processing
  • README with complete variable descriptions and usage instructions

Methods: Fire severity was quantified using differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR) calculated from Landsat 8/9 imagery with harmonic phenological baselines. Panel structure enables fixed-effects regression controlling for time-invariant spatial characteristics.

Associated manuscript: Precipitation reverses fire severity relationships across global mountain fire regimes
