metadata.title: Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland
metadata.description:
Main data and methods used for Roberts et al. (2026) - "Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland"

Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems 10:1945186

 

Methods -

CEA energy demand model setup

To compare CEA powered by PV with crop-specific production globally, we derived a spatially-explicit energy demand per CEA. This type of comparison has been addressed in localized contexts in Weidner et al.[19], but lack a global scope as indicated in Bomford[23], Righini et al.[24,37], and Stanghellini & Katzin[27]. While there are many different greenhouse production models available[38], the specific aim of this study was to examine CEA systems and energy use on a global scale and this led to the construction of a model to address this aim. We developed a simple mechanistic model similar to the Van Henten model[39,40] as a way of incorporating experimental CEA crop production values and parameters[24] across a global spatial array (Supplementary Fig. 2). In order to make the model globally applicable, we made certain elements more generalized than they might be in a site-specific model, such as the building design, crop growing parameters and production system, building interaction with outside conditions, and the indoor environment control systems.

The CEA yields, harvest metrics, and light requirements were taken directly from Righini et al.[24]. In that study, the authors compiled and analysed CEA metrics across multiple studies as well as their own experiments for wheat[28–30], soybean[24], potato[28,31,32], and tomato[24]. CEA aims to homogenize crop outputs and yields regardless of the geographic location, seasons, and local growing conditions. We applied this assumption to our model and kept CEA yields constant for each crop across the global spatial array. The yields from individual studies in Righini et al.[24] were analysed for parameters such as light requirements (photoperiod and photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD)), the growing cycle length (days), and the resulting yields in terms of plant density, harvest index (ratio of harvested biomass to total plant biomass), fresh harvest yield per growing cycle, dry harvest yield per cycle, and annual fresh weight yield (as the sum of multiple growing cycles possible per year). The values from that study used in this CEA energy model are listed in Supplementary Table 2. Long-term and continuous datasets on CEA for different crops such as those included in this study were not available. Hence, we extrapolated from the experimental results that were available to assume multiple yields per year (3-4) that would be possible given the reported growing production times and days to harvest. The reference experimental studies all used soilless growing set-ups (e.g., hydroponic), so the same is assumed in our modelled CEA. Mills[34] also compared energy demands across CEA studies and found differences between and across crop types. Mills[34] acknowledges that for crops such as wheat, few studies are available and in some cases, there is a reliance on modelled crop simulations. Given the discrepancies and potentially large ranges between crops and individual studies, we chose to directly apply the RIghini et al. CEA data compilation as the main source of crop specific parameters.

Two types of CEA were evaluated, a high-tech closed greenhouse (GH) and a vertical farm (VF), to model the energy required for each set-up to achieve the target yields as compiled in Righini et al.[24]. The mechanistic greenhouse model assumed uniform internal conditions, also known as a “perfectly stirred tank”[39], and considered water vapour and energy balances in a similar way to the Van Henten model[38–40] (Supplementary Tables 1 & 3). 

We adapted the basic greenhouse balance equations for energy and water vapour from the van Henten model[39,40] to run the simplified model on global scales to calculate the CEA energy demand:

 dE/dt  = QSun + QHeat + QLamp - QVent - QLatent - QCon – QFIR – Qcool   (J m-2 s-1 = W m-2)

dMW/dt = WTrans + WEvap + WHum - WCond - WVent - WDehum     (kg {water vapor} m-2  s-1)

dE/dt = net change of energy

Q = rate of heat transfer from the various factors, inside and outside the growing space

dMW/dt = net change of water mass

W = rate of water vapor change over time from inside and outside factors

More detailed processes can be captured in van Henten[39,40] or other greenhouse models[38]; however, to represent the major drivers of energy use, we only focused on these specific aspects. The process for calculating the influence of solar radiation was the same for both GH and VF and was an adapted version of the equation[24]:

 

Energy Uselights = PPFD * photoperiod * 3600 * ηlights *10-6 (MJ m-2 day-1)

 

 ηlights= electrical efficacy

 

The walls in the VF had 0% light entering, whereas the GH had 82% of solar radiation entering the growing space[22]. For incoming solar radiation, the daily total values were per month for an average daily solar radiation (J m-2 day-1). This incoming average daily solar radiation load was converted to a PPFD (μmol m-2 s-1) as the total daily PPFD or Daily Light Interval (DLI) as mol m-2 day-1. The PPFD and photoperiod for each crop from Righini et al.[24] was converted into a DLI requirement per day. The difference between the actual DLI and this required DLI indicated the lighting (J m-2 day-1) shortfall. Dividing this shortfall by the electrical efficacy*16 of the lights gave the average daily supplemental lighting demand (MJ m-2 day-1) for each month of 2020. 

While there are other potential processes or factors that would contribute to CEA energy demand, such as water pumps and irrigation, mechanized automation, and computer and sensor controls, these are relatively minor compared to the major energy drivers such as supplemental lighting, growing space heating and cooling, and ventilation[24]. 

Between the two CEA set-ups, there were minor adjustments to the building dimensions, crop growing area, and wall insulation properties. The simplified building designs similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] were intended to capture the basic parameters of the indoor growing space and basic interactions with the outdoor environment. In this way, the major drivers of CEA energy demand could be compared while avoiding specific building designs that vary by specific location and use. In this simulation, the vertical farm and closed greenhouse each had supplemental lighting, temperature, and humidity controls to maintain the same light requirements, indoor conditions, and annual yields depending on the crop requirements. 

The model considered a 1 ha GH (75% of the building footprint is considered usable as growing area) and a 0.25 ha VF (with 4 stacked layers that utilize 75% of the building footprint for growing area). The VF yield was assumed to be four times per hectare of building footprint compared to the GH as a way to capture the increased production capacity potential for the VF. Additionally, the VF was assumed to be 8m in height and the GH was assumed to be 4m in height. The same indoor environment was assumed for both systems and in turn the capacity to maintain that growing space environment is what drives the energy demand (Supplementary Table 1 & 3). 

We used the average daily light (PPFD) requirements, photoperiod, and annual yields according to Righini et al.[24] and included updated lighting and indoor environmental parameters to meet the best available standards for LEDs and heat pumps (Supplementary Table 4). The values presented by Righini et al.[24] include their own data for tomato and soybean experiments as well as a compilation of previous experiments for wheat[28–30] and potato[28,31,32] trials. Each of the selected experiments may have differed in specific CEA designs; however, all were soilless systems that relied entirely on supplemental lighting for crop growth. The mechanistic greenhouse model had a time-step of one day for all indoor processes. The outdoor climate conditions were averaged for each month and recorded as the average daily temperature, relative humidity, and solar radiation flux for each grid cell per month. The model received the daily average (for each month) as input data and first calculated the influence of the outside factors on the indoor growing parameters (temperature, relative humidity, and light) for both VF and GH. Then for each growing space parameter, the corresponding CEA component was forced to correct the factor to bring it back into the target range. For heating and cooling this was done with a heat pump, for relative humidity with humidifier or ventilation, and LEDs for supplemental lighting. 

The energy requirement for each component to maintain the target growing conditions was summed for each average day per month. These daily energy totals were multiplied by the number of days per month to return a monthly energy demand based on the average day in that month. These monthly values were then summed to return an annual energy demand. This annual energy demand was divided by the annual CEA yield per building to give the energy use efficiency (MJ kg-1) for each crop and CEA system.

The resulting energy demand reflects the energy needed to maintain those constant internal conditions within the target ranges. By doing this, we were able to compare the plant specific growing parameters and yields from Righini et al.[24] between VF and GH systems.

 

CEA energy demand simulation inputs

The selected crops for the study were wheat, potato, soybean, and tomato to represent grain, legume, tuber, and vegetable crop types. The temperature control (15-23°C) and relative humidity range (60-85%) were set at levels similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] (Supplementary Table 3) We assumed a fixed biomass production per growing cycle and year (yield biomass per m2 and harvest index adapted from Righini et al.[24] instead of simulating crop growth over time and across growth stages. Because evapotranspiration is a complex process that varies between crops and plant stages, we applied a single generalised evapotranspiration rate of 4.5 mm day-1 for all crops[42–44]. Additionally, the energy to power water pumps and recirculation is relatively insignificant compared to other CEA processes and the water use itself might be over 90% lower (for both closed greenhouses and vertical farms) than comparable field systems[20,24,45]. For this reason, water use and energy for the irrigation and water pump and recirculation system were not included.

A heat pump is used to maintain the internal temperature within the target range with a Coefficient of Performance, for heating, (COP) of 4.0 and an Energy Efficiency Ratio, for cooling, (EER) of 13.0[46]. These COP and EER are general values in order to reflect that these efficiencies could be influenced by local conditions and product designs. The building wall insulation R-value was kept at 3 for the GH[47] and 15 for the VF[48]. Supplemental lighting from LEDs was set to 3.5 mmol J-1 to represent the current best available standard[22,27] (Supplementary Table 4).

ERA 5 Agrometeorological environmental data[49] (0.1° x 0.1° resolution) were used for daily measurements for solar radiation flux (J m-2), temperature (K at 2m height), and relative humidity (% at 2m height at 12h) for the year 2020. The daily values for each grid cell were averaged for each month in the year 2020. This averaged daily value per month for the climate parameters (solar radiation, temperature, relative humidity) were input into the CEA energy demand model at 1-day time steps. The use of a monthly averaged value for each climate factor was a trade-off to run the model efficiently on a global array while still capturing site and seasonal variations. The model outputs were calculated in total energy demand (MJ) per day and then summed for a monthly and annual total. The annual energy demand to crop yield (MJ kg-1) or energy use efficiency in each CEA system was then calculated per grid cell. Both monthly energy demand and annual energy use efficiency were downscaled to a 1km grid in order to compare to the higher resolution land use and solar PV potential model outputs. The resulting energy use efficiency as MJ kg-1 for each crop calculated by region for both CEA systems is shown in Fig. 2.

 

Global crop area, yield, and production

We used a data harmonisation approach based on the HILDA+ land use reconstruction model[2], to allocate 2020 crop production (t km-2) and crop harvest area (ha km-2) for the target crops to a 1km global grid array. This approach allowed us to harmonise the outputs of multiple crop models, datasets, and statistical inventories to produce crop area, yield, and production maps for each target crop. In HILDA+, the cropland areas were isolated and used to mask the CROPGRIDS crop-specific crop area data (reference year 2020)[36]. GAEZ v4 (reference year 2015)[35], along with the statistical data for FAO country level harvest area and production quantity totals (reference year 2020)[50] were used to assign the pixel-level harvest area (ha) and yields (t/ha) for the target crops. 

This was done by first normalizing the GAEZ v4 crop yield values, i.e. dividing them by their national and cropland-wide mean, as well as normalizing the CROPGRIDS crop area values by their national and cropland-wide sum (all constrained by HILDA+ cropland and at least 5% CROPGRIDS crop coverage). This normalization was done in order to align each input dataset with the same consistent spatial array and projection. The normalized values, crop yield and area, were then multiplied by FAO crop yield and harvested area in 2020, respectively. The crop production (t) was finally derived by a pixel-based multiplication of country- and crop-specific yield (t ha-1) and harvested areas (ha). Each crop then had a specific harvest area (ha), yield (t ha-1), and production (t) per grid cell for the year 2020. In order to harmonise these different datasets, steps were taken to minimise inter-dataset variability. FAO statistics only report crop area harvested, which could include multiple harvests on the same area, so the CROPGRIDS crop cultivation area layer was used to set a fraction of crop area per grid cell prior to allocating the FAO area harvested within each country’s grid cells. Upper thresholds for crop area were set to limit any instance where the area from multiple harvests were applied to the same grid cell. In this way we were able to remove inconsistencies or data artifacts that would otherwise inflate the crop area beyond what was available in the grid cell (i.e., more than 100 ha crop area for a 100 ha grid cell). The data harmonisation process of crop area, yield, and production is simplified in Supplementary Fig. 4.

 

PV-powered CEA comparison with 2020 crop area, yield, and production

The CEA crop yields[24] were kept constant across the global array in order to test the area and PV energy capacity to scale these experimental values globally. The multiple datasets[35,36,50] used across the analysis reported the reference yields and production in harvested biomass. For this reason, we used CEA production and yield values for harvested biomass. For different research questions, this metric could be changed to dry harvest weight, calories, or other specific nutritional or agronomic units. The first step to calculate the comparison against 2020 crop production was to determine the CEA building area needed to meet 2020 production (t km-2) per grid cell. The annual CEA yields were calculated per growing area and were set per grid cell to reflect the CEA systems (0.75ha growing area per 1ha GH building area and 0.75ha growing area per 0.25ha VF building area). The 2020 production array was divided by the annual CEA yield (per growing area) per crop to give the CEA building area needed for year-round CEA production in each grid cell. This CEA footprint requirement was summed per hectare for GH or per 0.25 hectare for VF per grid cell.

To calculate the solar PV area needed for the CEA, the monthly solar PV potential (kWh m-2) was derived from Saxena et al.[33]. The area available for PV per grid cell was calculated as the harvest area subtracted by the CEA building area per grid cell. The surface area coverage of the solar PV was assumed to be 75% of a given area[22], so the potential energy available to the CEA was reduced by this factor. This PV potential was then multiplied by an efficiency factor[51] (26.8%) for conversion to usable electricity. The total CEA energy demand per building (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) per grid cell was multiplied by the CEA building area requirement to calculate the total CEA energy demand per grid cell. The monthly PV area requirement to directly power the CEA was calculated by multiplying the potential PV energy by the CEA energy demand per grid cell. The process is summarized visually in Supplementary Fig. 3 and all CEA component inputs are summarized in Supplementary Tables 1-4.

For year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for each grid cell became the fixed PV area needed to power the required CEA area for that grid cell. No energy storage was assumed from one day to the next, so each day had only the monthly 1-day average to fulfil the CEA demand. We also analysed continuous 9-month CEA production capacity as a way to reduce the energy demand and the required PV area to power the CEA. The reduction in yield capacity was taken into account and the CEA area needed to meet 2020-Production per grid cell was re-calculated. For the shortened 9-month production cycle, the 9-month stretch with the lowest PV area requirements to meet indoor energy demands were calculated per grid cell. Similar to the year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for this 9-month cycle, determined the PV area needed for that grid cell. The resulting area (ha) of PV needed to power a year-round or 9-month CEA is displayed spatially in Supplementary Fig. 7.

This CEA building area plus PV area was the total area that was then compared to the crop harvest area per grid cell. The land area requirement balance (ha) was calculated by subtracting the CEA building footprint plus PV area from the crop area per grid cell. If the area balance was negative, then not enough area was available for the CEA-PV to meet 2020 production in that grid cell. If the balance was zero or positive, the CEA-PV matched 2020 production and any positive value could be considered a lower required land area than 2020 production area in ha. 

Only the grid cells with a positive area balance were used to calculate the potential extra or surplus production by allowing the model to utilise all crop area available and CEA production above 2020 production values. This extra-production was calculated by incrementally adding CEA units (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) and the required PV area per building. This process was done iteratively until the crop harvest area in that grid cell reached zero. The sum of this extra production according to the CEA building area added, was then added to that grid cell total production quantity. The spatial distribution of areas where CEA met 2020 production can be seen in Fig. 3. The global totals and comparison between CEA systems for harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production, production quantity (t) met by CEA, lower CEA-PV land area requirements compared to 2020 production (ha), and extra production (t) by CEA are given in Fig. 4. The regional breakdowns relative to the global totals as well as the breakdown within each region are given in Supplementary Figs. 8&9.

 

Yield gap analysis

The yield gap analysis and comparison were done to apply a single metric for comparing crop production challenges globally. For this study we used the GAEZ v4 crop-wise Yield Achievement Ratio[35] (YAR) global gridded (5 arc minutes) dataset for the most recent average (2009-2011). The YAR was calculated by GAEZ as the ratio of actual (average) yields to the attainable yields for each grid cell. The attainable yields were calculated as the biophysical influences (e.g., solar radiation, water, nutrients, temperature) on yield (potential yield) while considering location specific constraints (e.g., soil or terrain, pest pressure, management). For the crops analysed in this study, GAEZ only has YAR data for wheat, soybean, and potato, so we limited the yield gap analysis to these crops. The ratio of actual/ attainable yields is inversely proportional to the yield gap, as a higher ratio indicates a smaller yield gap. 

We used the GAEZ YAR data that had already been divided into bins corresponding to the crop-wise YAR. The 2020 crop-wise harvest area (ha) was compared to the corresponding YAR to calculate the distribution of crop harvest area per YAR bin. This distribution (percent of harvest area (ha)) per YAR bin was plotted to complement the global YAR maps plotted directly from the GAEZ dataset.

CEA-PV system performance compared to 2020 production was then evaluated against the reference crop yield gaps. Only grid cells where there was spatial agreement between the CROPGRIDS and GAEZ YAR datasets were considered. To analyse CEA-PV relationships with crop yield gaps, only the grid cells where CEA-PV demonstrated the ability to meet 2020 production were considered. Including only these CEA-PV net area positive areas was done to focus on the technical potential of CEA in alleviating yield gap constraints. In our analysis, CEA-PV net negative could not meet the same production values as 2020 production without additional crop area, it was assumed that CEA in these areas would be able to aid in yield gap closures. The area (ha) that was net positive CEA-PV crop area was summed for each YAR bin and the percent of the net positive CEA-PV crop area was plotted alongside the total crop harvest area distribution. Supplementary Fig. 1 provides a general overview of the yield gap analysis process.

 

Electricity grid constraints

The Arderne et al.[52] electrical grid dataset was used to evaluate the current electrical grid coverage in areas that overlap with areas that meet 2020 production (CEA-PV technical capacity areas). Where there was at least medium-voltage electricity, a 2km buffer was set as the maximum distance for connection to these electricity grids. The grid cells where there was overlap of this grid network and buffer with these CEA-PV grid cells that met 2020 production were summed, as well as those that were outside of this 2km buffer. The grid cells were then multiplied by the crop harvest area (ha) in that grid cell and then summed crop at the country- and regional-levels. The proportion of harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production within the 2km electricity grid was then calculated for country and region as seen in Fig. 5. The spatial overlap of areas where CEA met 2020 production and the electricity grid can be seen in Supplementary Fig. 10.

 

Aridity Index

The Global Aridity Index Database as described in Zomer et al.(52) was used to compare where CEA matched 2020 production against aridity zones. The aridity index was divided into bins according to the index value. These index values were overlaid on the grid cells where CEA matched 2020 production. The harvest area (ha) was then multiplied by the number of grid cells within each index bin. The harvest area (ha) where CEA matched 2020 production was plotted according to the aridity index bin and results are given in Supplementary Fig. 11.

 

Model assumption sensitivity

            A deterministic sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate CEA-PV equivalent capacity reactions to changes in model assumptions. The sensitivity analysis evaluated changing assumptions around three parameters directly influencing CEA-PV area requirements and subsequent equivalent-capacity calculations: CEA crop yield, CEA energy demand, and PV conversion efficiency. Changes to each assumption were considered individually and for their combined effects on CEA-PV equivalent capacity. The main “baseline” analysis for GH and VF applied the experimental CEA yields described above and calculated the CEA building area required to match 2020 crop production in each grid cell, while the PV area requirement was determined from the corresponding CEA energy demand and a baseline PV conversion efficiency of 26.8%.

For the yield sensitivity analysis, the annual CEA yield for each crop was reduced by 10%, 25%, and 50%. The required CEA building area was then recalculated directly from 2020 crop production using the reduced yield while retaining the same GH- or VF-specific growing areas and corresponding year-round or 9-month growing cycles. The greater CEA area required under lower yields also increased growing area and associated PV area requirements to match 2020 crop production. For the energy sensitivity, CEA energy demand per unit growing area was increased by 10%, 25%, and 50%, while CEA yields and building area requirements were maintained at baseline input values. In turn, the corresponding PV area requirement increased to meet the increased energy demand. For the PV efficiency sensitivity, conversion efficiency was reduced from the baseline input value of 26.8% to 22%, while CEA crop yields and energy demands were kept constant. The PV area requirements were then required to provide the same amount of energy to meet CEA energy demands.

Additionally, the joint effects of combining CEA yield reductions, energy demand increases, and PV conversion efficiency reductions were evaluated. For each joint effect scenario, the revised CEA building area and PV requirements were compared to the available crop-wise harvested area in each grid cell using the same approach as the baseline analysis to calculate equivalent capacity. The sensitivity analysis tested the change in absolute area (ha), production (t), and less crop area required (ha) and corresponding global percentages for the CEA systems, year-round and 9-month growing cycles, and four crops. The sensitivity analysis therefore tested how these CEA systems performed under less favourable model assumptions rather than representing probabilistic uncertainty ranges.

metadata.title: Global Trends in Hydroclimatic Variables (1979–2023) from ERA5 at 0.25° Resolution
metadata.description:
This dataset provides global gridded trend estimates (Z-values) for key hydroclimatic variables over the period 1979–2023, derived from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset. The analysis was performed to detect long-term changes in climate and water cycle drivers at a spatial resolution of 0.25° (~25 km).

Variables included (all in .mat format):

  • Z_air_temperature.mat – near-surface at 2m air temperature trends

  • Z_cloud_cover.mat – total cloud cover trends

  • Z_ETo.mat – reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Penman-Monteith) trends

  • Z_long_radiation.mat – net longwave radiation trends

  • Z_net_radiation.mat – net radiation trends

  • Z_PET.mat – potential evapotranspiration (Priestley–Taylor) trends

  • Z_precipitation.mat – total precipitation trends

  • Z_short_radiation.mat – net shortwave radiation trends

  • Z_soil_moisture.mat – volumetric soil moisture trends

  • Z_soil_temperature.mat – soil temperature trends

  • Z_solar_radiation.mat – incoming solar radiation trends

  • Z_VPD.mat – vapor pressure deficit trends

  • Z_wind_speed.mat – near-surface at 2m wind speed trends

Methodology:

  • Long-term trends were calculated using the Mann-Kendall test for trend detection.

  • Significance levels were evaluated at α = 0.05.

  • Trend magnitudes are expressed as Z-values (normalized test statistics).

Spatial and Temporal Coverage:

  • Time span: 1979–2023 (45 years)

  • Spatial resolution: 0.25° × 0.25° global grid

  • Dataset source: ERA5 reanalysis (ECMWF)

Applications:
This dataset can be used for:

  • Hydroclimatic and environmental change assessments

  • Attribution studies on drivers of evaporative demand and water cycle intensification

  • Regional and global climate modeling validation

  • Agricultural and hydrological impact studies

File format:
All files are provided as MATLAB .mat files containing 2D gridded arrays corresponding to the global extent.

Note: All figures presented in the dataset description can be reproduced using the accompanying MATLAB script plot_global_trends_ERA5_Zmaps.m, which loads the .mat files and generates the global Z-value maps for each variable.

metadata.title: Lund University Global Drought Dataset (LUGD), 1981–2025: Weekly 0.1° SPEI with Accumulation Timescales from 1 Week to 48 Months – Southern Hemisphere
metadata.description:
The SPEI was calculated for 12 accumulation timescales ranging from 1 week to 48 months. The temporal index represents a pseudo-weekly time step, defined as four time steps per month starting on the 1st, 9th, 16th, and 23rd day of each month.

Daily precipitation (P) was obtained from the Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation dataset (MSWEP V2), which combines rain-gauge observations, satellite retrievals, and atmospheric reanalysis products to produce globally gridded precipitation estimates at 0.1° spatial resolution from 1979 to 2025. Daily potential evapotranspiration (PET) was obtained from the Bristol global PET dataset, which provides global PET estimates at 0.1° spatial resolution for the period 1981–2025. Bristol PET is calculated using the FAO Penman–Monteith formulation based on meteorological variables from ERA5-Land.

The climatic water balance was first calculated as D=P−PET, for accumulation timescales of 1 week, 2 weeks, and 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, and 48 months, capturing drought variability from short-term events to multi-year conditions. The accumulated water balance series was then fitted to a three-parameter log-logistic distribution and transformed to a standardized normal distribution N(0,1), i.e. SPEI, following the method of Vicente-Serrano et al. (2010).

metadata.title: Monthly climatologies of GHI and DNI for Cyprus retrieved from satellite measurements
metadata.description:
The published dataset has been created using high quality and fine resolution satellite retrievals of aerosols  from the MIDAS climatology (Gkikas et al., 2021), as well as information for clouds from CMSAF (Pfeifroth et al., 2017). The surface solar radiation has been simulated using the libRatran radiative transfer model (Mayer and Kylling, 2005). More information about the methodology used to create the dataset can be found in the corresponding study:

I. Fountouakis et al., (2021): Effects of aerosols and clouds on the levels of surface solar radiation and solar energy in Cyprus, submitted to the journal Remote Sensing

metadata.title: ERA5–SARAH-3 Meteorological Cutouts for Renewable Energy Modelling with PyPSA-Spain
metadata.description:
Description

This repository provides a 30-year collection of meteorological cutouts for renewable energy assessment and power system modelling in the Iberian Peninsula and nearby offshore areas. The datasets combine ERA5 meteorological information with satellite-derived solar radiation data from SARAH-3 and have been specifically prepared for use with PyPSA-Spain and the atlite framework.

ERA5 provides the meteorological variables required for wind, temperature-dependent and hydrological modelling, while SARAH-3 supplies the direct and diffuse surface solar radiation fields used for photovoltaic generation modelling.

The cutouts are defined on a regular latitude–longitude grid with a spatial resolution of 0.3° × 0.3° (approximately 30 km) and hourly temporal resolution. SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are retained over land and offshore grid cells located within 50 km of the coastline.

All variables are integrated into a common atlite-compatible NetCDF structure, enabling the modelling of wind, solar and other weather-dependent energy-system processes.

Data Sources

ERA5

ERA5 is the global atmospheric reanalysis produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) within the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S).

ERA5 provides most of the meteorological variables contained in these cutouts. The variables derived from ERA5 are:

  • height: Surface elevation
  • wnd100m: Wind speed at 100 m above ground level
  • wnd_azimuth: Wind direction information derived from the 100 m wind field
  • roughness: Surface roughness length
  • influx_toa: Top-of-atmosphere solar radiation
  • albedo: Surface albedo
  • temperature: Air temperature at 2 m above ground level
  • soil temperature: Soil temperature at level 4
  • runoff: Surface and subsurface runoff information used by the atlite hydrological workflow

Source:

https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/

SARAH-3

Solar radiation data are obtained from the Surface Solar Radiation Data Set – Heliosat, Edition 3 (SARAH-3), developed by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF).

SARAH-3 provides satellite-derived surface solar radiation information over the study region. The following radiation variables are derived from SARAH-3:

  • influx_direct: Direct surface solar radiation
  • influx_diffuse: Diffuse surface solar radiation

The cutouts also include solar position variables calculated during data processing:

  • solar_altitude: Solar altitude angle
  • solar_azimuth: Solar azimuth angle

Within these cutouts, SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are provided over land and offshore grid cells located at most 50 km from the coastline. For marine grid cells located farther than 50 km from the coast, these variables are set to NaN.

Source:

https://doi.org/10.5676/EUM_SAF_CM/SARAH/V003

Terms of Use

These cutouts contain processed meteorological data derived from ERA5, provided by the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), and SARAH-3, provided by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF).

SARAH-3

Contains modified EUMETSAT CM SAF SARAH-3 data (2026).

metadata.description: Model code and simulation output for a global sensitivity study of earthen berms in dryland valleys. metadata.title: MMDEC: Multimodal Maritime Dataset on the English Channel
metadata.description:
The rapid proliferation of tracking sensors—ranging from vessel and vehicle tracking systems to smartwatches, cameras, and Earth observation sensors—has led to an unprecedented influx of high-frequency, high-volume data. Yet, despite this abundance, many trajectories remain incomplete, contain errors, or are entirely missing. A vast reservoir of tracking data remains unexplored or underutilized, holding valuable insights that could enhance monitoring and decision-making.

The MUlti-Sensor Inferred Trajectories (MUSIT) project is dedicated to unlocking this potential by integrating and refining data from heterogeneous sources. Through advanced AI algorithms and spatio-temporal methodologies, MUSIT reconstructs and enhances trajectories, filling in gaps and minimizing errors to provide a more accurate and insightful picture of moving objects’ behavior.

By fusing multi-sensor data, MUSIT not only improves trajectory accuracy but also enriches it with semantic information, adding context and meaning to movement patterns. The project explores cross-domain representation models within the ICT sector, pushing the boundaries of what is possible in trajectory analysis.

 

---

 

The MMDEC dataset contains data from various sources and sensors (AIS, satellite images, meteorology, oceanography, ports locations, marine protected areas,...) within an Area of Interest (AOI) covering the western Celtic Sea, the English Channel, and a part of the North Sea, and a 3-month time from July 1, 2023, to October 1, 2023.

metadata.title: The effects of light intensity and flow speed on biogeochemical variability within a fringing coral reef in Onna-son, Okinawa, Japan
metadata.description: Global warming and ocean acidification are driving gradual declines in seawater dissolved oxygen concentrations and pH. Predicting how these changes will affect shallow, near-shore environments including coral reefs is challenging due to high natural variability on both spatial (10 m to km) and temporal (diel to seasonal) scales. To make predictions, it is first necessary to identify and quantify the drivers of this natural variability. While significant efforts have been devoted to characterising the influence from metabolic processes on coral reef seawater chemistry, less attention has been devoted to physical processes such as flow speed and light intensity. Here, we measured seawater flow, photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), pH, and dissolved oxygen (DO) at three reef habitats (reef flat, lagoon, and outflow channel) in a fringing coral reef system in Okinawa, Japan for a duration of 3 weeks in October of 2019. During the study, circulation was primarily wave-driven with mean flow speeds ranging from 14-26 cm/s. Flow direction became increasingly consistent at higher flow speeds, which traced visual patterns in the benthos observed from satellite imagery. Multiple linear regression models of daytime changes in pH and DO versus daily mean flow speed and PAR described 25-74% of the observed variability across all sites while at night, flow speed alone accounted for 35-69% of the observed variability. The results demonstrate that flow speed, trajectory, and PAR play important and variable roles in controlling biogeochemical variability within coral reefs and need to be considered in assessing their vulnerability to global climate change.

metadata.title: Cartographie fine de la couverture de Macrocystis pyrifera sur l'archipel de Kerguelen à partir d'images Sentinel-2 acquises en 2020
metadata.description:
Cette donnée représente une cartographie fine de la couverture de Macrocystis pyrifera (MP) sur l’archipel de Kerguelen à partir d'images Sentinel-2 acquises en 2020. Etant donné la proximité de MP avec Durvilleae Antarctica (DA) (du point de vue de leur signature spectrale), les résultats intègrent aussi cette dernière.

Les données d’Observation de la Terre utilisées sont les images satellitaires libres et gratuites Sentinel-2 (A et B). La chaîne de traitement mise en place est entièrement basée sur le langage R. Les téléchargements et prétraitements ont été effectués grâce à une librairie complète, sen2r, créée par Luigi Ranghetti (Ranghetti et al., 2020).
Les résultats de détection des algues brunes à partir de la chaîne sont proches de l’exhaustivité avec un Kappa global de 0.993. C’est l’indice du grNDVI de Wang et al. (2007) qui a été utilisé pour réaliser ces produits.

Un produit final utilisable par un utilisateur n’ayant pas forcément été initié à la télédétection a été favorisé. Dans ce but une couche shapefile représentant la présence moyenne d’algue brune sur la zone (c.à.d. sur toute l’étendue temporelle disponible) est ici mise à disposition.

Cette donnée a été réalisée dans le cadre du stage de master2 d'Alexis Pré co-encadré par l'UMR Espace-Dev à la station SEAS-OI et le service SIG des Terres Australes et Antarctiques Françaises.

metadata.title: FluxCubes30: A 30-m, 27-year (1999–2025) global flux-tower-centered GPP spatial cutout dataset based on optimal footprint and cross-calibrated Landsat observations
metadata.description:
As Earth system science advances into the deep-learning era, geoscience foundation models require high-resolution training samples with explicit spatial context. To complement point-scale eddy-covariance ground observations, we present FluxCubes30, a global flux-tower-centered, high-resolution (30 m), 27-year (1999–2025) gross primary productivity (GPP) spatial cutout dataset.

This dataset encompasses 404 core sites across major regional flux networks. It was generated by harmonizing Landsat 7, 8, and 9 observations through a cross-calibration algorithm to drive an ecosystem light-use-efficiency (eLUE) model. The model is forced by Landsat-based Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) and top-of-atmosphere photosynthetically active radiation (PAR_TOA). The production pipeline incorporates a dynamic footprint optimization algorithm and propagates pixel-level 95% confidence uncertainty for each 30 m grid cell.

As an AI-ready spatiotemporal benchmark, FluxCubes30 reconstructs decadal carbon-sink histories for sites with short operational records, captures micro-refugia following extreme disturbances, and preserves agricultural irrigation signals that are typically smoothed out by coarse-resolution products.

Dataset Characteristics

  • Temporal Coverage: 1999–2025.

  • Spatial Unit: 7 km x 7 km site-centered cutouts.

  • Spatial Resolution: 30 m.

  • Coordinate Reference System: WGS84 geographic coordinates, EPSG:4326.

  • Main Output Variables: EVI, eLUE-modeled GPP (g C m-2 d-1), and Propagated GPP Uncertainty.

File Organization The root directory contains the master index, documentation, and compressed archives organized by regional flux networks (e.g., JapanFlux.rar, Demo_Sites.rar). For networks that contains a substantial number of sites (e.g., AmeriFlux), the network is further divided into sub-files names as  NETWORK + (SITE_NAME_INITIAL_LETTER).zip (e.g., AmeriFlux (A).zip).

  • IndexMeta.csv: The master metadata index used for site lookup, model parameters, and relative file paths.

  • FluxCubes30_User_Guide_v1.0.pdf: The comprehensive product user guide.

  • DataRead_Example.R: An R script demonstrating how to batch read the metadata, CSVs, and multi-band GeoTIFFs.

Within each individual site folder (e.g., AU-Ade):

  • <Site_ID>_timeseries.csv: Site-level time-series containing Landsat observation-level EVI, PAR, GPP_EC, GPP_eLUE, and uncertainty bounds.

  • <Site_ID>.png: A four-panel quick-look visualization.

  • spatial_cutouts/: A directory containing three multi-band GeoTIFF cubes (EVI, GPP_eLUE, GPP_uncertainty) and a band_date_index.csv mapping each GeoTIFF band to its specific observation date.

Usage Notes & Scaling Factors To optimize storage, all dynamic spatial cubes are stored as signed 16-bit integers. The NoData value across all rasters is -32768. Users must apply the following scaling factors to recover physical values before analysis:

  • EVI: Divide raw values by 10000.

  • GPP_eLUE: Divide raw values by 100 (Unit: g C m-2 d-1).

  • GPP_uncertainty: Divide raw values by 100 (Unit: g C m-2 d-1).

For a detailed description of the model parameterization, quality control, and data reading examples, please refer to the attached User Guide.

metadata.title: Global rRNA Universal Metabarcoding of Plankton database (GRUMP)
metadata.description:
We introduce the Global rRNA Universal Metabarcoding Plankton database (McNichol and Williams et al., 2025), 1194 samples covering extensive latitudinal and longitudinal transects, including depth profiles, in all major ocean basins from 2003-2020. Unfractionated (>0.2 µm) seawater DNA samples were amplified using the 515Y/926R universal 3-domain rRNA primers, quantifying the relative abundance of amplicon sequencing variants (ASVs) from Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukaryotes with one denominator. Thus, the ratio of any organism (or group) to any other in a sample is directly comparable to the ratio in any other sample within the dataset, irrespective of gene copy number differences. This obviates a problem in prior global studies that used size-fractionation and different primers for prokaryotes and eukaryotes, precluding comparisons between abundances across size fractions or domains.

Sample Collection Samples were collected by multiple collaborations, which used slightly different sample collection techniques. These collection techniques will be outlined by individual cruise.

For the Atlantic Meridional Transects (AMT 19 and AMT 20), 5–10 L of whole seawater was collected from the sea surface using a Niskin bottle and was then filtered onto 0.22 µm Sterivex Durapore filters (Millipore Sigma, Burlington, MA, USA). Samples were collected by Stephanie Sargeant and Andy Rees, Plymouth Marine Laboratory (PML) as part of the Atlantic Meridional Transect (AMT) (Rees, Smyth and Brotas, 2024) research cruises 19 (2009) and 20 (2010) onboard UK research vessel RRS James Cook (JC039 and JC053 – (Rees, 2010a, 2010b). Sterivex filters were capped and stored in RNAlater® (ThermoFisher) at -80 °C until analysis.

For samples taken in the FRAM Strait (Wietz et al., 2021), whole seawater was collected using Remote Access Samplers (RAS; McLane) on seafloor moorings F4-S-1, HG-IV-S-1, Fevi-34, and EGC-5. Moorings were operated within the FRAM / HAUSGARTEN Observatory covering the West Spitsbergen Current, central Fram Strait, and East Greenland Current as well as the Marginal Ice Zone. RAS performed continuous, autonomous sampling from July 2016 – August 2017 in programmed intervals (weekly to monthly). Nominal deployment depths were 30 m (F4, HG-IV), 67 m (Fevi), and 80 m (EGC). However, vertical movements in the water column resulted in variable actual sampling depths, ranging from 25 to 150 m. Per sampling event, two lots of 500 mL of whole seawater was pumped into bags containing mercuric chloride for fixation. After RAS recovery, the two samples per sampling event were pooled, and approximately 700 mL of pooled water was filtered onto 0.22 µm Sterivex cartridges. Filtered samples were stored at -20°C until DNA extraction. For MOSAiC whole seawater was collected from the upper water via a rosette sampler equipped with Niskin bottles through a hole in the sea ice next to the RV Polarstern. If possible, duplicate samples, with two Niskins per depth were collected during the up-casts near the surface (~5 m), 10 m, chlorophyll max (~20–40 m), 50 m, and 100m. in these Niskins and. 1-4 litres was filtered on to Sterivex-filters (0.22 µm pore size) using a peristaltic pump in a temperature controlled lab at 1°C in the dark, only using red light. The number of Sterivex-filters used per sampling event varied between two during Polar Night and 3-4 during Polar day, depending on the biomass found in the samples. Sterivex filters with were stored at -80°C until further processing took place in the laboratory.

GEOTRACES cruises (Anderson et al., 2014), including transects GA02, GA03, GA10, and GP13, collected whole seawater using a Niskin bottle, filtering 100 mL of whole seawater between the surface and 5601 m onto 0.2 µm 25 mm polycarbonate filters. After filtration, 3 mL of sterile preservation solution (10 mM Tris, pH 8.0; 100 mM EDTA; 0.5 M NaCl) was added, and samples were stored in cryovials at -80°C until DNA extraction.

During the 2017 and 2019 SCOPE (Simons Collaboration on Ocean Processes and Ecology) - Gradients cruises, 0.7-4 L of whole seawater was collected at sea using the ships underway system, which is approximately 7 m below the surface, as well as the rosette sampler for depths between 15 – 125 m by Mary R. Gradoville, Brittany Stewart, and Esther Wing (Zehr lab) (Gradoville et al., 2020). This water was filtered onto 0.22 µm 25 mm Supor membrane filters (Pall Corporation, New York) and stored at -80°C until DNA extraction.

The collection of Southern Ocean transects include the 1) IND-2017 dataset, which were taken during the Totten Glacier-Sabrina Coast voyage in 2017 as part of the CSIRO Marine National Facility RV Investigator Voyage IN2017_V01, 2) the Kerguelen-Axis Marine Science program (K-AXIS) in 2016 on the Australian Antarctic Division RV Aurora Australis 2015/16 voyage 3, 3) Global Ocean Ship-based Hydrographic Investigations Program (GO-SHIP) P15S cruise in 2016 as a part of the CSIRO Marine National Facility RV Investigator Voyage IN2016_V03, and 4) the Heard Earth-Ocean-Biosphere Interactions (HEOBI) voyage in 2016 as part of the CSIRO Marine National Facility RV Investigator Voyage IN2016_V01. For these cruises, 2 L of whole seawater was filtered onto 0.22 µm Sterivex-GP polyethersulfone membrane filters (Millipore). This water was collected from the ships underway during IND-2017 by Amaranta Focardi (Paulsen Lab, Macquarie University), from between 5 and 4625 m during K-AXIS by Bruce Deagle and Lawrence Clarke (Australian Antarctic Division), from between 5 and 6015 m during GO-SHIP P15S by Eric J. Raes, Swan LS Sow and Gabriela Paniagua Cabarrus (Environmental Genomics Team, CSIRO Environment), Nicole Hellessey (University of Tasmania) and Bernhard Tschitschko (University of New South Wales), and from between 7-3579 m during HEOBI by Thomas Trull (CSIRO Environment). After filtration, samples were stored at -80°C until analysis.

As part of GO-SHIP, there were several additional transects (i.e., I08S, I09N, P16 S/N), including some that also traversed into the Southern Ocean (i.e., I08S, P16S) or Arctic Ocean (P16N). For I08S and I09N, 2 L of whole seawater was filtered onto 0.22 µm 25 mm filters (Supor® hydrophilic polyethersulfone membrane) by Norm Nelson (I08S) and Elisa Halewood (I09N), UCSB, as part of the U.S. Global Ocean Ship-based Hydrographic Investigations Program aboard the R/V Roger Revelle during the cruises in 2007. Sucrose lysis buffer was added to filters, which were then stored at -80°C until DNA extraction. For P16N and P16S, samples were collected at various depths by Elisa Halewood and Meredith Meyers (Carlson Lab, UCSB) onto 0.22 µm 25 mm Supor filters during two latitudinal transects of the Pacific Ocean in 2005 and 2006 as part of the GO-SHIP repeat hydrography program (then known as CLIVAR). Samples were stored as partially extracted lysates in sucrose lysis buffer at -80°C until DNA extraction.

Finally, for samples from the Production Observations Through Another Trans-Latitudinal Oceanic Expedition (POTATOE) cruise, 20 L of whole seawater was collected from the sea surface between 1-2 m and filtered onto 0.22 µm Sterivex® filters during a “ship of opportunity” cruise on the RVIB Nathaniel B Palmer in 2003 (Baldwin et al., 2005). Sterivex filters were stored dry at -80°C until DNA extraction.

All datasets had corresponding environmental data. We included date, time, latitude, longitude, depth, temperature, salinity, oxygen for all transects, and nutrient data where available. However, some cruises have other environmental data which can be found at the British Oceanographic Data Centre (https://www.bodc.ac.uk/) for both AMT cruises, at the CSIRO National Collections and Marine Infrastructure Data Trawler (https://www.cmar.csiro.au/data/trawler/survey_details.cfm?survey=IN2016_V01) for IND-2017 and HEOBI, at the CLIVAR and Carbon Hydrographic Data Office (https://cchdo.ucsd.edu/) for GO-SHIP P15S, P16N and P16S, at the Australian Antarctic Division Datacenter (https://data.aad.gov.au/aadc/voyages/) for the K-AXIS cruise, at (https://doi.org/10.6075/J0CCHLY9https://doi.org/10.6075/J0CCHLY9) for the I08S and I09N cruises, at the MGDS (Marine Geoscience Data System: https://www.marine-geo.org) for POTATOE, at (https://scope.soest.hawaii.edu/data/gradients/documents/) for both SCOPE-Gradients cruises, and at PANGAEA (https://www.pangaea.de/) for FRAM Strait and MOSAiC. Finally, we have also used satellite data to estimate the euphotic zone depth where photosynthetic available radiation (PAR) is 1% of its surface value (Lee et al., 2007; Kirk, 2010). We approximated the euphotic zone depth using the light attenuation at 490nm (Kd 490) product and the relationship Z eu(1%) = 4.6/Kd 490. We also used the script Longhurst-Province-Finder (https://github.com/thechisholmlab/Longhurst-Province-Finder) to assign each sample to the Longhurst Province in which it was sampled in, another useful column to help subset data and investigate specific regions of the ocean.

DNA Extraction For AMT cruises, DNA was isolated using the Qiagen AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini kit (Hilden, Germany) with modifications to be compatible with RNAlater® and to disrupt cell membranes (Varaljay et al., 2015). Briefly, the filter was removed from the Sterivex housing and immersed in RLT+ buffer that had been amended with 10 µl 1N NaOH per 1ml buffer, followed by a 2 minute agitation in a Mini-Beadbeater-96 (Biospec Inc., Bartlesville, OK, USA) with 0.1- and 0.5 mm sterile glass beads (BioSpec).

DNA was isolated from the FRAM Strait and MOSAiC samples using a PowerWater kit (QIAGEN, Germany).

DNA from GEOTRACES was isolated and purified using a phenol/chloroform-based method by Steven Biller, Paul Berube, Keven Dooley, and Medline Williams (Chisholm lab, MIT) (Biller et al., 2018).

DNA from the SCOPE-Gradients cruises was isolated using the extraction method described by (Gradoville et al., 2020).

DNA from IND-2017, K-AXIS, HEOBI, and P15S was isolated and purified in 2017-2018, using a modified phenol:chloroform:isoamyl based extraction protocol of the DNeasy PowerWater Sterivex Kit (Brown et al., 2018; Raes et al., 2018). HEOBI samples were extracted by Swan LS Sow and Jodie van de Kamp in 2017 (Environmental Genomics Team, CSIRO Environment). P15S samples were extracted by DNA was isolated and purified by Swan LS Sow, Eric J. Raes, Bronwyn Holmes and Jodie van de Kamp in 2017-2018 (Environmental Genomics Team, CSIRO Environment). K-AXIS samples were extracted by Swan LS Sow and Bronwyn Holmes in 2017 (Environmental Genomics Team, CSIRO Environment). IND-2017 samples were extracted by Swan LS Sow (Environmental Genomics Team, CSIRO Environment).

For I08S, I09N, P16N, P16S, and POTATOE, the DNA was isolated and purified using the method described in (Boström et al., 2004), with modifications detailed in (Manganelli et al., 2009; Signori et al., 2014). An additional bead-beating step was added using 0.1mm glass beads (Biospec 11079101) for two minutes at maximum speed on a VWR Analog Vortex Mixer (58816-121). DNA was precipitated in low-EDTA buffer to protect from degradation and quantified using PicoGreen dsDNA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific). A detailed extraction protocol is available at https://osf.io/k4c5u. To minimize potential contamination, all DNA extracts were done in molecular biology-grade plasticware with filter tips, and all PCR steps were conducted in plasticware that had been exposed to UV radiation for at least 10 minutes to inactivate any contaminating DNA templates.

Sequencing methods and pipeline Relative abundance information was generated by PCR amplification of extracted DNA using the 515Y/926R universal primer pair (Parada, Needham and Fuhrman, 2016) which amplify both 16S and 18S simultaneously. All samples except for FRAM, for which raw sequences were supplied, were amplified using the protocol available at (https://www.protocols.io/view/fuhrman-lab-515f-926r-16s-and-18s-rrna-gene-sequen-vb7e2rn). Briefly, PCR reaction reagent master mix was made by adding 12 µl of PCR water (VWR), 10 µl of 5’ Master Mix (0.5 U taq, 45 mM Kcl, 2.5 mM Mg2+, 200 µM each dNTP), 1.5 µl of 1:1, 515F:926R barcoded primer mix (0.3 mM each primer) and 1 µl of DNA per reaction for a final volume of 25 µl. For the samples taken on the I8S, I9N, P16N, P16S, AMT-19, AMT-20, POTATOE, GA02, GA03, GA10, GP13, GRADIENTS 2, and GRADIENTS 3 cruises, 5' master mix (Quantabio) was used, while for samples taken on cruises P15S, K-AXIS, IND-2017, and HEOBI, GoTaq master mix (Promega) was used and finally, for samples taken during the FRAM Strait and MOSAiC cruises U Phusion Polymerase (Thermo Fisher, Germany) was used. PCR was performed under the following conditions: initial denaturing at 95°C for 120 seconds, followed by 30 cycles of 95°C for 45 seconds, 50°C for 45 seconds, and then 68 °C for 90 seconds, and then a final elongation step at 68°C for 300 seconds. PCR products were then stored at 4 °C before being cleaned using the Agencourt AMPure XP PCR purification protocol, and then DNA concentration was quantified using the Pico-Green dsDNA Quant-iT Assay Kit. Given we used barcoded primers, samples were then pooled, and then this pool was cleaned and concentrated with SPRIselect (Beckman Coulter B23317) beads, and then this cleaned pool was quantified using the Qubit dsDNA HS Assay Kit. Finally, the ratio of 16S:18S was calculated with the Bioanalyzer Chip: High Sensitivity DNA Kit.

Most sequencing was done at Tufts Medical School using HiSeq Rapid Run technology (2 x 250 bp), except for FRAM and MOSAiC which were sequenced using MiSeq technology (2 x 300 bp) and GA03/GP13 which were sequenced at USC’s genome sequencing center Molecular Genomics Core, with the same parameters as Tufts. Sequences were demultiplexed manually (https://github.com/jcmcnch/demux-notes) and denoised to amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) with a custom analysis pipeline based on QIIME2 and DADA2 (Callahan et al., 2016; Bolyen et al., 2019) which can be found on GitHub (https://github.com/jcmcnch/eASV-pipeline-for-515Y-926R). The main difference between this pipeline and standard workflows is that it contains an initial 16S/18S splitting step, which is accomplished using bbsplit against curated 16S and 18S databases derived from SILVA and PR2. This results in two ''pools'' of data (16S and 18S rRNA) that are then denoised separately, and later merged if desired. Note that standard pipelines require a merging of forward and reverse reads where they overlap, which for these primers leads to removal of all 18S sequences because their forward and reverse 18S reads do not overlap. We used a universal trim length of 220 for forward and 180 for reverse 18S reads so that ASVs could be directly compared to each other across cruises (also because forward and reverse 18S reads do not overlap, so we needed a single overall length and concatenated forward + reverse reads to create intercomparable ASVs). The 16S forward and reverse do overlap, so trimming of them is not necessary, and 16S amplicons fully span the amplified region. Two corrections were made to both 16S and 18S ASV tables before they were merged. The first adjusts for a known bias against longer 18S sequences during Illumina sequencing (Yeh et al., 2021) and the second adjusts for random variations in sample quality using the DADA2 output statistics. Briefly, bioanalyzer traces were taken for all samples except the FRAM Strait and MOSAiC samples, to determine the 16S and 18S bioanalyzer fractions prior to sequencing, which was calculated by:

Bioanalyzer 16S fraction= (16S bioanalyzer (nmol/L))/(16S+18S bioanalyzer (nmol/L) )

Bioanalyzer 18S fraction= (18S bioanalyzer (nmol/L))/(16S+18S bioanalyzer (nmol/L) )

and this was considered the “expected” outcome from the sequencing run. The same fractions were then calculated after the bbsplit step (which sorts 16S and 18S sequences into separate bins) in the analysis pipeline (Figure 1), using the number of 16S and 18S sequences measured by the sequencer.

These ratios were calculated by:

16S sequence fraction= (Total 16S sequences)/(Total 16S+total 18S sequences)

18S sequence fraction= (Total 18S sequences)/(Total 16S+total 18S sequences)

Once both the bioanalyzer ratios and the sequence ratios for 16S and 18S were obtained, we then calculated the correction factor for each sequence type by:

16S correction factor= (16S bioanalyzer fraction)/(16S sequence fraction)

18S correction factor= (18S bioanalyzer fraction)/(18S sequence fraction)

Finally, both the 16S and 18S data were multiplied by their respective correction factor using this script (https://github.com/Nwilliams96/Project-2-Universal-Primer-Pipeline), and for FRAM Strait and MOSAiC data, which did not have bioanalyzer traces, we used the same correction factor used for the Southern Ocean samples, as it was predicted they would have a similar level of Eukaryotic bias. The final dataset contains merged abundance information from both 16S and 18S ASVs using the same denominator. Correction factors and calculations are available in Supplementary Table 1 (McNichol and Williams et al., 2025).

In the final dataset, meta barcode information was derived from organisms that range from small Bacteria and Archaea (16S) to protists (photosynthetic and non-photosynthetic; 16S chloroplasts & nuclear 18S) as well as larger planktonic organisms such as arthropods, salps, and jellyfish (nuclear 18S) which are derived from tissue fragments, larvae, eggs, etc. that were captured on 0.2 µm filters. Data users should note that most photosynthetic protists (with the exception of dinoflagellates) will be represented by both chloroplast 16S and nuclear 18S. The taxonomy levels are joined from three databases: PR2 (Vaulot, 2023), SILVA (Quast et al., 2012) and ProPortal (Kelly et al., 2012). The levels are as follows: Domain – SILVA Level 1 Taxonomy and PR2 Level 1 Taxonomy, Supergroup – PR2 Level 2 Taxonomy, Division – PR2 Level 3 Taxonomy, Phylum – SILVA Level 2 Taxonomy, Class - SILVA Level 3 Taxonomy and PR2 Level 4 Taxonomy, Order - SILVA Level 4 Taxonomy and PR2 Level 5 Taxonomy, Family - SILVA Level 5 Taxonomy and PR2 Level 6 Taxonomy, Genus - SILVA Level 6 Taxonomy and PR2 Level 7 Taxonomy, Species - SILVA Level 7 Taxonomy and PR2 Level 8 Taxonomy, Proportal_ASV_Ecotype – ProPortal assignment.

Scripts necessary to exactly reproduce the analysis are available at https://github.com/jcmcnch/Global-rRNA-Univeral-Metabarcoding-of-Plankton, with modifications to the merge script which can be found at https://github.com/Nwilliams96/Project-2-Universal-Primer-Pipeline-Modifications.

metadata.title: Northern Hemisphere historical in-situ Snow Water Equivalent dataset (NorSWE, 1979-2021)
metadata.description:
Description (in English, French follows)

The Northern Hemisphere historical in situ snow water equivalent dataset (NorSWE) includes snow water equivalent (SWE, or water equivalent of snow cover by WMO, 2018) observations from manual snow surveys, snow pillows, automated passive gamma radiation sensors (GMON), and from airborne passive gamma radiation surveys for the period 1979-2021 compiled from nine different sources covering North America, Russia, Finland, Norway and Switzerland. Exceptionally, to expand coverage over Europe we also include single point manual SWE observations (type_mes=1) from eleven sites in Switzerland. SWE is the primary variable of interest. Snow depth (SD) is included when available and derived bulk snow density is calculated from SD and SWE. NorSWE is described in detail in Mortimer and Vionnet (in prep). Sites intersecting the Global Mountain Biodiversity Assessment (GMBA) Mountain Inventory v2 (Snethlage et al., 2022; https://www.earthenv.org/mountains) with a 25 km buffer or a 2° slope mask derived from the GETASSE30 DEM are assigned a mountain mask flag of 1.

Processing and quality control generally follows that described in Vionnet et al. (2021). Quality control involved range thresholding: ranges for SD, SWE and bulk density are 0-3 m (0-8 m where mmask = 1), 0-3000 kg m-2 (0-8000 kg m-2 where mmask =1), and 25-700 kg m-3. Where station elevation was not included in the original station metadata or it was deemed to be erroneous, elevation was taken from the United States Geological Survey’s National Elevation Dataset (Gesh et al., 2022). NorSWE was originally compiled to support evaluation of gridded SWE products over the modern satellite era (1979-2021) and focused on observations from snow course and airborne gamma SWE. In v2, we expanded the dataset to include automated data over North America to support hydrological modelling applications. In v3, we added data from Norway and Switzerland (Marty, 2020).

NorSWE is provided as a netCDF (NorSWE-NorEEN_1979-2021_v3.nc, compressed into zip file) and following the conventions of the Canadian Snow Water Equivalent Dataset (CanSWE) described in Vionnet et al. (2021) with the addition of a mountain mask variable. The final dataset includes 10 153 locations spanning the years 1979 to 2021.

 

Description (Francais)

Cet ensemble de données de l’Équivalent en Eau de la couverture Neigeuse (EEN, OMM, 2018) comprend des observations manuelles des lignes de neige, des mesures automatiques des coussins à neige et des capteurs gamma passif (GMON), et des estimations de l’EEN issues de mesures de radiation gamma aéroportée pour la période 1979-2021. Cette base de données compile des données issues de neuf sources couvrant l’Amérique du Nord, la Russie et la Finlande. L’EEN est la quantité d’intérêt principal. L’information sur la hauteur de neige (HN) est incluse lorsqu’elle est disponible et la masse volumique moyenne du manteau neigeux est calculée à partir de l’HN et de l’EEN. NorEEN est décrit en détail dans Mortimer and Vionnet (en préparation). Les sites montagneux sont indiqués par le code mmask (valeur = 1). Le masque de montagne combine le Global Mountain Biodiversity Assessment (GMBA) Mountain Inventory v2 (Snethlage et al., 2022; https://www.earthenv.org/mountains) (plus une zone tampon de 25 km) et un masque de topographie complexe (2°) calculée selon le modèle numérique de terrain (MNT) GETASSE30.

Le traitement des données et le contrôle de qualité (CQ) suivent la méthodologie proposée par Vionnet et al. (2021). Pour le CQ, les observations en dehors de plages de valeurs prédéterminées ont été exclues : HN 0-3 m (0-8 m mmask = 1), EEN 0-3000 kg m-2 (0-8000 kg m-2 mmask = 1), et masse volumique moyenne du manteau neigeux 25-700 kg m-3. Si l’altitude de la station manquait ou était erronée, l’altitude du site a été extraite du fichier national d’élévation de la Commission Géologique des USA (Gesh et al., 2022). Originalement, la base de données décrite dans ce document a été mise en place pour évaluer de produits d’EEN sur grille d’échelle moyennes à large (4-50 km) couvrant la période moderne de la télédétection satellitaire (1979-2021). Pour cette raison, seules les observations des lignes de neige et les estimations de EEN dérivées de mesures de radiation gamma aéroportées avaient été incluses dans la version 1. Pour la version 2, les données historiques des stations automatiques couvrants l’Amérique du Nord ont été incluses en support des applications hydrologiques. Pour la version 3, les données historiques des stations de stations en Norvège et la Swisse ont été incluses (Marty, 2020).

La base de données est distribuée au format NetCDF (NorSWE-NorEEN_1979-2021_v3.nc, comprimée dans une archive zip) selon les conventions de la base de données historiques canadiennes d’Équivalent en Eau de la Neige (CanEEN, Vionnet et al., 2021) et comprenant une variable supplémentaire indiquant les sites montagneux. La base de données inclut des mesures issues de 10,153 sites uniques durant la période de 1979 à 2021.
