metadata.title: Global AIS-based Apparent Fishing Effort Dataset
metadata.description:
Overview

This dataset contains version 3.0 (March 2025 release) of the Global Fishing Watch apparent fishing effort dataset. Data is available for 2012-2024 and based on positions of >190,000 unique automatic identification system (AIS) devices on fishing vessels, of which up to ~96,000 are active in a given year. Fishing vessels are identified via a machine learning model, vessel registry databases, and manual review by GFW and regional experts. Vessel time is measured in hours, calculated by assigning to each AIS position the amount of time elapsed since the previous AIS position of the vessel. The time is counted as apparent fishing hours if the GFW fishing detection model - a neural network machine learning model - determines the vessel is engaged in fishing behavior during that AIS position. 

Data are spatially binned into grid cells that measure 0.01 or 0.1 degrees on a side; the coordinates defining each cell are provided in decimal degrees (WGS84) and correspond to the lower-left corner. Data are available in the following formats: 

  1. Daily apparent fishing hours by flag state and gear type at 100th degree resolution
  2. Monthly apparent fishing hours by flag state and gear type at 10th degree resolution
  3. Daily apparent fishing hours by MMSI at 10th degree resolution

The fishing effort dataset is accompanied by a table of vessel information (e.g. gear type, flag state, dimensions).

File structure

Fishing effort and vessel presence data are available as .csv files in daily formats. Files for each year are stored in separate .zip files. A README.txt and schema.json file is provided for each dataset version and contains the table schema and additional information. There is also a README-known-issues-v3.txt file outlining some of the known issues with the version 3 release.

Files are names according to the following convention:

  • Daily file format: 

    • [fleet/mmsi]-daily-csvs-[100/10]-v3-[year].zip

    • [fleet/mmsi]-daily-csvs-[100/10]-v3-[date].csv

  • Monthly file format: 

    • fleet-monthly-csvs-10-v3-[year].zip

    • fleet-monthly-csvs-10-v3-[date].csv

  • Fishing vessel format: fishing-vessels-v3.csv

  • README file format: README-[fleet/mmsi/fishing-vessels/known-issues]-v3.txt

File identifiers:

  • [fleet/mmsi]: Data by fleet (flag and geartype) or by MMSI

  • [100/10]: 100th or 10th degree resolution

  • [year]: Year of data included in .zip file

  • [date]: Date of data included in .csv files. For monthly data, [date]corresponds to the first date of the month

Examples: fleet-daily-csvs-100-v3-2020.zip; mmsi-daily-csvs-10-v3-2020-01-10.csv; fishing-vessels-v3.csv; README-fleet-v3.txt; fleet-monthly-csvs-10-v3-2024.zip; fleet-monthly-csvs-10-v3-2024-08-01.csv

Key documentation

  • For an overview of how GFW turns raw AIS positions into estimates of fishing hours, see this page.

  • The models used to produce this dataset were developed as part of this publication: D.A. Kroodsma, J. Mayorga, T. Hochberg, N.A. Miller, K. Boerder, F. Ferretti, A. Wilson, B. Bergman, T.D. White, B.A. Block, P. Woods, B. Sullivan, C. Costello, and B. Worm. "Tracking the global footprint of fisheries." Science 361.6378 (2018). Model details are available in the Supplementary Materials.

  • The README-known-issues-v3.txt file describing this dataset's specific caveats can be downloaded from this page. We highly recommend that users read this file in full.

  • The README-mmsi-v3.txt file, the README-fleet-v3.txt file, and the README-fishing-vessels-v3.txt files are downloadable from this page and contain the data description for (respectively) the fishing hours by MMSI dataset, the fishing hours by fleet dataset, and the vessel information file. These readmes contain key explanations about the gear types and flag states assigned to vessels in the dataset.

  • File name structure for the datafiles are available below on this page and file schema can be downloaded from this page. 

  • A FAQ describing the updates in this version and the differences between this dataset and the data available from the GFW Map and APIs is available here. 

Use Cases

The apparent fishing hours dataset is intended to allow users to analyze patterns of fishing across the world’s oceans at temporal scales as fine as daily and at spatial scales as fine as 0.1 or 0.01 degree cells. Fishing hours can be separated out by gear type, vessel flag and other characteristics of vessels such as tonnage. 

Potential applications for this dataset are broad. We offer suggested use cases to illustrate its utility. The dataset can be integrated as a static layer in multi-layered analyses, allowing researchers to investigate relationships between fishing effort and other variables, including biodiversity, tracking, and environmental data, as defined by their research objectives. 

A few example questions that these data could be used to answer:

  • What flag states have fishing activity in my area of interest?

  • Do hotspots of longline fishing overlap with known migration routes of sea turtles?

  • How does fishing time by trawlers change by month in my area of interest? Which seasons see the most trawling hours and which see the least?

Caveats

This global dataset estimates apparent fishing hours effort. The dataset is based on publicly available information and statistical classifications which may not fully capture the nuances of local fishing practices. While we manually review the dataset at a global scale and in a select set of smaller test regions to check for issues, given the scale of the dataset we are unable to manually review every fleet in every region. We recognize the potential for inaccuracies and encourage users to approach regional analyses with caution, utilizing their own regional expertise to validate findings. We welcome your feedback on any regional analysis at research@globalfishingwatch.org to enhance the dataset's accuracy.

Caveats relating to known sources of inaccuracy as well as interpretation pitfalls to avoid are described in the README-known-issues-v3.txt file available for download from this page. We highly recommend that users read this file in full. The issues described include: 

  • Data from 2024 should be considered provisional, as vessel classifications may change as more data from 2025 becomes available. 

  • MMSI is used in this dataset as the vessel identifier. While MMSI is intended to serve as the unique AIS identifier for an individual vessel, this does not always hold in practice.

  • The Maritime Identification Digits (MID), the first 3 digits of MMSI, are the only source of information on vessel flag state when the vessel does not appear on a registry. The MID may be entered incorrectly, obscuring information about an MMSI’s flag state.

  • AIS reception is not consistent across all areas and changes over time.

Alternative ways to access

  1. Query using SQL in the Global Fishing Watch public BigQuery dataset: global-fishing-watch.fishing_effort_v3

  2. Download the entire dataset from the Global Fishing Watch Data Download Portal (https://globalfishingwatch.org/data-download/datasets/public-fishing-effort)

title: Global AIS-based Apparent Fishing Effort Dataset

metadata.title: Uncertainty-aware Machine Learning Bias Correction and Filtering for OCO-2 | 2014-2024
metadata.description:
Overview


This is a dataset to explore the effect of applying a new bias correction and quality filtering approach to increase the accuracy of atmospheric CO2 measurements derived from the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2) satellite. This is not an official OCO-2 data product.

 

Data Description

The dataset contains OCO-2 retrieved XCO2 B11.2 that have been corrected and filtered with a new machine learning approach from 2014 to the end of 2024. There is one file for each year. The following variables are contained in the files:

sounding_id, xco2_ML*, xco2, xco2_x2019, xco2_quality_flag_ML*, xco2_quality_flag, bias_correction_uncert_ML*, xco2_uncertainty, latitude, longitude, time, land_water_indicator, operation_mode

* new variables that contain the new bias coorected xco2, quality flag, and uncertainty and are not contained in the official OCO-2 Lite Files.

 

xco2_ML: XCO2 Machine Learning corrected XCO2 on x2019 scale

xco2_quality_flag_ML: XCO2 ternary quality flag:  0 = best quality data, 1 = good quality data for increasing sounding throughput if needed, 2 = poor quality data (do not use)

bias_correction_uncert_ML: XCO2 bias correction uncertainty

 

For the full set of variables contained in the LiteFiles and description of each variable please refere to the data user guide of the official OCO-2 lite files: https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/OCO2_L2_Lite_FP_11.2r/summary?keywords=oco2

 

Current Bias Correction Approach


The operational bias correction method uses a multiple linear regression-like approach to adjust errors in XCO2 relative to elements of the state vector derived from the ACOS retrieval. Adjustments are currently made manually, guided by various success metrics like TCCON observation agreement, retrieval variability reduction, and flux model coherence.

 

New Bias Correction Approach


1. Computational Optimization: Replaces manual tuning with computational methods, enhancing transparency, traceability, and reproducibility.
2. Non-linear Error Modeling: Allows more flexibility in modeling retrieval errors, reducing biases, particularly in previously unusable data.
3. Independent Flux Inversion Models: Excludes flux inversion models from bias correction development, maintaining OCO-2 measurement independence.
4. Quantified Correction Uncertainties: Provides uncertainty quantification for each bias correction at the per sounding level.

 

Data Usage


If you find anything unexpected in the data please report your findings to Steffen.mauceri@jpl.nasa.gov and william.r.keely@jpl.nasa.gov so we can resolve any issues.


Additional Resources and Citation

Two preprints are currently available that describe the approach in detail and should be cited if the data is used. We will update the citations as soon as the papers are published:

https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.174164198.80749970/v1
https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.174164203.37422284/v1

title: Uncertainty-aware Machine Learning Bias Correction and Filtering for OCO-2 | 2014-2024

metadata.title: Giant kelp forests act as natural barriers to motorboat noise: Dataset
metadata.description:
Description of the data and file structure

The "GiantKelpForestData" dataset includes the following sheets:

  1. "SPL": Contains sound pressure level (SPL) data along with the following variables:
    • "year"; "area"; "transect"; "distance_hydrophone_boat" for LMM 
  2. "HydrophoneCalibration": Contains SPL values for each boat pass recorded by each hydrophone to compare the hydrophones with an ANOVA
  3. "KelpDensity": Includes the number of individual kelp counted in each quadrant (2 per transect point) to estimate density
  4. "N°Pneumatocyst": Records the height of kelp plants where pneumatocysts were counted to estimate density

The "PSD_kelp" and "PSD_control" files contain power spectral density (PSD) values for each area (kelp forest and control) for the years 2022 and 2024. For visualization, the PSD values expressed in dB were used.

Files and variables

File: PSD_kelp.csv

Description: 

Variables
  • year: year of data collection
  • area: study area (kelp forest/control area)
  • transect: transect number 
  • point: point transect where measurements were taken
  • frequency: frequency in Hz 
  • psd (uPa): psd value in uPa
  • psd (dB): psd value in dB
File: PSD_control.csv

Description: 

  • year: year of data collection
  • area: study area (kelp forest/control area)
  • transect:  transect number 
  • point: point transect where measurements were taken
  • frequency:  frequency in Hz 
  • psd (uPa): psd value in uPa
  • psd (dB): psd value in dB

File: GianKelpForestData.xlsx

Description: 

Variables
  • year:  year of data collection
  • area:  study area (kelp forest/control area)

metadata.title: Raw data : "Soil organic carbon stocks and dynamics under contrasting organic matter management practices - Results from a 65-year-old experiment in Belgium"
metadata.description:
Long-term field experiments (LTEs) are key for evaluating the long-term effect of agricultural practices on soil organic carbon (SOC) storage. In this work, we studied the long-term effect of organic matter (OM) management practices on SOC in a 65-year LTE under arable cropping in Belgium. To evaluate SOC dynamics, a time series (1959-2021) of topsoil SOC content was analyzed for three subperiods in which N fertilization remained unchanged. Topsoil and subsoil SOC stocks were calculated by the equivalent soil mass method for one individual sampling campain in 2018. 

Cattle manure (CM) application led to the most significant SOC storage, increasing topsoil SOC stock and content by approximately 20% over the long term. Other individual OM management practices – pig slurry (PS) application, cereal straw incorporation and cover crops (CC) cultivation – induced smaller, non-significant SOC increases of about 5%. Nevertheless, their combined effects were cumulative, resulting in significant SOC accruals. In contrast to the topsoil, SOC stock in the subsoil was unaffected by the OM management practices.

Annual humified C inputs calculated from the amount and quality of livestock manures and (cover) crops residues correlated strongly with SOC content in the topsoil (r=0.8), which underlines that the amount and quality of C inputs are key drivers of SOC storage. Changes in N fertilization over time and N fertilization adjustments among treatments significantly affected SOC dynamics. This highlights the complexity of interpreting time series of data from LTEs, for which the evolution of management practices over time may act as confounding factors.
references: Sail, S., Huyghebaert, B., Vanwindekens, F., Abras, M., & Hardy, B. (2025). Soil organic carbon stocks and dynamics under contrasting organic matter management practices - Results from a 65-year-old LTE in Belgium. European Journal of Agronomy (accepted)
metadata.notes:
SOC_content_data : soil organic carbon (SOC) content in the topsoil (0-25 cm) per plot from 1959 to 2021. The plots are replicated six times.

SOC_stocks_data : soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks in five soil layers (0-10, 10-25, 25-33, 33-55 and 55-80 cm) per plot (in triplicates). The stocks were calculated by the Equivalent Soil Mass method. The plots are replicated six times. 

C_inputs_data : Estimated annual humified C inputs per treatment and per OM_input_type : main crop residues, cover crops and external organic matters

Metadata : describes each column content of the files mentionned above.

title: Raw data : "Soil organic carbon stocks and dynamics under contrasting organic matter management practices - Results from a 65-year-old experiment in Belgium"

metadata.title: Global Monthly Reach-Level Water Surface Slopes from SWOT
metadata.description:
This dataset provides global, monthly, reach-level median water surface slope (WSS) derived from the SWOT Level 2 River Single-Pass Vector Product, Version C, aggregated from August 2023 through May 2025. For each reach and month, we compute the median WSS after quality control. We also provide a per-reach annual file that combines the 12 monthly values into an overall median of available months. Companion variables include potential explanatory data from SWORD v16 and GEOGLOWS retrospective daily discharge sampled on the calendar day corresponding to each reach’s monthly median WSS timestamp.

The dataset supports the manuscript: Chen, Y., Dhital, S., Cohen, S., Baruah, A., & Devi, D. (2025). Spatial and Temporal Variability in Global River Slopes from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) Satellite (under revision). These data are suitable for hydrologic and hydraulic modeling across spatial scales, particularly studies that consider temporal variability in WSS.

In this study, “Integrating connectivity and habitat availability to identify key wetlands for a critically endangered marsh passerine and guide its national-scale conservation”, published in Ornithological Applications, we analyze habitat availability at the national level for the Eastern Iberian Reed Bunting and perform several connectivity analyses to identify critical locations for its conservation.

The methods are described in detail in the methods section and in the Supplementary Material file due to limitations in the length of the paper. The data used, except for the habitat and suitability maps generated for each of the 64 wetlands, are described or available in the body of the manuscript, in the supplementary material, or are open access. The maps of each of the wetlands, as well as those of habitats, suitability, and standard deviation of variation of the 10 models predicting Eastern Iberian Reed Bunting breeding occurrence can be found in this repository.

metadata.title: LAI measurements for the assessment of successional trajectories in submontane non-serotinous Pinus spp. forests
metadata.description:
This dataset compiles field measurements obtained with a LAI-2200C Plant Canopy Analyzer (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA) to generate continuous LAI profiles and capture the structural variability of submontane Pinus spp. forests. The measurements provide detailed information on canopy gap distribution, both vertically and horizontally, allowing for the assessment of successional trajectories in non-serotinous pine stands.

Measurements were carried out by comparing light transmittance above the canopy (reference readings) and below the canopy (sample readings). The difference between the two was used to estimate LAI through radiative models assuming random leaf distribution and ellipsoidal orientation, which may not be accurate for all species or canopy types.

Instrument: LAI-2200C Plant Canopy Analyzer (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA). Spectral range: 320–490 nm. Measurement geometry: Five concentric rings with zenith angles of 7°, 23°, 38°, 53°, and 68°.

Sampling protocol: Measurements were taken every 0.5 m during floristic inventories (~900 samples). A maximum optical coverage of 270° was used to exclude the operator from the field of view. Data processing: FV2200 software (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA). Quality control: Measurements under unstable light conditions were avoided.

metadata.title: WHiCH (Western Himalaya Canopy Height) Map 2020, Pakistan
metadata.description:
The western Himalayas region is a key biodiversity hotspot and a habitat for several species. This region needs an accurate spatial assessment of tree canopy height for improved estimates of aboveground biomass, carbon sequestration, and related forest ecosystem services. In this work, we used a deep convolution neural networks model, U-Net, for estimating canopy heights using Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation Mission (GEDI) with multi-band Sentinel-2 datasets. We produced a 10 m canopy height map of the study region for 2020. Overall, we achieved a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 7.52 m and a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 5.71 m on test set, outperforming existing global canopy height models in this topographically challenging region.

metadata.title: ENCORE Insights: Country Dashboard
metadata.description:
The ENCORE Insights: Country Dashboard  enables regulators, policymakers, civil society and financial institutions to understand how each of the European Union (EU)'s 27 economies depends on nature and is exposed to nature loss as a result. It combines data about the extent of sectors and subsectors' nature dependency with data on their monetary value to help identify the most critical parts of the economy in terms of exposure to nature degradation. Importantly, it quantifies those dependencies across countries' supply chains and differentiates between their domestic and foreign exposure to allow for more targeted policy responses. 

The Country Dashboard has been developed under the EU Horizon-funded Nature-3B project by Global Canopy.

Data is accessible via the Dashboard at https://countries.encorenature.org. All underlying data is exportable directly from the dashboard interface, and the full methodology and data sourcing are documented in the accompanying Methodology Document. This DOI links to the continuous live version of the interactive dashboard.

metadata.title: High-resolution China Coastal Wetland (HCCW, 2016–2024) Version 1.0 Dataset
metadata.description:
Abstract Coastal wetlands face severe degradation under global change and high-intensity human activities. Assessing China's recent large-scale ecological restoration requires high spatial resolution data. However, existing products are inadequate for fine-scale management, suffering from coarse resolution (mostly 30 meter) or insufficient samples. We propose a novel method, Rapid Automated Multiclass Coastal Wetland Classification (RAMCWC), based on fusing spatiotemporal features and adaptive sample iteration. We produced the first 10-meter resolution annual map series of China's coastal wetlands (High-resolution China Coastal Wetland, HCCW, 2016–2024), achieving a mean annual overall accuracy of 96.11%.

Dataset Specifications This repository contains the vector dataset derived from the HCCW product.

  • Temporal Coverage: 2016–2024 (Annual)

  • Spatial Resolution of Source Data: 10 meters (Sentinel-1/2)

  • Format: Vector Polygon (.shp compressed in .zip)

  • Coordinate Reference System: WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)

Attribute Table Description The classification codes (gridcode) used in the vector files are defined as follows:

  • 1: [Salt Marsh]

  • 2: [Mangrove]

  • 3: [Tidal Flat]

metadata.title: Global hydrology and water quality data from 1980-2019, derived from the dynamical surface water quality model (DynQual) at 5 arcmin spatial resolution
metadata.description:
Global ~10km (5 arcmin) output data from the dynamical surface water quality model (DynQual) from 1980-2019, with annual and monthly temporal resolution. Simulations are made following the ISIMIP3a protocol (https://protocol.isimip.org/#/ISIMIP3a).

Output data includes:

  • Discharge (m3 s-1)
  • Channel storage (m3) 
  • Water temperature (K)
  • Total dissolved solids (TDS) load (g s-1)
  • Biological oxygen demand (BOD) load (g s-1)
  • Fecal coliform (FC) load (million cfu s-1)
  • Salinity; as indicated by TDS concentrations (mg l-1)
  • Organic pollution; as indicated by BOD concentrations (mg l-1)
  • Pathogen/bacterial pollution; as indicated by FC concentrations (cfu 100ml-1)

Note. a minimum discharge threshold of 0.1 m3 s-1 was used when computing salinity (TDS), organic (BOD) and pathogen (FC) concentrations, as uncertainties in absolute values of water availabilities have large impacts on resulting in-stream concentrations. Thus, if the the average discharge for the month was below 0.1 m3 s-1, concentrations are not calculated (assigned as NA).

Full time series of variables can be retrieved from: https://public.yoda.uu.nl/geo/UU01/OWKPGL.html. Here you can also find in-stream water quality aggregated to 0.5 degree (i.e. 30 arcmin) spatial resolution (daily, monthly and annual), which is alternatively also avaliable here: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10155483.
metadata.notes: As published in: Jones, E. R., Bierkens, M. F. P., Wanders, N., Sutanudjaja, E. H., van Beek, L. P. H., and van Vliet, M. T. H.: DynQual v1.0: a high-resolution global surface water quality model, Geosci. Model Dev., 16, 4481–4500, https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-16-4481-2023, 2023.

metadata.title: A global gridded CO2 flux dataset inferred from OCO-2 retrievals using the GONGGA inversion system (v2025)
metadata.description:
Data Description

Here we provide a global monthly CO2 flux dataset at 1° × 1° spatial resolution for the period 2014.9-2024.12. The dataset is generated using the GONGGA (Global ObservatioN-based system for monitoring Greenhouse GAs) inversion system by assimilating OCO-2 (Observing Carbon Observatory 2) v11.2r column CO2 retrievals that scaled to the WMO X2019 standard. The dataset contains fluxes from biosphere (Net Ecosystem Exchange, NEE) (both prior and posterior), ocean (both prior and posterior), biomass burning emissions and fossil fuel emissions.

We also provide the posterior model simulated values corresponding to all measurements contained in the lastest release of NOAA’s ObsPack database (obspack_co2_1_GLOBALVIEWplus_v10.1_2024-11-13 and obspack_co2_1_NRT_v10.1_2025-02-07).

Change from v2024

  • Assimilation of OCO-2 v11.2r retrievals
  • Update of prior fluxes

Data version specification

v202x.ori refers to original GONGGA flux data with 3-hourly time resolution and  2° latitude × 2.5° longitude spatial resolution, v202x refers to GONGGA flux data resampled to monthly time resolution and 1° latitude × 1° longitude spatial resolution for facilitating comparisons with other GCP inversion results.

metadata.title: Soil organic carbon and soil organic matter measurements across European habitats, including permafrost regions and global seagrass sediments
metadata.description:
A collation of datasets and derived carbon metrics is provided for soil samples with data on total soil carbon, soil organic carbon (SOC) and soil organic matter (SOM) for soil samples from Europe, permafrost regions and global seagrass sediments. Soils were sampled to different depths.

metadata.title: DFC30
metadata.description:
This repository provides datasets used in the paper "JSPSR: Joint Spatial Propagation Super-Resolution Networks for Enhancement of Bare-Earth Digital Elevation Models from Global Data".

This work selected (1) the Copernicus GLO-30 DEM (COP30) dataset as the low-resolution DSM source, (2) the Forest And Buildings removed Copernicus DEM (FABDEM) dataset and FathomDEM dataset as the comparison reference DTM source, (3) the HighResCanopyHeight dataset as the Canopy Height Map (CHM) source, and (4) the GRSS Data Fusion Contest 2022 (DFC2022 or grss_dfc_2022) dataset as the high-resolution image, DTM and land use mask sources, to build a dataset for real-world DEM SR problems, denoted here as DFC30 (DFC30.zip).

The DFC30 dataset was preprocessed to 8 m and 3 m resolution samples for network training and evaluation, denoted as DFC30-8m (DFC30_8m.zip) and DFC30-3m (DFC30_3m.zip), respectively. 

This version (v3) fixed minor flaws found in previous preprocessed datasets.

The upload process was not pleasant, so the author lost interest in downloading the data to verify its integrity. Please get in touch with the author if the file extraction fails.

metadata.title: Canopy fuel maps for Pinus pinaster in interior Spain
metadata.description:
Thirthy meter resolution maps of canopy fuel attributes for pure maritime pine polygons of the Spanish Forest Map in the Autonomous comunities of Aragon, Castilla y León, La Rioja, Madrid, Castilla la Mancha and Extremadura, Spain, in EPSG3035 and EPSG25830. Mapped attributes are canopy base height (CBH, m), canopy bulk density (kg/m3), canopy fuel load (CFL, Mg/ha) and canopy height (CH, m) Maps were obtained using random forest models relating canopy fuel attributes with airborne laser scanning data, landsat time series imagery, topographic and climate metrics. Models were trained using data from the fourth National Forest Inventory cycle in Spain. Coefficients of determination were, 88.44% for CH,  81.28% for CFL, 76.45% for CBD and 58.23% for CBH. 

The process to create this dataset is described in "Estimating crown fuels in Pinus pinaster Aiton forests of interior Spain using remote sensing and national forest inventory data". Accepted version. 

For fire spread simulation use the ETRS89 UTM30N (EPSG25830) versions.

metadata.title: Vineyard's Leaf Area / Photosynthesis Service – Very High Resolution
metadata.description:
The Vineyard's Leaf Area / Photosynthesis Service provides information on the leaf area and photosynthesis status of vineyard fields for a user-selected period. Two products are delivered through this EO service: Leaf Area and Photosynthesis. For each product, one EO index has been selected as the most suitable to provide information on the corresponding variable. The Leaf Area Index (LAI) is used to provide information on leaf area, while the Fraction of Absorbed Photosynthetically Active Radiation (fAPAR) is used to provide information on photosynthesis. 

This EO service can provide leaf area and photosynthesis products at both High Resolution (HR) and Very High Resolution (VHR). The system selects the best input data from the available options based on the user’s preferences. For the VHR option, both LAI and fAPAR products can be generated using either Satellogic or WorldView-2 images.

This service is part of the set of Earth Observation (EO) services developed in order to illustrate, test, validate and demonstrate the LEONSEGS capabilities. The defined use cases are implemented and tested in two Areas of Interest (AoIs), located in Spain and Austria. This service is only provided for the Spanish use case, focused on vineyard monitoring.

This record provides examples of the outputs produced by the LEONSEGS system in response to a user requesting the Vineyard’s Leaf Area Status service at VHR level.

Outputs:
• The Leaf Area Index (LAI), used to provide information on leaf area.
• The Fraction of Absorbed Photosynthetically Active Radiation (fAPAR), used to provide the photosynthesis.

For each EO index product, the following files are provided:
      - GeoTIFF raster containing the original index values
      - Categorized GeoTIFF raster
      - RGB visualization GeoTIFF
      - PNG legend associated with the RGB visualization
      - Raster footprint geometry (.wkt)
      - ISO 19115/19139 metadata (.xml)
      - STAC metadata (.geojson)

The categorized values have been specifically adjusted for vineyard crops according to crop phenology; therefore, these values are not applicable to other crop types.

This stack contains 31 covariate features combining Sentinel-2 bare-soil reflectance, vegetation history, terrain/hydrology, Sentinel-1 radar statistics, and SoilGrids 0–30 cm soil priors. The Sentinel-2 bare-soil bands are median composites from cloud-masked observations where PVIR<0.25

  2. BS_B3: Bare-soil median composite of Sentinel-2 B3, green band.
  3. BS_B4: Bare-soil median composite of Sentinel-2 B4, red band.
  4. BS_B5: Bare-soil median composite of Sentinel-2 B5, red-edge 1 band.
  5. BS_B6: Bare-soil median composite of Sentinel-2 B6, red-edge 2 band.
  6. BS_B7: Bare-soil median composite of Sentinel-2 B7, red-edge 3 band.
  7. BS_B8: Bare-soil median composite of Sentinel-2 B8, near-infrared band.
  8. BS_B8A: Bare-soil median composite of Sentinel-2 B8A, narrow near-infrared band.
  9. BS_B11: Bare-soil median composite of Sentinel-2 B11, shortwave infrared 1 band.
  10. BS_B12: Bare-soil median composite of Sentinel-2 B12, shortwave infrared 2 band.
  11. bare_soil_count: Number of valid bare-soil Sentinel-2 observations used per pixel.

metadata.title: Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics: Annual mangrove extent, 1984-2023
metadata.description:
This dataset provides annual global mangrove extent maps from 1984 to 2023 at 30 m spatial resolution, derived from the Landsat archive. The data are distributed in ESRI Shapefile format, using the Behrmann equal-area projection and the WGS 1984 geographic coordinate system. The attribute field gridcode indicates data availability: a value of 1 represents pixels derived from valid Landsat observations, whereas a value of 2 represents pixels gap-filled using the closest previous valid observation.

The easiest way to access and use the data is through Google Earth Engine, where the datasets are available in the Earth Engine Data Catalog: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/publisher/mangrovedatahub2.

For a quick overview or simple exploratory analysis, feel free to use our Google Earth Engine app: https://zhenzhang.users.earthengine.app/view/globalmangrovedynamic.

For using the dataset, please cite our paper: Zhang, Z., Murray, N., Song, X. P., Bunting, P., Worthington, T., Fatoyinbo, L., ... & Friess, D. A. Unexpected expansion and regrowth in Earth’s mangrove forests over the past four decades. Science 392,1082-1087 (2026). DOI:10.1126/science.aec9773

metadata.title: Canada1Water Leaf Area Index - Monthly Normals
metadata.description:
Abstract

ESA Copernicus Global Land Operations Leaf Area Index with global gap-free coverage at 11-day interval and 1km resolution was selected for Canada1Water use. This LAI product is more ready for use in application such as HGS as it is gap-free and quality assured.

The 756 NetCDF files were downloaded for 11-day intervals for time periods between 1999 and 2019. There are 21 years with 12 months and 3 LAI grids for each month. First, a daily normal was calculated using the mean value of each of the 36 time intervals within the 21 years. Then, a monthly normal was further calculated using the mean of the 3 time intervals in each month using the daily normal grids. This results in 12 final LAI grids – 1 for each month of the year, representing the normal over the 21 year period.

Note that Canada1Water is re-serving LAI using a scaling factor of 30 that needs to be applied to the Geotiff for correct use.

Visit the Canada1Water Data Portal here: 

https://portal.canada1water.ca/

Source Data Citation:
European Space Agency (ESA) (2019). Leaf Area Index 1km 11-day (LAI1km) version 2.2. Dataset. Available online from the European Space Agency's Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Open Data Portal: https://land.copernicus.eu/global/products/lai

metadata.title: Associational defense reduces grazing and deforestation in a kelp forest ecosystem: implications for restoration
metadata.description:
This repository supports a research project investigating whether the chemically and structurally defended brown alga Desmarestia herbacea can function as an associational defense to reduce sea urchin grazing on juvenile bull kelp (Nereocystis luetkeana). Using a combination of field surveys, field manipulations, and laboratory feeding assays, this project evaluates whether co-occurrence with Desmarestia can improve kelp survival and inform restoration strategies in urchin-dominated systems.

Overview

This repository contains the data and, if applicable, the code required to reproduce the results presented in the associated journal article:

Wiley, B. W., E. M. Carrasco, M. Sedeño, and P. E. Bourdeau. (2026) "Associational defense reduces grazing and deforestation in a kelp forest ecosystem: implications for restoration" Journal of Applied Ecology

All figures and tables in the paper should be reproducible by running the scripts provided in this repository.

Data Description

  • Data collected by: Brayden Wiley (Cal Poly Humboldt), in collaboration with the Cher-Ae Heights Indian Community of the Trinidad Rancheria and the Bourdeau Lab
  • Date of data collection: [2024-05-10] to [2025-09-10], using the YYYY-MM-DD standard

metadata.title: Vineyard's Leaf Area / Photosynthesis Service – High Resolution
metadata.description:
The Vineyard's Leaf Area / Photosynthesis Service provides information on the leaf area and photosynthesis status of vineyard fields for a user-selected period. Two products are delivered through this EO service: Leaf Area and Photosynthesis. For each product, one EO index has been selected as the most suitable to provide information on the corresponding variable. The Leaf Area Index (LAI) is used to provide information on leaf area, while the Fraction of Absorbed Photosynthetically Active Radiation (fAPAR) is used to provide information on photosynthesis. 

This EO service can provide leaf area and photosynthesis products at both High Resolution (HR) and Very High Resolution (VHR). The system selects the best input data from the available options based on the user’s preferences. For the HR option, both LAI and fAPAR products can be generated using either Sentinel-2 or Landsat 8/9 data.

This service is part of the set of Earth Observation (EO) services developed in order to illustrate, test, validate and demonstrate the LEONSEGS capabilities. The defined use cases are implemented and tested in two Areas of Interest (AoIs), located in Spain and Austria. This service is only provided for the Spanish use case, focused on vineyard monitoring.

This record provides examples of the outputs produced by the LEONSEGS system in response to a user requesting the Vineyard’s Leaf Area Status service at HR level.

Outputs:
• The Leaf Area Index (LAI), used to provide information on leaf area.
• The Fraction of Absorbed Photosynthetically Active Radiation (fAPAR), used to provide the photosynthesis.

For each EO index product, the following files are provided:
      - GeoTIFF raster containing the original index values
      - Categorized GeoTIFF raster
      - RGB visualization GeoTIFF
      - PNG legend associated with the RGB visualization
      - Raster footprint geometry (.wkt)
      - ISO 19115/19139 metadata (.xml)
      - STAC metadata (.geojson)

The categorized values have been specifically adjusted for vineyard crops according to crop phenology; therefore, these values are not applicable to other crop types.

For a given EO product, multiple examples may be available, representing the full range of satellite missions: Landsat 8, Landsat 9, Sentinel-2A, Sentinel-2B, and Sentinel-2C.

metadata.title: Global Fishing Watch IUU Fishing Risk Insight v1 2012-2025
metadata.description:
The Global Fishing Watch Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated (IUU) Fishing Risk Insights dataset provides computed insights per vessel at an annual scale (from January to December). 

  • The dataset and associated documentation can be found here
  • We have also developed a Fact Sheet that outlines the background research that contributed to the development of the IUU fishing risk insights included in this dataset. 
  • Finally, the list of citations used to develop the indicators can be found here.

The IUU fishing risk insights have been identified through a literature review and consultation with experts and practitioners who support maritime authorities with fisheries intelligence. The 11 insights included in this dataset are observable behaviors we have found to be associated with an increased risk of IUU fishing, and that can be calculated using publicly available datasets. They are either derived from:

  • Automatic Identification System (AIS) data, 

  • Reported cases of IUU fishing (from Regional Fisheries Management Organization (RFMO) IUU vessel lists) or 

  • Forced labor information drawn from an internally maintained list of reported forced labor vessels that have been matched to AIS. 

The dataset also includes vessel identity fields, including Maritime Mobile Service Identities (MMSI), IMO number, callsign, flag, and shipname from both AIS and registry sources. Vessel identity is not an IUU risk insight, rather the information may be used to contextualize results and filter for vessels or fleets of interest.

The plan is to calculate and update the dataset every 12 months. 

 

IMPORTANT DISCLAIMER

The outputs of this dataset are not designed to make definitive determinations of IUU fishing or to replace legal, investigative, or judicial processes. Rather, this dataset aims to serve as an early-warning and decision-support tool that must be combined with additional evidence, regulatory and geographic knowledge, and expert judgement before reaching any conclusions. Where appropriate, validation of risk signals may be supported through inspections, enforcement records, or other independent verification mechanisms. Please read more details about the data caveats on our website.

metadata.title: OCO-2/3 v10/11 10-second average XCO2 data used in a recent v11-v10 comparison
metadata.description:
NASA's Atmospheric Carbon Observations from Space (ACOS) Level 2 full physics (L2FP) retrieval algorithm has been used to estimate of the total column dry-air mole fraction of carbon dioxide (XCO2) from satellite measurements of reflected solar radiation.  A recent update of the L2FP code (Version 11, or 'v11'), has been used to retrieve XCO2 from data from the Orbiting Carbon Observatory 2 (OCO-2) satellite, as well as from the near-identical Orbiting Carbon Observatory 3 (OCO-3) instrument mounted on the International Space Station (ISS).  The performance of this v11 update, along with the associated screening-out of bad data and the post hoc bias correction of the remaining data, has been assessed by Taylor et al. (2026), in part by comparing to the previous versions ('v10') of the bias-corrected XCO2 from OCO-2 and OCO-3.  Part of this analysis used a reduced-volume version of the data, achieved by averaging the original XCO2 retrievals across 10-second spans.   Four files containing the 10-second average XCO2 retrievals used in the Taylor et al. analysis are presented here:

  1. OCO-2 v11  (20140906-20240731):   OCO2_b11.2_10sec_GOOD_r3.nc4

  2. OCO-2 v10  (20140906-20220228):   OCO2_b10c_10sec_GOOD_r7.nc4

  3. OCO-3 v11  (20190806-20250331):   OCO3_b11_10sec_GOOD_r4.nc4

  4. OCO-3 v10  (20190806-20231112):   OCO3_b10.4-lite_10sec_GOOD_190806-231112.h5

Below, we give some details on the OCO-2 and OCO-3 viewing approach, the CO2 and XCO2 values retrieved from their data, and the weighted average used to compute the 10-second averages presented here.

The Orbiting Carbon Observatory 2 (OCO-2) satellite, as well as the near-identical Orbiting Carbon Observatory 3 (OCO-3) instrument mounted aboard the ISS with a pointing mechanism that allows it to mimic OCO-2's thin-swath scan, measure solar radiance reflected from the Earth's surface in two CO2 absorption bands (1.6 and 2.0 um), as well as in the O2 A-band.  By comparing the CO2 / O2 absorption ratio, the dry air mixing ratio of CO2 may be estimated along the observed path, i.e. averaged across the full atmospheric column, though with sensitivity peaking near the Earth's surface.  A radiative transfer model that accounts for the effects of thin clouds and aerosols, water vapor, and surface albedo variations, is used, and the vertical profile of CO2 mixing ratio is estimated from the radiance data.  This CO2 profile is then collapsed to a scalar vertical average (XCO2), which is then bias corrected post hoc against Earth-based Fourier spectrometer data from the Total Carbon Column Observation Network (TCCON), which itself is tied to CO2 measurement standards using in situ aircraft CO2 profile measurements.

OCO-2 & OCO-3 take measurements in a thin swath (nominally 10-km wide) underneath the satellite/ISS, with a 3 Hz cross-scan rate.  Each cross-scan is divided into 8 individual fields of view (FOVs) of approximate size 2.3km x 1.3km.  These small FOVs increase the chances of seeing through clouds and can reveal details of point-source CO2 emissions, but are generally much finer-scale than can be modeled by the atmospheric transport models used in global CO2 flux inversions, which typically use grid boxes 100s of km on a side.  Rather than assimilating each fine-scale FOV XCO2 value individually and comparing them to modeled XCO2 values that change much more slowly, it is convenient to average the original OCO-2/3 data to coarser scales beforehand, then assimilate these averaged values in the flux inversions.  This averaging has the beneficial side-effect of reducing the OCO-2/3 data volume considerably.  In the files presented here, the data have been averaged across 10-second spans, equivalent to an along-track distance of ~67.5 km for OCO-2 (or ~73 km for OCO-3) on the Earth's surface.

The bias-corrected XCO2 retrievals at the original fine-scale resolution are available at NASA's Goddard Earth Sciences (GES) Data and Information Services Center (DISC) as 'Lite' files.  The file collections corresponding to the XCO2 retrievals that are used as input to the four 10-second average files given above are (for reference):

  1.  "OCO-2 Level 2 bias-corrected XCO2 and other select fields from the full-physics retrieval aggregated as daily files, Retrospective processing V11.2r (OCO2_L2_Lite_FP)", https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/OCO2_L2_Lite_FP_11.2r/summary?keywords=OCO2_L2_Lite_FP,
  2. "OCO-2 Level 2 bias-corrected XCO2 and other select fields from the full-physics retrieval aggregated as daily files, Retrospective processing V10r (OCO2_L2_Lite_FP)", https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/OCO2_L2_Lite_FP_10r/summary?keywords=OCO2_L2_Lite_FP,
  3. "OCO-3 Level 2 bias-corrected XCO2 and other select fields from the full-physics retrieval aggregated as daily files, Retrospective processing V11r (OCO3_L2_Lite_FP)",  https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/OCO3_L2_Lite_FP_11r/summary?keywords=OCO3_L2_Lite_FP.  
  4. "OCO-3 Level 2 bias-corrected XCO2 and other select fields from the full-physics retrieval aggregated as daily files, Retrospective processing v10.4r (OCO3_L2_Lite_FP)",  https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/OCO3_L2_Lite_FP_10.4r/summary?keywords=OCO3_L2_Lite_FP.  

The original XCO2 values contained in these data collections, along with other auxiliary variables provided for analysis purposes, have been averaged in the same manner across each 10-second span, with the approach used with the Version 10 release of the OCO-2 XCO2 data, as described in Section 3.2.1 of Byrne et al. (2023) and Section 3.1.1 of Baker et al. (2022): each value in the span is weighted with the inverse square of its retrieved XCO2 uncertainty value, taken from variable 'xco2_uncertainty' from the 'Lite" file.  Data inside each 10-second span are averaged separately based on viewing mode and surface type, as indicated by variable 'data_type'.  Only data with a 'good' retrieval quality flag (variable 'xco2_quality_flag' in the 'Lite' file equal to zero) are included in the average;  the number of such 'good' data values (1-240) included in each average value is indicated in variable 'N_total_shots'.  It has been found that 10-second spans with fewer 'good' retrievals tend to be affected more by the unwanted effects of aerosols and undetected clouds: these may be mitigated somewhat by not using 10-sec averages for spans with low 'N_total_shots' values.  Variable 'assimilate_flag' separates those data that are not taken in glint viewing mode over either land or water, or in nadir mode over land, from data taken in other modes (target mode, or in transition to/from target mode, or nadir mode over water, or mixed land/water scenes) that are generally not assimilated in flux inversions; for OCO-3, it indicates which scenes are part of a Snapshot Area Map (SAM); and it also flags 5% of the assimilable data by orbit for use as withheld evaluation data, for use in inversion studies.  The uncertainty on the 10-sec average XCO2 value is given in variable 'xco2_uncertainty'; this accounts for correlations in error between individual scenes (+0.3 over land, +0.6 over ocean) as described in Section 3.2.1 of Baker et al (2022), as well as variability in the averaged XCO2 values not captured by the retrieval uncertainties.  

References

Baker, DF, E Bell, KJ Davis, JF Campbell, B Lin & J Dobler, A new exponentially-decaying error correlation model for assimilating OCO-2 column-average CO2 data, using a length scale computed from airborne lidar measurements, Geosci. Model Dev., 15, 649–668, https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-15-649-2022, 2022.

Byrne, B, DF Baker, et al., National CO2 budgets (2015-2020) inferred from atmospheric CO2 observations in support of the Global Stocktake, Earth System Sci. Data, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-2022-213, 2023.

Taylor, TE, CW O'Dell, et al., The OCO-2 and OCO-3 ACOS version 11 XCO2 data products: a benchmark record  for space-based global carbon cycle research, submitted to Earth and Space Science
references: Taylor, TE, CW O'Dell, et al., The OCO-2 and OCO-3 ACOS version 11 XCO2 data products: a benchmark record for space-based global carbon cycle research, submitted to Earth and Space Science

metadata.title: Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics: Mangrove change layers, 1984-2023
metadata.description:
This dataset provides global mangrove change layers derived from the Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics (CGMD) annual mangrove extent product, covering the period 1984-2023. The data describe multiple dimensions of mangrove dynamics, including loss, gain (including regeneration and expansion), degradation, growth.

All data are provided in ESRI Shapefile format.

File descriptions

1. AnnualLoss&Gain1984–2023.zip

This file contains annual mangrove loss and gain layers derived from year-to-year comparisons.

  • File naming: Change_{year}_{year+1}.shp
    (e.g., Change_2000_2001.shp represents changes between 2000 and 2001)
  • Attribute field: ChangeType (string):
    • loss – mangrove loss between two consecutive years
    • gain – mangrove gain between two consecutive years
    • stable – no change (persistent mangrove)

2. AnnualDegradation&Growth1984–2023.zip

This file contains year-to-year within-mangrove changes in canopy condition, including degradation and growth.

  • File naming: Degradation_{year}_{year+1}.shp
  • Attribute field: landcover (integer):
    • 1 – degradation (canopy thining or short-term loss)
    • 2 – growth (canopy cover increase)
    • 3 – degraded (persistently lower canopy cover after degradation)
    • 4 – after growth (persistently higher canopy cover after growth)

3. 2010To2023_Loss&Gain.zip

This file contains aggregated mangrove loss and gain between 2010 and 2023.

  • Includes two shapefiles: Loss (2010 → 2023) and Gain (2010 → 2023).

4. 1980sTo2010_Loss&Gain.zip

This file summarizes mangrove changes from the 1980s baseline to 2010.

  • Includes two shapefiles: Loss (1980s → 2010) and Gain (1980s → 2010).

5. Regeneration2010to2023.zip

This file represents mangrove regeneration between 2010 and 2023.

  • Definition: Gain occurring in areas that were previously mangroves before 2010 but had been lost and later regenerated.

6. Expansion2010to2023.zip

This file represents mangrove expansion between 2010 and 2023.

  • Definition: Gain occurring in areas that were not identified as mangroves during the 1980s–2010 baseline period.

For visualization or simple analysis, please use our Google Earth Engine app: https://zhenzhang.users.earthengine.app/view/globalmangrovedynamic.

For using the dataset, please cite our paper: Zhang, Z., Murray, N., Song, X. P., Bunting, P., Worthington, T., Fatoyinbo, L., ... & Friess, D. A. Unexpected expansion and regrowth in Earth’s mangrove forests over the past four decades. Science 392,1082-1087 (2026). DOI:10.1126/science.aec9773

Note: The archive AnnualLoss&Gain1984–2023.zip contains a shapefile named Change_2018-2023.shp, which contains valid mangrove change data for 2018-2023. However, its attribute table has not been prepared for end users and may be difficult to interpret. We therefore recommend excluding this shapefile from your analyses.

metadata.title: Global monthly land surface water mapping using three water indices from Landsat-8 and Sentinel-2
metadata.description:
Summary of Version 2.0 Updates
This version (v2.0) extends the data record to include the period from January 2022 to December 2024. Combined with the previous version (v1.0), this repository now provides a continuous global record of surface water dynamics from 2019 through 2024.

Description
This dataset provides monthly global land surface water mapping using water indices derived from Earth observation satellite data. It was generated using imagery from two satellite missions: Landsat-8 and Sentinel-2.

The dataset includes three water indices:

  • NDWI2 (Normalized Difference Water Index)
  • MNDWI (Modified Normalized Difference Water Index)
  • WI2015 (Water Index 2015)

Methodology
A pixel was classified as water if the average index value within each month exceeded 0, and as non-water otherwise. The dataset maintains a spatial resolution of 300 m. Each dataset is provided in GeoTIFF format, which can be visualized and analyzed using GIS software. This dataset can be used for hydrological studies, flood monitoring, and water resource management.

Temporal Coverage

  • Version 2.0 (New): January 2022 to December 2024
  • Version 1.0: January 2019 to December 2021

This dataset provides the foundational data for the following manuscript published in Scientific Data: A Global Multi-Sensor Dataset of Surface Water Indices from Landsat-8 and Sentinel-2 Satellite Measurements (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-025-05562-z).

metadata.title: HERA-WB: a multi-decadal, sub-daily water balance dataset for Europe (1951-2020)
metadata.description: Freshwater availability shapes ecosystems and human societies. Anthropogenic activities, including land use and climate change, have altered the hydrological cycle. We introduce HERA-WB (Hydrological European ReAnalysis – Water Balance), a spin-off of the HERA high-resolution hydrological reanalysis for Europe generated with the OS LISFLOOD hydrological model. The model is forced by bias-corrected, downscaled ERA5-Land climate reanalysis and incorporates dynamic maps of land use, water demand, and reservoirs to represent human influence. From this simulation we derive 17 hydrological variables characterising blue and green water fluxes across 2,214 European catchments. The dataset spans the period 1951-2020, with a 6-hourly temporal resolution. We assess the performance of the reanalysis against benchmark datasets from four key hydrological variables: river discharge, surface soil moisture, snow water equivalent, and actual evaporation. We further propose a tiered classification of the variables according to the strength of their independent evaluation, to guide users on the confidence warranted for each. HERA-WB combines a temporal coverage and resolution rarely available together for a dataset of this kind. It highlights the capabilities of global hydrological models like OS LISFLOOD to provide skilful simulations beyond river discharge. By providing internally consistent, co-located estimates of blue and green water fluxes, the dataset can support the development and benchmarking of machine-learning hydrological models as constraints or as targets for evaluating process consistency. Furthermore, the spatial and temporal coverages of HERA-WB enable the analysis of dynamics governing changes in freshwater availability, informing continental to local water policies.

title: HERA-WB: a multi-decadal, sub-daily water balance dataset for Europe (1951-2020)

metadata.title: Global gridded canopy height and height distributions from GEDI and ICESat-2 for EDv3 initialization at 0.01° resolution
metadata.description:
This dataset provides gridded forest canopy structure inputs developed for the lidar-based initialization of the Ecosystem Demography model (ED v3.0), as described in Ma et al. (2023). It includes mean canopy height and canopy height histograms derived from NASA GEDI and ICESat-2 observations, together with tree canopy cover from the Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS), at a spatial resolution of 0.01°.

These products characterize spatial variation in canopy height and the distribution of observed canopy heights within each grid cell. They were developed to connect satellite observations of forest structure with mechanistic ecosystem modeling and can support initialization and evaluation of other forest and vegetation models.

Data contents

The repository contains five GeoTIFF files:

  • Global_GEDI_v2_gridded_rh100_avg.tif: Mean canopy height, in meters, calculated from filtered GEDI L2A version 002 RH100 observations.

  • Global_GEDI_v2_gridded_rh100_hist_count.tif: GEDI canopy height histograms, recording the number of retained observations in each height bin within each grid cell.

  • Global_ICESat2_v5_gridded_sup_h_canopy_avg.tif: Mean canopy height, in meters, derived from filtered ICESat-2 ATL08 version 005 observations.

  • Global_ICESat2_v5_gridded_sup_h_canopy_hist_count.tif: ICESat-2 canopy height histograms, recording the number of retained observations in each height bin within each grid cell.

  • CGLS_forest_percent_2019_001deg.tif: Tree canopy cover percentage for 2019, aggregated from the native 100 m CGLS product to 0.01°.

Source observations and processing

The study used GEDI observations acquired from March 2019 through August 2021 and ICESat-2 observations acquired from October 2018 through October 2021. GEDI observations cover approximately 51°S–51°N, while ICESat-2 provides observations beyond this latitude range.

Observations were quality filtered and assigned to 0.01° grid cells. The filtering criteria documented in the paper were:

  • GEDI: quality_flag = 1, sensitivity > 0.95, and RH100 > 5 m.

  • ICESat-2: dem_removal_flag = 0, canopy_flag = 1, cloud_flag_atm < 4, and h_canopy > 5 m.

Canopy height histograms contain 90 bins spanning 5–50 m at 0.5 m intervals. Each histogram layer records sample counts rather than normalized probabilities. Mean canopy height summarizes the retained observations within each grid cell. The products pool observations across the acquisition periods and do not represent annual time series.

Use in model initialization

In the associated study, canopy height histograms were used to index height-based lookup tables generated by ED v3.0. Model states associated with each height bin were weighted by the observed sample counts, preserving variation in canopy height within a grid cell. Tree canopy cover was then used to scale forest estimates to the whole grid cell.

The histograms describe the distribution of sampled canopy heights across footprints or segments within a grid cell; they are not vertical foliage profiles or distributions of individual tree heights. Spatial coverage and sampling density vary because both lidar missions collect observations along orbital tracks. Cells without retained observations should not be interpreted as having zero canopy height.

Associated publication

Ma, L., et al. (2023). Spatial heterogeneity of global forest aboveground carbon stocks and fluxes constrained by spaceborne lidar data and mechanistic modeling. Global Change Biology, 29, 3378–3394. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.16682

Please cite this dataset and the associated publication when using these products.

title: Global gridded canopy height and height distributions from GEDI and ICESat-2 for EDv3 initialization at 0.01° resolution

metadata.title: Unprecedented warming and increased herbivory drive collapse of Japan's kelp forests
metadata.description: Kelp forests underpin entire ecosystems and provide key services for human society, yet are threatened by anthropogenic stressors, most notably ocean warming and overgrazing. While Japanese kelp forests have substantial historical and cultural value, responses to recent environmental change remain poorly resolved. Here, we assessed how recent Kuroshio-associated warming and increased herbivory were linked to kelp forest collapse across approximately 200 km of the Izu Peninsula (central-eastern Japan). We combined 40 years of in situ kelp biomass (1980–2024) and 12–14 years of canopy-cover records (2009–2025) with satellite-derived sea-surface temperature and marine heatwave metrics. Herbivorous fish assemblages and bite rates were surveyed monthly (2021–2022) across reefs spanning healthy, mosaic, and barren states. Laboratory experiments quantified lethal and sub-lethal thermal thresholds of juvenile Ecklonia cava using temperature-ramping (20–33 °C) and growth trials (22 vs 28 °C). Spatial analyses compared thermal-threshold exceedance and seasonal grazing-window expansion with observed canopy loss, evaluating whether warming and herbivory were consistent with the spatial extent of decline. Warming along the Izu coast intensified during the recent Kuroshio Large Meander, increasing from 0.15 °C decade-1 (1982–2016) to 2.98 °C decade-1 (2017–2024), with cumulative marine heatwave intensity rising from 2.34 to 63.22 °C·day decade-1. Over the same period, canopy-forming E. cava cover fell from ~75% to zero, and peak biomass declined from 2.37 kg DW.m⁻² to zero, indicating local extirpation and likely regional functional loss. Laboratory assays showed rapid physiological decline above 29.5 °C and mortality at 32–33 °C; temperatures exceeded during summer 2023/2024. The grazing season by warm-adapted herbivorous fishes expanded by up to 86 days, amplifying kelp loss across heat-stressed reefs. Together, extreme thermal stress and expanded herbivory were strongly associated with a shift from kelp forests to barren reefs, highlighting how physiological stress and trophic processes can contribute to rapid kelp loss in warming boundary-current systems.

title: Unprecedented warming and increased herbivory drive collapse of Japan's kelp forests

This is a dataset designed to provide geospatial layers of Urban Water Producing Systems in the state of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil.

The catchment polygons are the main novel output for these dataset. The catchments were delineated via a fast-algorithm that uses topological network analysis and raster DEM processing for fine-tuning. Geometries and areas are estimated and subject to revision.

metadata.title: 202609 - Vessel detections from Sentinel 2
metadata.description:
Vessel detections with Sentinel-2 satellite imagery from 2019 to 14 days ago. Multiyear detection of vessels with respective length, speed and orientation estimates based on deep-learning models applied to electro-optical imagery (RGB and near-infrared) at 10-m resolution covering most exclusive economic zones and marine protected areas across the ocean.

Sentinel-2 detections are  based on electro-optical imagery at 10-m resolution. Compared with our published Sentinel-1 detections based on SAR imagery at 20-m resolution, Sentinel-2 allows detecting smaller vessels with all types of vessel materials, in contrast with the weakness of SAR imagery on revealing vessels made of wood and fiberglass. Sentinel-2 also images the wakes of moving vessels, which further increase the detectability of small vessels and allow us to infer the vessels’ speed and orientation.The rich information contained in the optical imagery can be used to map not only vessel presence, but also vessel activities such as vessel encounters and bottom trawling. Sentinel-2 also covers more area of the ocean than Sentinel-1, and the novel neural-net detection approach does not require the exclusion of near-shore regions (as opposed to the CFAR approach), allowing detection of vessels in highly-packed areas all the way to the shoreline where most human activity is concentrated. Overall, with Sentinel-2 imagery we are able to detect about 3 times more vessels, “see” a broader range of vessel lengths and types, and infer more information of vessel activities than in our previous mapping using Sentinel-1 imagery.

title: 202609 - Vessel detections from Sentinel 2

metadata.title: Mapping crown length and canopy depth across global forests at 1 km from multi-platform lidar and satellite data
metadata.description: Crown length (CL) describes the vertical extent of an individual tree's live crown. Canopy depth (CD) describes the vertical extent of the canopy within a forest stand. Both inform fire behaviour, vegetation and habitat models, yet their global distributions remain poorly resolved. We present global maps of mean CL and CD at 1 km resolution for 2020. We first retrieved CL for individual trees segmented from lidar point clouds, as tree height minus crown-base height. Within each of 1147 reference records on six continents, mean CL was the average of the tree values and CD was the 95th-percentile tree height minus the lowest crown base. Both were related to satellite and environmental predictors using random forest models. Tree-level CL agreed with field measurements and manual annotations with R² = 0.62 and RMSE = 2.63 m. Across 46 validation plots, RMSE was 1.90 m for mean CL and 2.09 m for CD. In the 30 % hold-out set, the mapping models achieved R² = 0.64 for CL and 0.72 for CD, with RMSE of 2.15 m and 2.98 m. Global mean CL and CD were 7.0 m and 14.2 m. Long crowns and deep canopies occurred in equatorial rain forests and humid temperate forests. Savannas, Mediterranean woodlands and dry forests had the smallest values. These maps give the first globally consistent view of the crown layer beneath the canopy top. They can constrain crown geometry in vegetation models, canopy fuel depth in fire models and vertical habitat structure in biodiversity studies.

title: Mapping crown length and canopy depth across global forests at 1 km from multi-platform lidar and satellite data

MATLAB code, model inputs, processed results, and figure scripts supporting Dominant Controls on Soil Carbon and Nutrient Dynamics Across Ecosystems: A Global Sensitivity Analysis.

The study examines 81 soil biogeochemical parameters across 17 sites using elementary-effects screening and variance-based sensitivity analysis (VBSA). metadata.title: Dataset for "Characteristics of the Fluorescence of Water-Soluble Organic Matter in Forest, Remote, and Urban Aerosols in Japan, Atmos. Environ."
metadata.description:
This dataset is for “Characteristics of the Fluorescence of Water-Soluble Organic Matter in Forest, Remote, and Urban Aerosols in Japan” by Wei et al. in Atmospheric Environment. The contents are described in the sheet “Readme” of the Excel file named “Dataset_cw260904.xlsx”. The dataset contains the data used in the manuscript, including average fluorescence spectra, fluorescence indices, atmospheric fluorescence volumes, normalized fluorescence volumes, and PARAFAC components of water-soluble organic matter (WSOM) in atmospheric aerosol samples collected at forest, remote, and urban sites in Japan. The dataset also includes the correlations of the atmospheric fluorescence volumes of the PARAFAC components with the concentrations of water-soluble organic carbon (WSOC) and meteorological parameters. The dataset further provides fluorescence indices and atmospheric fluorescence volumes for three subfractions of WSOM obtained from aerosol and rainwater samples collected in Nagoya. The excitation-emission matrix (EEM) spectra of WSOM in aqueous extracts were measured using a fluorescence spectrophotometer (FP-6600, JASCO) with a 1-cm path length quartz cell. The ranges of the excitation and emission wavelengths were 235-500 nm and 300-600 nm, respectively. The drEEM toolbox for MATLAB was used to preprocess the EEMs and to perform parallel factor (PARAFAC) analysis. The concentrations of WSOC and water-soluble inorganic ions were measured using a total organic carbon analyzer and ion chromatography, respectively.

The dataset was obtained in the study conducted under JSPS KAKENHI (JP26281007, JP23H00515, and JP19KK0265); ArCS II (JPMXD1420318865); and ERDF from ERCA (JPMEERF20232001). Other acknowledgments are provided in the associated manuscript.

metadata.title: Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics: Global mangrove stand age in 2023
metadata.description:
This dataset provides global mangrove stand age in 2023 at a spatial resolution of 30 m, derived from the annual mangrove extent maps of the Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics (CGMD) dataset.

Stand age is defined as the number of consecutive years of mangrove presence, counted backwards from 2023 to the first year of the most recent uninterrupted period detected by CGMD. Mangroves continuously present throughout 1984–2023 are assigned to the ≥40-year age class, as their establishment may predate the satellite record.

The attribute fields include

  • age — Mangrove stand age in years. A value of 40 represents stands aged ≥40 years.
  • Area_ha — Mangrove patch area in hectares, calculated using the World Behrmann equal-area projection.
  • Region — Geographic region in which the mangrove patch is located.

The dataset is currently under embargo and will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the associated manuscript. Please contact us if you require access before its public release.

title: Continuous Global Mangrove Dynamics: Global mangrove stand age in 2023

metadata.title: Downscaled GRACE Total Water Storage Change (TWSC) Dataset on a 1 km grid at daily intervals for Naryn – Kara Darya basins and Fergana valley (2002–2023)
metadata.description:
This dataset contains daily estimates of terrestrial water storage changes (TWSC) derived from the downscaling of Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) observations over the Naryn–Kara Darya basins and the Fergana Valley in Central Asia. The dataset covers the period from 1 April 2002 to 31 December 2023 and is provided on a 1 km grid.

The downscaling is performed by integrating GRACE/-FO data with hydrological forcing datasets, including precipitation, evapotranspiration, and river discharge from the Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation (MSWEP), the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM), and the Global Flood Awareness System (GloFAS), respectively.

The dataset is produced in support of a forthcoming manuscript on GRACE downscaling and terrestrial water storage dynamics in Central Asia. The final version will be uploaded after peer review.

Variables:
- twsc — daily terrestrial water storage change, expressed as equivalent water height in mm/day; dimensions: (time, lat, lon).
- lat — latitude of grid-cell centres, in degrees north.
- lon — longitude of grid-cell centres, in degrees east.
- time — days since 1970-01-01 00:00:00, with daily timestamps at 12:00.

title: Downscaled GRACE Total Water Storage Change (TWSC) Dataset on a 1 km grid at daily intervals for Naryn – Kara Darya basins and Fergana valley (2002–2023)

metadata.title: Developing a dynamic semi-distributed hydrological model considering interactions between soil moisture and evapotranspiration: application of bulk transfer method
metadata.description: Empirically-derived relationships are mainly used to estimate evapotranspiration (ET) in water balance models. Due to a lack of effective factors and correct conceptual relationships, the resulting ET may be inaccurate. Therefore, a hydrological model was developed by combining water balance and bulk transfer theory, called semi-distributed coupled water balance and bulk transfer (SD-CWBT). According to it, a dynamic interrelationship between ET and soil moisture was correctly established to estimate ET via physical concepts. Global gridded ET retrievals, which provide the spatiotemporal distribution of ET at a global scale, including ECMWF Reanalysis v5-Land (ERA5-Land), TERRA, Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM), and Operational Simplified Surface Energy Balance (SSEBop), were employed to evaluate the model. The results indicated the SD-CWBT, with Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE), and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of [0.6, 0.95], [0.68, 0.96], and [12.61, 0.99] for the streamflow and groundwater level simulation, respectively, had better performance compared to the alternatives. Furthermore, the estimated spatiotemporal distributions of ET agreed well with the climatic-vegetation conditions.

metadata.title: Zooplankton Samples Collected in the Bering Sea On Board the F/V Northwest Explorer from September to October, 2002
metadata.description:
Zooplankton samples collected between September 8 and October 6, 2002 as part of the BASIS survey by the F/V Northwest Explorer . A total of 44 rope trawl stations were sampled along the Aleutian chain in the Bering Sea basin or within the proximity of the Aleutian Islands and stations on or adjacent to the Eastern Bering Sea shelf. Zooplankton were collected using a bongo net (mesh sizes: 333 and 505 microns) towed obliquely between the surface and 200 meters, or 20 meters from the sea floor. Zooplankton samples were split onboard the vessel with a Matoto splitter and sample halves were preserved in formalin and frozen. Formalin preserved specimens have been sent to the Polish sorting center for species identification; frozen specimens will be used for stable isotope analysis. Surface water samples were collected and filtered for stable isotopes, coccolithophores, and chlorophyll. Filters were frozen and 250 ml of the filtered water was retained for nutrient analysis (NO 2 , NO 3 , PO 4 , and SiO 3 ). [Reference: Murphy, J., N. Davis, O. Ivanov, M. Rohr, S. Elmajjati, and W. Barber. 2003. Cruise report of the 2002 F/V Northwest Explorer BASIS survey in the Bering Sea, September- October. (NPAFC Doc. 676 Rev. 1) 23 p. NMFS, Auke Bay Laboratory, Juneau, AK; School of Aquatic& Fishery Sciences, University of Washington; Pacific Fisheries Research Centre (TINRO-Centre), Vladivostok; Alaska Quaternary Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks; Institute of Marine Science, University of Alaska Fairbanks.] This report is available at http://www.npafc.org/restricted_doc/2003%20Documents_PDF/676(Rev1)(USA).pdf
