metadata.title: Ranked ephemeral wetland candidates for South Carolina, USA, derived from lidar, Sentinel-1 SAR, and soil survey data
metadata.description:
Introduction

Ephemerally-flooded wetlands, characterized by seasonal flooding and drying cycles, play crucial roles in water regulation, biogeochemical cycling, and biodiversity conservation. However, despite their ecological significance, ephemeral wetlands face threats from anthropogenic disturbances, a rapidly changing atmospheric equilibrium, and weakened regulatory protections. Recognizing the importance of these ecosystems is crucial for their conservation and sustainable management. There is currently no statewide map of ephemeral wetlands across all geographic zones. To address this gap, we developed a Wetland Atlas for South Carolina, focusing on the major river basins focusing on ephemeral wetlands. This digital atlas will provide a comprehensive inventory of identified wetland locations, allowing stakeholders to prioritize areas for protection and restoration efforts. By adopting a landscape approach and leveraging existing protected lands, we aim to enhance conservation strategies and promote spatial connectivity among ephemeral wetlands across the state.


The National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) was established in 1974 and led by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service “to inventory wetland area, location, type, and trends — the foundational information needed to better manage wetlands and their many benefits” (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 2025, para. 3). The NWI provides spatial boundaries and attribute information describing wetlands ranging from small, ephemeral features (<1 ha) to large, complex riverine and estuarine systems spanning thousands of hectares. The original NWI maps were delineated by hand using aerial imagery, soils data, and other available information. Collectively, these data provide one of the most comprehensive spatial inventories of wetlands in the United States and support applications at continental, state, county, and local scales. NWI data are used for wetland management and conservation as well as recreational applications, including birding, hunting, fishing, and boating (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 2025).
The accuracy of the NWI is known to be an issue for wetlands due to “the age of the data, include a relatively large (0.5 ac.) minimum mapping size, relatively coarse resolution of the source imagery, and inclusion of many features that do not meet the current common definition of ‘wetland’” (Gale, 2021, p. 1). Gale (2021) led a North Carolina statewide effort where 103,000 acres of field surveys were used to assess the NWI. The surveys included 4,655 individual wetlands with sizes ranging from <0.01 to 1,271 ac. and found that “>90% of field verified wetlands were below the NWI minimum mapping size of 0.5 ac.” (Gale, 2021, p. 1). Overall, these results suggest that the NWI underestimates approximately 60,000 ac. of wetlands in the state (Gale, 2021).


South Carolina shares a similar climate and ecoregions as North Carolina including the Blue Ridge, Piedmont, Southeastern Plains, Mid-Atlantic Coastal Plain, and also includes the Southeastern Coastal Plain that is not present in North Carolina. We make the assumption that given these similarities between SC and NC that there are similar issues with the NWI in SC.


One of the classification issues with ephemeral wetlands is that these tend to be small and are seasonally inundated depressions that the National Wetlands Inventory has systematically under-mapped because they are too small for the imagery NWI was compiled from, dry for much of the year, and often under forest canopy. This project asks a narrow question of closed depressions (sinks) across the state within existing protected areas mapped under the USGS PAD-US: Do they resemble the wetlands NWI did map based on soil, terrain, land cover, and radar backscatter? The output is a ranked list of unmapped sinks that have similar characteristics to existing NWI wetlands across all SC counties and ecoregions.


Specifically, we use a positive-unlabeled (PU) approach with a gradient boosting machine learning (ML) algorithm. The PU approach was used because we know where existing NWI boundaries are, including their attributes and classification schemes, but we do not know where other wetlands exist, based on the assumption that small ephemeral wetlands were likely underrepresented during the NWI mapping efforts. To support the identification of these unknown wetlands, we generated a sink layer for every county in SC. For this research, we identified sinks or topographic depressions derived from USGS DEMs that are characterized by interior drainage (Lindsay, 2023), using primarily 1-m lidar-derived DEMs, but in some instances we had to fall back to older 3-m DEMs due to the lack of updated coverage for some counties. These hydrological depressions do not have surface outflows and thus represent areas that have the potential to retain or pond water, but this does not mean they are wetlands. Lane et al. (2018) provide a detailed discussion of the water storage capacity of depressional non-floodplain wetlands. It is acknowledged that the identification of sinks does not indicate a wetland, but we use the sinks as landscape characteristics to build a ranking system of potential wetlands that closely match NWI-characterized wetlands. Thus, our work generates a ranking rather than a probability.


Scope and interpretation

This report summarizes the clustered positive-unlabeled sink model. Counties are grouped into clusters based on measured predictor behavior, and one model is fitted per cluster, so scores are comparable within a cluster and are not comparable between clusters. Positive prevalence of labeled NWI wetlands in the training data differs substantially from cluster to cluster due to physiographic differences across the landscape. Coastal and near-coastal counties tend to have relatively flat landscapes and thousands of sinks, as compared to the western Piedmont/Blue Ridge counties, which are characterized by more prominent elevation changes, well-defined drainage, and fewer input sinks and NWI wetlands available to serve as positive labeled sinks. Additionally, the NWI itself contains errors in both directions: some areas mapped as wetland are not actually wetlands, and some real wetlands exist but were not mapped. This omission error is skewed by size, as smaller wetlands are more difficult to delineate given the methods and complexities of wetland identification. This impacts the analysis because a binary labeling approach is used: positive NWI-labeled sinks are used to estimate the probability that an unlabeled sink more closely matches the labeled NWI sinks within each cluster. Elkan and Noto (2008) identify this issue and propose methodologies to address it: “Under the assumption that the labeled examples are selected randomly from the positive examples, we show that a classifier trained on positive and unlabeled examples predicts probabilities that differ by only a constant factor from the true conditional probabilities of being positive” (p. 1). A classifier that scores unlabeled sinks by their similarity to the positive sinks is expected to produce lower values than a classifier trained against the true population would. In other words, the output probabilities reported here are lower than they would be if we were working with a known true population of NWI wetlands to train the model on unlabeled sinks. Elkan and Noto (2008) do discuss methods to calculate a corrected classifier value, but we do not attempt that in this work.


The model produces a single probability score per unlabeled sink, and sinks are ranked within each cluster on a scale from 0 to 1, where 0 indicates no similarity to the NWI positive set and 1 indicates a 100% probability of matching the NWI positive labeled data set. Thus, each unlabeled sink is tagged with a score that essentially functions as a ranking from 0 to 1 within each cluster. We present those findings and model performance in this work. An additional output not presented here is the final GIS layer, in which every unlabeled sink in every county is identified with its score. Those data will be available on ArcGIS.com. A high-scoring sink is a candidate for field verification, not a wetland determination or delineation.
metadata.notes:
HOW TO USE THESE DATA

FILES
  sc_wetland_candidates_v5_k5_ranked.gpkg   statewide layer, 57,627 features
  <County>_wetland_candidates_v5_k5_ranked.gpkg   43 county files, 1,358,271 features total
  ranked_layers_v5_k5.json    per-file and per-cluster counts
  README_v5_k5_ranked.txt     field definitions and caveats

Every file contains one feature layer named "wetland_candidates", plus two
attribute tables, "run_metadata" and "rank_metadata", holding provenance and
field definitions. ArcGIS Pro and QGIS both list those tables.

WHICH FILE TO USE
  Statewide file: unmapped candidates scoring 0.5 or higher. This is the
  discovery product and the right starting point for most users.

  County files: every scored depression in that county, including those the
  National Wetlands Inventory already maps and those excluded from the target
  class. Use these to see what the model rejected, or to select candidates
  below the 0.5 cut.

READING THE SCORE
  wetland_probability is NOT a calibrated probability. This is a
  positive-unlabeled model: the score ranks a depression against the
  NWI-mapped wetlands of its own cluster. Cluster positive prevalence ranges
  from roughly 17% to 65%, so the same score carries different weight in
  different parts of the state. Treat 0.5 as a display convenience, not a
  decision boundary.

  Use the rank fields rather than raw score when comparing sites:
    rank_in_cluster     1 = highest scoring candidate in that cluster, statewide
    pctile_in_cluster   100 = top of the cluster, near 0 = bottom
    rank_in_county      same ranking within one county

  Ranks are computed over all unmapped candidates in the full county files,
  before any threshold. In the statewide file the ranks are therefore not
  consecutive from 1, and its lowest percentile is 84.7, meaning the 0.5 cut
  corresponds to roughly the top 15% of each cluster.

  Only unmapped candidates are ranked. Mapped and excluded depressions have
  NULL in all three rank fields.

LABEL CLASSES
  unmapped_candidate   no NWI polygon overlaps the depression. Unlabeled, NOT
                       negative. Only these can be discoveries.
  nwi_positive         NWI regime A or C with no h/x modifier. Already mapped.
                       These were the training positives.
  excluded             mapped by NWI but not the target: regime B, F or H, an
                       h/x modifier, or mapped open water. Scored, never
                       trained on.

COMMON SELECTIONS
  Top quarter of a cluster:       pctile_in_cluster >= 75
  Top 100 in a cluster:           rank_in_cluster <= 100
  Top candidates within a county: rank_in_county <= 50
  Note that a per-county selection is not a statewide "best" selection,
  because the score at the cut differs between counties.

CLUSTERS
  Counties were grouped by which predictors work for them, not by landform,
  and one model was trained per cluster. The cluster field records which model
  scored each depression; cluster_tier records whether the county helped
  define the cluster ("fit") or was assigned to it afterward ("assigned").
  Cluster membership is not stable across model runs, so do not build an
  argument on any single county's membership.

  Ranked candidates per cluster: 0: 36,968  1: 122,385  2: 258  3: 69,564
  4: 225,465. Cluster 2 is very small and none of its candidates reach 0.5,
  so it appears only in the county files.

COVERAGE
  43 of South Carolina's 46 counties. Cherokee, Lexington and Saluda were
  never scored, because they had too few NWI positives to join a cluster.
  On a map they will read as having no candidates. They were not evaluated.

PROJECTION AND AREA
  EPSG:26917 (NAD83 / UTM zone 17N).

title: Ranked ephemeral wetland candidates for South Carolina, USA, derived from lidar, Sentinel-1 SAR, and soil survey data

metadata.title: Simulated OCO-2 data, split tables, trained model weights, and predictive artifacts for amortized probabilistic CO2 retrieval
metadata.description:
Simulated OCO-2 soundings and everything needed to reproduce the amortized probabilistic retrieval described in the accompanying paper.

Version 3 adds the operational a priori of every reference sounding in February, March and July 2020 (oco2_apriori.tar.gz): the a priori state vector and its covariance, and the a priori XCO2 and its pressure-weighting function. These are the prior baselines added to the paper in its second revision. Every other archive is unchanged from version 2.

Version 2 adds, to the February 2020 delivery already in version 1: the reference-disjoint, within-reference, all-February and training-size split tables, each with the standardization constants estimated from its own training partition (oco2_splits.tar.gz); the trained checkpoints of all six models on each of the three splits reported in the paper (oco2_model_weights_v2.tar.gz); the two held-out months, March and July 2020, as the archives the scoring jobs consumed — spectra, ACOS profile covariances, covariates and the month split table (oco2_month_202003_full.tar.gz, oco2_month_202007_full.tar.gz); and the per-sounding predictive artifacts from which every table and figure in the paper is regenerated without a GPU (oco2_scoring_artifacts.tar.gz).

Version 1's archives are included unchanged. oco2_model_weights.tar.gz is the original submission's checkpoints, kept for provenance and superseded by the _v2 archive. The paper's numbers come from the reference-disjoint split table group_split_v1_cov.csv and the _v2 weights.

CONTENTS.md describes each archive and SHA256SUMS.txt covers all of them. The code that reads them is at https://github.com/acallesalda/oco2-amortized-uq, archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22667577; scripts/get_data.sh downloads, verifies and unpacks everything to the paths the code expects.

The simulation experiment, its a priori and the operational ACOS L2FP retrievals were produced at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology.

metadata.title: Data for Manuscript entitled "Extended global terrestrial evapotranspiration and gross primary production dataset from 1982 to near present"
metadata.description:
Overview

This repository contains the comprehensive calibration dataset, model source code, and global spatial-temporal simulation results for the PML-V2.2 (Penman-Monteith-Leuning) model. It provides all the necessary inputs, parameters, and scripts to reproduce the site-level model validations and evaluate global water-carbon cycle dynamics (Evapotranspiration and Gross Primary Production).

Reference

If you use this dataset or code in your research, please cite the following related paper:

Xu, Z., Zhang, Y., Kong, D., Ma, N., & Zhang, X. (2026). Extended global terrestrial evapotranspiration and gross primary production dataset from 1982 to near present. Earth System Science Data, 18(7), 5663–5695. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-5663-2026

Repository Structure & File Descriptions

For ease of downloading, the repository is organized into three main compressed archives (.zip).

1. calibration.zip (Site-level Calibration & Validation Data)

This folder contains the 8-day temporal resolution datasets used to calibrate and validate the model across global flux tower sites.

  • sites_qc_pml_v22.csv: Metadata for the flux sites used in the calibration process (e.g., site ID, coordinates, and final customized plant functional type IGBP1) after quality control.

  • input_qc_8d_pml_v22.csv: 8-day composite meteorological and remote sensing driving data (forcings) required to run the model.

  • input_output_qc_8d_pml_v22.csv: A comprehensive dataset containing the inputs, benchmark observations (ET_obs, GPP_obs), and calibrated PML-V2.2 model outputs.

  • parameters_IGBP1_pml_v22.csv: Optimized PML-V2.2 model parameters, grouped and calibrated based on the customized plant functional type (IGBP1).

  • site_metrics_cal_cv.csv: Site-level statistical performance metrics (e.g., NSE, KGE, Bias, RMSE, R) evaluated during the calibration and cross-validation phases.

2. code.zip (Model Source Code)

  • Contains the core algorithms (R and Rcpp/C++ implementations) for the PML-V2.2 model. It also includes the example scripts used to extract data, run site-level simulations, evaluate consistency, and generate the final figures presented in the manuscript.

3. figure.zip (Global Patterns & Trends)

This folder provides the underlying data for the manuscript's key global figures.

  • figure_9_10_PML_V2.2c_global_pattern_*.nc (6 NetCDF files): Global spatial patterns of Evapotranspiration (ET), Gross Primary Production (GPP), Water Use Efficiency (WUE), and ET component fractions (Ec_fraction, Ei_fraction, Es_fraction).

Note: Values in these NetCDF files are explicitly clamped to the plotting limits used in the manuscript figures for direct visualization consistency.

  • figure11_PML_V2.2c_global_mean.csv: Global mean annual time-series data for the core variables (ET, GPP, WUE, Ec, Es, Ei) used to evaluate long-term interannual trends.

Usage Notes & Support

  • Quick Start: To reproduce the workflows or utilize the data, please download and extract the three .zip files into a single working directory. The provided example R scripts in the code directory are pre-configured to read data seamlessly from the unzipped calibration and figure folders.

  • Recommendation: It is highly recommended to use our latest data updates to ensure high accuracy!

  • Contact: For any support or inquiries, please contact Zhenwu Xu at xuzhenwu@igsnrr.ac.cn.
